And it had been like that for months.

Every day was the same thing. She'd want something, she couldn't tell me what it was, and the whole house would fall apart. 

Breakfast. Getting dressed. Bathtime. Bedtime. It didn't matter. 

Any moment where she needed something and couldn't say it turned into a war.

I tried everything people told me to try. 

I made routines. I gave warnings before transitions. I got down on her level and spoke calmly. I did time-outs. I did time-ins. I read every parenting article about managing toddler behavior.

None of it worked. 

And the more I paid attention, the more I realized the tantrums weren't about discipline at all.

Because they always started the same way. 

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I could see it in her face right before the meltdown — she knew what she wanted to say, she just couldn't get it out. She was trapped. 

And the frustration had to go somewhere. So it came out through her body.

I knew that. Deep down I knew that. But I didn't know what to do about it.

So I tried working on her speech. I started narrating everything I did. I read to her every night. 

I bought flashcards and sat on the floor pointing at pictures saying "can you say dog?”

She'd stare at me. I'd wait. She'd stare. I'd try again. Nothing. And then she would start to cry. And then the crying would turn into a full meltdown. 

I would be sitting there on the floor with a stack of flashcards wondering how something that was supposed to help just made everything worse.

It kept happening. Every time I tried to practice with her it ended the same way. I'd put her on the spot, she'd freeze, the frustration would build, and she'd explode. 

The flashcards made her cry. Asking her to repeat words made her cry. Even pausing after I said something and waiting a few extra seconds to see if she'd try — stressed her out.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point. 

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician about the meltdowns. How many we were having. How physical they were getting. How nothing I tried was helping.

She asked about routine and sleep and discipline. She said it could be behavioral. She said some kids just have bigger emotions at this age. 

She told me to stay consistent and gave me a handout on managing toddler behavior.

I sat in the parking lot staring at the handout. It was the same advice I'd been following for months. 

“Stay calm. Give warnings. Be consistent. Redirect.”

I'd been doing all of it. And my daughter was still hitting me in the face at grocery stores.

That night after we put her to sleep I started googling. "Why won't my toddler stop melting down." "2 year old tantrums getting worse." "Toddler aggressive when frustrated."

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

The pediatrician closed her chart. She said we didn't need the behavioral evaluation anymore.

She just wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.

The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words.

Every page has a red start button and icons they can press to hear each word.

There are themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, the house, the park, getting dressed. 

It has all the words they actually need to communicate. 

And each page has its own game that my daughter would play over and over.

The book says a word, she finds the matching picture, she presses it, and then tries to say it.  

She was practicing without it feeling like practice.

And she had free access to all of this whenever she wanted.

Which is the part I didn't understand until I watched that video. 

My daughter needed to be in control. She needed to decide when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.

Because that’s when kids actually learn to talk. When they're the one driving it. Not when we're hovering with flashcards begging them to say a word.

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound. So beyond learning words she's starting to piece together how they're built.

It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

It's safety tested for little hands.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it. 

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying this is a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight because I was skeptical too.

But if your child is melting down every day and you've tried every behavioral strategy in the book and nothing is changing — it might not be a behavior problem. It might be a communication problem. 

And this book might be the thing that finally gives them the words they need so they don't have to scream for them anymore.

The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a sale right now.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom whose daughter went from 6 words and daily meltdowns to actually telling me what she needs. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

P.P.S. — I keep getting asked what age this is good for. My daughter started using it at 2 and she's still using it now. I know friends whose kids started as young as 12 months. The book has enough in it that it grows with them. Worth the money either way.

My son had 6 months left.

Every single thing I did with Maya, plus 20 hours a week of professional therapy on top.

Children don't build speech by hearing language. They build it by trying to say it.

Maya did that on her own.

bodyText:
There's one Bible verse that keeps me up at night as a mom.

"Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it." Proverbs 22:6.

Read that again.

When he is old, he will not depart from it.

That means what you put into them right now, during these little years, is what stays with them. The stories they hear. The songs they sing. The names they learn. The feelings they associate with God and Jesus and church and prayer.

All of that gets built now. Not later. Now.

But it also means something that most Christian parents don't want to think about.

The window closes.

You can't build a foundation after the house is already standing. You can't go back and plant seeds once the ground has already hardened. You can't undo years of nothing with a single conversation when they're fifteen and already questioning everything.

The foundation gets built while they're little. Or it doesn't get built at all.

And I think deep down, every Christian mom knows that.

We feel it every Sunday when we rush to get them dressed for church. We feel it every night when bedtime comes and we realize we didn't read them a single Bible story. We feel it when we see another mom's kid singing worship songs and our kid is on their third hour of screen time.

We know. We just don't know what to do about it.

I didn't.

I've been a Christian my whole life. Church every Sunday since I was a girl. Married a man who shares my faith. We pray before meals. We go to service. We say the right things.

But when it came to actually teaching my kids about Jesus at home, consistently, in a way that was real and daily and part of the fabric of their little lives?

I wasn't doing it.

And the worst part is I had every intention of doing it.

When my daughter was born, I told myself she would grow up different. She would know the stories I grew up hearing. She would know who Noah was and who David was and why the birth of Jesus matters. She would hear the songs. She would learn to pray. She would have the foundation I wished I'd had more of as a kid.

But then reality hit.

Toddlers don't sit still. Dinner is chaos. Bedtime is a negotiation. Baths turn into water fights. And by the time both kids are finally down, I'm so exhausted that the idea of pulling out a children's Bible and doing a devotional feels like climbing a mountain.

So I'd hand one of them my phone instead.

Just for a few minutes. Just so I could breathe.

And then a few minutes would become thirty. And then it was bedtime. And another day went by where my kids heard more from YouTube than they ever heard about God.

I never felt good about it. Not once.

But I kept telling myself there was still time. She's only two. She's only three. We'll start next month. I'll find the right devotional. I'll figure it out.

Except I never did.

And that verse kept echoing in the back of my mind.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

When he is old, he will not depart from it.

I wasn't training her in anything. I was hoping it would happen by osmosis. Like going to church on Sundays would be enough. Like being a Christian household automatically meant my kids would become Christians.

But that's not what the verse says.

It says train. That's an action word. That's something you do on purpose. That's something you build with intention, day after day, while they're still young enough to absorb it.

And I was letting those days slip by.

The moment it really hit me was last Thanksgiving.

We were at my sister's house. Her youngest had just turned three, same age as my daughter. Same church. Same family values. Same faith background.

About an hour after we arrived, her little girl came walking through the kitchen carrying this small colorful device I'd never seen before. She had it tucked under her arm like a favorite stuffed animal.

She sat down on the living room rug, turned a little dial on the front, pressed a button, and the thing started reading her a Bible story out loud.

She sat there and listened to the entire story of Noah. No fidgeting. No asking for help. No adult telling her to sit down and pay attention. She was just sitting there, cross-legged, completely absorbed.

When it finished, she turned the dial again and played another one.

Later that evening, while we were all cleaning up in the kitchen, she started singing Jesus Loves Me out of nowhere. Not the way kids mumble through a song they barely know. She knew every single word. She was singing it like it was her favorite song in the world.

Meanwhile, my daughter was in the other room on my phone. Watching the same cartoon she watches every single day.

I can't describe exactly what I felt standing in that kitchen, but it wasn't good.

It was guilt. And frustration. And something that almost felt like jealousy, which sounds awful to say about a three-year-old. But it wasn't jealousy toward my niece. It was anger at myself.

Because my sister's kid knew Bible stories by name. She could tell you about Noah and David and Goliath and baby Jesus.

My daughter, same age, same church, same Christian parents, couldn't tell you a single one.

And the worst part was I couldn't blame her. She didn't know those stories because I never taught them to her.

I just kept assuming faith would show up on its own.

That night, after all the kids were asleep, I asked my sister about it. I tried to sound casual but I think she could tell it was eating at me.

I asked her when she started doing Bible lessons with her daughter. How she found the time with three kids. What curriculum she used.

She laughed.

She said she didn't do any of that.

She told me she had the exact same problem I did. She wanted her kids growing up knowing Jesus but she could never find a way to make it consistent. The children's Bible lost her daughter's attention after one page. The Bible apps on the iPad led to the kid swiping to something else within minutes. Worship music during dinner just got talked over.

Then a mom at her church told her about something called FaithNest.

She said it was a screen-free Bible storyteller designed for little kids. No iPad. No YouTube. No Wi-Fi. The child just picks which Bible story they want, presses a button, and it reads the whole story to them page by page.

If they can't read yet, it reads for them. If they're starting to learn, they can follow along with the words as they hear them.

It comes with 11 Bible stories. Noah. David and Goliath. Jonah. The birth of Jesus. The Easter story. All told in a way that's gentle enough for a two-year-old to follow without getting overwhelmed.

And it comes with classic Christian songs that every family already knows. Jesus Loves Me. This Little Light of Mine. All the ones you grew up singing at church and Sunday school.

My sister said she bought it not expecting much. She figured it would end up in the toy bin within a week like everything else she'd tried.

But her daughter picked it up the first day. Figured out how to use it in minutes. And then she just kept going back to it.

Every day. Multiple times a day. Without being told. Without being sat down. Without a single lesson plan.

She just chose it on her own.

That's what hit me the hardest.

My sister didn't teach her daughter all those Bible stories. She didn't create a routine or carve out extra time or become some kind of homeschool Bible teacher.

She just put this thing in her daughter's hands and her daughter did the rest.

I ordered one from my sister's couch that same night.

It arrived about a week later. I didn't make a big deal about it. I just set it on the playroom floor next to her other toys and waited.

Within an hour, she picked it up.

By the end of the day, she had listened to three stories.

By the end of the week, she was carrying it around the house the same way my niece was at Thanksgiving.

The first time I heard her singing Jesus Loves Me by herself, I was standing at the kitchen sink and I literally froze.

She was in the bathtub. Singing it like it was the most natural thing in the world. Nobody played it for her. Nobody told her to sing it. She just had it in her head because she'd been pressing that button and listening to it over and over on her own terms.

That was the moment I finally understood what Proverbs 22:6 actually means.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

It doesn't say lecture them. It doesn't say force them. It doesn't say sit them down every night for a structured Bible lesson and make sure they pay attention.

It says train. And training can look like giving them something they reach for on their own. Something that puts faith in their hands in a way that feels like play instead of instruction. Something they choose.

That's what FaithNest did for my daughter. And for me.

We've had it for four months now. She uses it almost every day. She has favorite stories she replays over and over. She knows the characters by name. She sings the songs at random. In the car. At the dinner table. Before bed. At grandma's house.

And it started real conversations between us that I never expected. She'll listen to a story and then come find me and ask questions. "Mama, why did God send the big water?" "Mama, what happened to the giant?"

Those little conversations have become the closest thing we have to Bible time. And they happen naturally because she's already engaged before I ever say a word.

I told three friends at church about it. Two of them bought one that same week. One of them told her mom, who is a grandmother of five, and she bought four as Christmas gifts.

That's what keeps happening. Parents find it. Their kids love it. And then they buy more for every kid in their life.

I keep thinking about that verse.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

The verse doesn't say think about it. It doesn't say plan to do it. It doesn't say feel guilty about not doing it and tell yourself you'll start next week.

It says do it. Now. While they're little. While the ground is still soft. While they're still forming their picture of the world and deciding what feels familiar, comforting, and true.

Because once that window closes, you don't get to reopen it.

Last I checked, FaithNest was running 50% off with free shipping. I don't know how long that lasts. I do know they've sold out multiple times this year because my sister tried to buy another one for a baby shower gift and had to wait for a restock.

They also have a 30-day guarantee. If your child doesn't love it, you get your money back. I didn't even know about that until after I'd already decided we were keeping ours forever.

I don't know what your house looks like right now.

Maybe you're already doing an amazing job with Bible time and your kids are way ahead of where mine were.

But if you're anything like I was, standing in your sister's kitchen watching her three-year-old sing hymns while your kid watches cartoons on your phone, just know this.

The gap isn't as big as it feels. One small thing closed it for us in a week.

And that verse? It stopped keeping me up at night. Because I finally started living it.

bodyText:
"You're being paranoid. Boys just talk later." That's what my husband told me every time I brought up our son's speech.

Then his 2 year checkup came and he only had 6 words.

"This is significantly behind for his age."

That's what the pediatrician told me at the appointment. 

After 8 months of everyone in my life telling me the opposite.

She said we needed to get him evaluated by a speech pathologist as soon as possible. 

She said the earlier we started, the better his chances of catching up. 

She wrote me the referral and told me not to wait.

I sat in the parking lot for 20 minutes crying. Not because I was scared. Because I was relieved. 

Someone had finally believed me.

I drove home and told my husband what she said.
 
He didn't take it the way I hoped he would.
 
He said "she's just being cautious. Pediatricians have to say things like that so they don't get sued."
 
I didn't argue with him. I was done arguing about it.
 
I sat on the couch after he went to bed and cried on the phone to my sister for an hour.
 
She said "you don't need him to agree with you to do something about it. Just do it."
 
So the next morning I called for the referral. The waitlist for a private speech pathologist near me was 6 months.

My husband seemed relieved when I told him. 

He said "well, that gives him plenty of time to catch up on his own."

I didn't respond. I didn't have anything left to say.

But I knew one thing — I wasn't going to sit around for 6 months hoping he was right. 
 
So I started doing my own research.
 
I joined 4 different Facebook groups for late talker parents. I followed every speech pathologist I could find on Instagram. I read Reddit threads until 1am looking for what actually worked for kids like mine.
 
Two days in, I saw a post that stopped me.
 
A mom whose son had been in the exact same spot as mine — 2 years old with barely any words — found something that worked.
 
It was a sound book. Not a normal one — it was designed by speech pathologists specifically for how toddlers actually build language.
 
She said her son got obsessed with it right away. Every page had pictures he could press to hear the word out loud. 

There was also a game mode — the book would say a word, and he had to find the picture that matched.
 
He'd sit with it for 30 minutes at a time saying the words along with the book. It was practice for him, but without any pressure.
 
And once the words felt easier to say, he started using them everywhere.
 
I sat there staring at the post for a while.
 
Because I'd read stories like this before. I'd already spent almost $300 trying every product that promised the same thing. Lovevery flashcards. Speech Blubs. Ms. Rachel's merch. A pile of VTech and Melissa & Doug toys that my son barely touched.
 
Every kid is different, I told myself. What worked for her son might not work for mine.
 
But it was $50 and I was desperate so I ordered it.
 
The box came 3 days later. My husband saw it on the counter and picked it up.
 
"Fifty bucks for a book that talks?"
 
I told him yes. He shrugged and put it back down.
 
The first week I didn't see much. He held it, pressed some buttons, wandered off. I remember thinking great, another $50 down the drain. My husband didn't even bring it up.
 
But by week two, he'd started sitting with it every morning after breakfast. On his own. 

I didn't put it in front of him. He'd get up, pull it off the shelf, and sit on the rug flipping pages.
 
The game mode was what really got him. The book would call out a word and he had to find the picture that matched. He was thrilled every time he got it right. He'd play it over and over.
 
By week three I heard him. He was mumbling the words back to the book while he played. Not to me. To the book. But he was saying them.
 
By week four he was making sounds along with the book. Not real words yet. But attempts. Effort.
 
Something was happening.
 
My husband noticed too. He didn't say anything about it. But he stopped rolling his eyes when I put the book on the floor.
 
Then one Saturday morning, everything changed.
 
My husband was in the kitchen making coffee. Our son was on the rug in the living room with the book. I was folding laundry.
 
My son stood up. Walked into the kitchen. Tugged on my husband's pant leg, and said "dada."
 
Clear as day.
 
My husband turned around. Looked at me. Looked at our son. Looked back at me.
 
And he broke.
 
Not cried. Broke. He picked up our son and buried his face in his hair and stood there in the middle of the kitchen sobbing.
 
I put down the laundry and walked over. 

My husband looked at me over our son's shoulder and said "I'm so sorry."
 
I didn't say anything. I just put my hand on his back.
 
That was the last time my husband ever dismissed anything I said about our kid.
 
Two weeks later our son said his cousin's name for the first time. 

Three weeks after that he asked for milk instead of screaming at the fridge.
 
After that he wouldn't stop. He was trying new words every single day. Some clear, some garbled, some just attempts. But he was doing it. He was talking.
 
At his 2.5 year checkup the pediatrician spent 10 minutes just watching him tell her about the trucks on the street outside her window.
 
He'd gone from 6 words to over 50.
 
She wrote down the name of the sound book, and said "keep doing whatever you're doing."
 
My husband was in the room this time.
 
He drove us home and told his mother on speaker phone what the pediatrician had said. 

His mother — the same one who told me boys just talk later — got quiet for a second and then said "Rachel, I owe you an apology."
 
I heard her. But I couldn't stop listening to my son. 

He was in the back seat calling out every vehicle we passed. Big truck. Red car. School bus. 

He was just narrating the world to himself now.
 
The sound book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words in it.
 
Every page has a red start button and pictures he could press to hear each word.
 
There were themed pages for the zoo, the doctor's office, construction, the solar system, feelings, opposites — 23 themed worlds in total.
 
And each page had its own little game he'd play over and over.
 
My son had free access to any of them, whenever he wanted, just by pressing a picture.
 
That's the part I didn't realize was so important.
 
He was in control. He decided when to press it, which words to hear, and how many times to hear it.
 
That's when learning actually sticks. When the kid is the one driving it.
 
There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches him each letter's sound. 

So beyond learning words, he was starting to piece together how they were built.
 
It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.
 
It's safety tested for little hands.
 
And the pages are thick and tear-proof so he can't rip them no matter how rough he plays with it.
 
And unlike an iPad, when he's done with it he's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.
 
It's the only thing that finally worked.
 
I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight. I was skeptical just like you.
 
But I am saying if you're where I was — worried about your kid's speech and being told by everyone in your life to relax — trust your gut. Get the book.
 
I found out yesterday they've been selling out constantly. If it's out of stock when you look, sign up for the restock alert. It usually comes back within a few days.
 
The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a back to school sale right now.
 
P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom who spent 8 months being told she was overreacting and turned out to be right. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that made all the other stuff we were doing actually stick.
 
P.P.S. — Getting so many DMs asking what the book is called. It's the KiddoSpark 500 Words Sound Book. The link is at the bottom of the post. They just restocked but they've been going fast.
 
P.P.P.S. — My husband asked me to add this. If you're a dad reading this and your wife has been telling you something is off with your kid — please just listen to her. I almost cost my son a year of progress by not listening to mine.

bodyText:
My daughter hit me in the face at the grocery store. In front of everyone.

She wanted something off the shelf but she couldn't tell me what it was. And I kept grabbing the wrong thing. 

So she hit me.

I put her in the cart and walked out without buying anything. 

I just sat in the car and cried.

My daughter was 2 years old, and she only had 6 words. 

And it had been like that for months.

Every day was the same thing. She'd want something, she couldn't tell me what it was, and the whole house would fall apart. 

Breakfast. Getting dressed. Bathtime. Bedtime. It didn't matter. 

Any moment where she needed something and couldn't say it turned into a war.

I tried everything people told me to try. 

I made routines. I gave warnings before transitions. I got down on her level and spoke calmly. I did time-outs. I did time-ins. I read every parenting article about managing toddler behavior.

None of it worked. 

And the more I paid attention, the more I realized the tantrums weren't about discipline at all.

Because they always started the same way. 

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I could see it in her face right before the meltdown — she knew what she wanted to say, she just couldn't get it out. She was trapped. 

And the frustration had to go somewhere. So it came out through her body.

I knew that. Deep down I knew that. But I didn't know what to do about it.

So I tried working on her speech. I started narrating everything I did. I read to her every night. 

I bought flashcards and sat on the floor pointing at pictures saying "can you say dog?”

She'd stare at me. I'd wait. She'd stare. I'd try again. Nothing. And then she would start to cry. And then the crying would turn into a full meltdown. 

I would be sitting there on the floor with a stack of flashcards wondering how something that was supposed to help just made everything worse.

It kept happening. Every time I tried to practice with her it ended the same way. I'd put her on the spot, she'd freeze, the frustration would build, and she'd explode. 

The flashcards made her cry. Asking her to repeat words made her cry. Even pausing after I said something and waiting a few extra seconds to see if she'd try — stressed her out.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point. 

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician about the meltdowns. How many we were having. How physical they were getting. How nothing I tried was helping.

She asked about routine and sleep and discipline. She said it could be behavioral. She said some kids just have bigger emotions at this age. 

She told me to stay consistent and gave me a handout on managing toddler behavior.

I sat in the parking lot staring at the handout. It was the same advice I'd been following for months. 

“Stay calm. Give warnings. Be consistent. Redirect.”

I'd been doing all of it. And my daughter was still hitting me in the face at grocery stores.

That night after we put her to sleep I started googling. "Why won't my toddler stop melting down." "2 year old tantrums getting worse." "Toddler aggressive when frustrated."

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

bodyText:
There's one Bible verse that keeps me up at night as a mom.

"Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it." Proverbs 22:6.

Read that again.

When he is old, he will not depart from it.

That means what you put into them right now, during these little years, is what stays with them. The stories they hear. The songs they sing. The names they learn. The feelings they associate with God and Jesus and church and prayer.

All of that gets built now. Not later. Now.

But it also means something that most Christian parents don't want to think about.

The window closes.

You can't build a foundation after the house is already standing. You can't go back and plant seeds once the ground has already hardened. You can't undo years of nothing with a single conversation when they're fifteen and already questioning everything.

The foundation gets built while they're little. Or it doesn't get built at all.

And I think deep down, every Christian mom knows that.

We feel it every Sunday when we rush to get them dressed for church. We feel it every night when bedtime comes and we realize we didn't read them a single Bible story. We feel it when we see another mom's kid singing worship songs and our kid is on their third hour of screen time.

We know. We just don't know what to do about it.

I didn't.

I've been a Christian my whole life. Church every Sunday since I was a girl. Married a man who shares my faith. We pray before meals. We go to service. We say the right things.

But when it came to actually teaching my kids about Jesus at home, consistently, in a way that was real and daily and part of the fabric of their little lives?

I wasn't doing it.

And the worst part is I had every intention of doing it.

When my daughter was born, I told myself she would grow up different. She would know the stories I grew up hearing. She would know who Noah was and who David was and why the birth of Jesus matters. She would hear the songs. She would learn to pray. She would have the foundation I wished I'd had more of as a kid.

But then reality hit.

Toddlers don't sit still. Dinner is chaos. Bedtime is a negotiation. Baths turn into water fights. And by the time both kids are finally down, I'm so exhausted that the idea of pulling out a children's Bible and doing a devotional feels like climbing a mountain.

So I'd hand one of them my phone instead.

Just for a few minutes. Just so I could breathe.

And then a few minutes would become thirty. And then it was bedtime. And another day went by where my kids heard more from YouTube than they ever heard about God.

I never felt good about it. Not once.

But I kept telling myself there was still time. She's only two. She's only three. We'll start next month. I'll find the right devotional. I'll figure it out.

Except I never did.

And that verse kept echoing in the back of my mind.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

When he is old, he will not depart from it.

I wasn't training her in anything. I was hoping it would happen by osmosis. Like going to church on Sundays would be enough. Like being a Christian household automatically meant my kids would become Christians.

But that's not what the verse says.

It says train. That's an action word. That's something you do on purpose. That's something you build with intention, day after day, while they're still young enough to absorb it.

And I was letting those days slip by.

The moment it really hit me was last Thanksgiving.

We were at my sister's house. Her youngest had just turned three, same age as my daughter. Same church. Same family values. Same faith background.

About an hour after we arrived, her little girl came walking through the kitchen carrying this small colorful device I'd never seen before. She had it tucked under her arm like a favorite stuffed animal.

She sat down on the living room rug, turned a little dial on the front, pressed a button, and the thing started reading her a Bible story out loud.

She sat there and listened to the entire story of Noah. No fidgeting. No asking for help. No adult telling her to sit down and pay attention. She was just sitting there, cross-legged, completely absorbed.

When it finished, she turned the dial again and played another one.

Later that evening, while we were all cleaning up in the kitchen, she started singing Jesus Loves Me out of nowhere. Not the way kids mumble through a song they barely know. She knew every single word. She was singing it like it was her favorite song in the world.

Meanwhile, my daughter was in the other room on my phone. Watching the same cartoon she watches every single day.

I can't describe exactly what I felt standing in that kitchen, but it wasn't good.

It was guilt. And frustration. And something that almost felt like jealousy, which sounds awful to say about a three-year-old. But it wasn't jealousy toward my niece. It was anger at myself.

Because my sister's kid knew Bible stories by name. She could tell you about Noah and David and Goliath and baby Jesus.

My daughter, same age, same church, same Christian parents, couldn't tell you a single one.

And the worst part was I couldn't blame her. She didn't know those stories because I never taught them to her.

I just kept assuming faith would show up on its own.

That night, after all the kids were asleep, I asked my sister about it. I tried to sound casual but I think she could tell it was eating at me.

I asked her when she started doing Bible lessons with her daughter. How she found the time with three kids. What curriculum she used.

She laughed.

She said she didn't do any of that.

She told me she had the exact same problem I did. She wanted her kids growing up knowing Jesus but she could never find a way to make it consistent. The children's Bible lost her daughter's attention after one page. The Bible apps on the iPad led to the kid swiping to something else within minutes. Worship music during dinner just got talked over.

Then a mom at her church told her about something called FaithNest.

She said it was a screen-free Bible storyteller designed for little kids. No iPad. No YouTube. No Wi-Fi. The child just picks which Bible story they want, presses a button, and it reads the whole story to them page by page.

If they can't read yet, it reads for them. If they're starting to learn, they can follow along with the words as they hear them.

It comes with 11 Bible stories. Noah. David and Goliath. Jonah. The birth of Jesus. The Easter story. All told in a way that's gentle enough for a two-year-old to follow without getting overwhelmed.

And it comes with classic Christian songs that every family already knows. Jesus Loves Me. This Little Light of Mine. All the ones you grew up singing at church and Sunday school.

My sister said she bought it not expecting much. She figured it would end up in the toy bin within a week like everything else she'd tried.

But her daughter picked it up the first day. Figured out how to use it in minutes. And then she just kept going back to it.

Every day. Multiple times a day. Without being told. Without being sat down. Without a single lesson plan.

She just chose it on her own.

That's what hit me the hardest.

My sister didn't teach her daughter all those Bible stories. She didn't create a routine or carve out extra time or become some kind of homeschool Bible teacher.

She just put this thing in her daughter's hands and her daughter did the rest.

I ordered one from my sister's couch that same night.

It arrived about a week later. I didn't make a big deal about it. I just set it on the playroom floor next to her other toys and waited.

Within an hour, she picked it up.

By the end of the day, she had listened to three stories.

By the end of the week, she was carrying it around the house the same way my niece was at Thanksgiving.

The first time I heard her singing Jesus Loves Me by herself, I was standing at the kitchen sink and I literally froze.

She was in the bathtub. Singing it like it was the most natural thing in the world. Nobody played it for her. Nobody told her to sing it. She just had it in her head because she'd been pressing that button and listening to it over and over on her own terms.

That was the moment I finally understood what Proverbs 22:6 actually means.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

It doesn't say lecture them. It doesn't say force them. It doesn't say sit them down every night for a structured Bible lesson and make sure they pay attention.

It says train. And training can look like giving them something they reach for on their own. Something that puts faith in their hands in a way that feels like play instead of instruction. Something they choose.

That's what FaithNest did for my daughter. And for me.

We've had it for four months now. She uses it almost every day. She has favorite stories she replays over and over. She knows the characters by name. She sings the songs at random. In the car. At the dinner table. Before bed. At grandma's house.

And it started real conversations between us that I never expected. She'll listen to a story and then come find me and ask questions. "Mama, why did God send the big water?" "Mama, what happened to the giant?"

Those little conversations have become the closest thing we have to Bible time. And they happen naturally because she's already engaged before I ever say a word.

I told three friends at church about it. Two of them bought one that same week. One of them told her mom, who is a grandmother of five, and she bought four as Christmas gifts.

That's what keeps happening. Parents find it. Their kids love it. And then they buy more for every kid in their life.

I keep thinking about that verse.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

The verse doesn't say think about it. It doesn't say plan to do it. It doesn't say feel guilty about not doing it and tell yourself you'll start next week.

It says do it. Now. While they're little. While the ground is still soft. While they're still forming their picture of the world and deciding what feels familiar, comforting, and true.

Because once that window closes, you don't get to reopen it.

Last I checked, FaithNest was running 50% off with free shipping. I don't know how long that lasts. I do know they've sold out multiple times this year because my sister tried to buy another one for a baby shower gift and had to wait for a restock.

They also have a 30-day guarantee. If your child doesn't love it, you get your money back. I didn't even know about that until after I'd already decided we were keeping ours forever.

I don't know what your house looks like right now.

Maybe you're already doing an amazing job with Bible time and your kids are way ahead of where mine were.

But if you're anything like I was, standing in your sister's kitchen watching her three-year-old sing hymns while your kid watches cartoons on your phone, just know this.

The gap isn't as big as it feels. One small thing closed it for us in a week.

And that verse? It stopped keeping me up at night. Because I finally started living it.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

The pediatrician closed her chart. She said we didn't need the behavioral evaluation anymore.

She just wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.

The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words.

Every page has a red start button and icons they can press to hear each word.

There are themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, the house, the park, getting dressed. 

It has all the words they actually need to communicate. 

And each page has its own game that my daughter would play over and over.

The book says a word, she finds the matching picture, she presses it, and then tries to say it.  

She was practicing without it feeling like practice.

And she had free access to all of this whenever she wanted.

Which is the part I didn't understand until I watched that video. 

My daughter needed to be in control. She needed to decide when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.

Because that’s when kids actually learn to talk. When they're the one driving it. Not when we're hovering with flashcards begging them to say a word.

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound. So beyond learning words she's starting to piece together how they're built.

It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

It's safety tested for little hands.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it. 

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying this is a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight because I was skeptical too.

But if your child is melting down every day and you've tried every behavioral strategy in the book and nothing is changing — it might not be a behavior problem. It might be a communication problem. 

And this book might be the thing that finally gives them the words they need so they don't have to scream for them anymore.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom whose daughter went from 6 words and daily meltdowns to actually telling me what she needs. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

P.P.S. — I keep getting asked what age this is good for. My daughter started using it at 2 and she's still using it now. I know friends whose kids started as young as 12 months. The book has enough in it that it grows with them. Worth the money either way.

bodyText:
There's one Bible verse that keeps me up at night as a mom.

"Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it." Proverbs 22:6.

Read that again.

When he is old, he will not depart from it.

That means what you put into them right now, during these little years, is what stays with them. The stories they hear. The songs they sing. The names they learn. The feelings they associate with God and Jesus and church and prayer.

All of that gets built now. Not later. Now.

But it also means something that most Christian parents don't want to think about.

The window closes.

You can't build a foundation after the house is already standing. You can't go back and plant seeds once the ground has already hardened. You can't undo years of nothing with a single conversation when they're fifteen and already questioning everything.

The foundation gets built while they're little. Or it doesn't get built at all.

And I think deep down, every Christian mom knows that.

We feel it every Sunday when we rush to get them dressed for church. We feel it every night when bedtime comes and we realize we didn't read them a single Bible story. We feel it when we see another mom's kid singing worship songs and our kid is on their third hour of screen time.

We know. We just don't know what to do about it.

I didn't.

I've been a Christian my whole life. Church every Sunday since I was a girl. Married a man who shares my faith. We pray before meals. We go to service. We say the right things.

But when it came to actually teaching my kids about Jesus at home, consistently, in a way that was real and daily and part of the fabric of their little lives?

I wasn't doing it.

And the worst part is I had every intention of doing it.

When my daughter was born, I told myself she would grow up different. She would know the stories I grew up hearing. She would know who Noah was and who David was and why the birth of Jesus matters. She would hear the songs. She would learn to pray. She would have the foundation I wished I'd had more of as a kid.

But then reality hit.

Toddlers don't sit still. Dinner is chaos. Bedtime is a negotiation. Baths turn into water fights. And by the time both kids are finally down, I'm so exhausted that the idea of pulling out a children's Bible and doing a devotional feels like climbing a mountain.

So I'd hand one of them my phone instead.

Just for a few minutes. Just so I could breathe.

And then a few minutes would become thirty. And then it was bedtime. And another day went by where my kids heard more from YouTube than they ever heard about God.

I never felt good about it. Not once.

But I kept telling myself there was still time. She's only two. She's only three. We'll start next month. I'll find the right devotional. I'll figure it out.

Except I never did.

And that verse kept echoing in the back of my mind.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

When he is old, he will not depart from it.

I wasn't training her in anything. I was hoping it would happen by osmosis. Like going to church on Sundays would be enough. Like being a Christian household automatically meant my kids would become Christians.

But that's not what the verse says.

It says train. That's an action word. That's something you do on purpose. That's something you build with intention, day after day, while they're still young enough to absorb it.

And I was letting those days slip by.

The moment it really hit me was last Thanksgiving.

We were at my sister's house. Her youngest had just turned three, same age as my daughter. Same church. Same family values. Same faith background.

About an hour after we arrived, her little girl came walking through the kitchen carrying this small colorful device I'd never seen before. She had it tucked under her arm like a favorite stuffed animal.

She sat down on the living room rug, turned a little dial on the front, pressed a button, and the thing started reading her a Bible story out loud.

She sat there and listened to the entire story of Noah. No fidgeting. No asking for help. No adult telling her to sit down and pay attention. She was just sitting there, cross-legged, completely absorbed.

When it finished, she turned the dial again and played another one.

Later that evening, while we were all cleaning up in the kitchen, she started singing Jesus Loves Me out of nowhere. Not the way kids mumble through a song they barely know. She knew every single word. She was singing it like it was her favorite song in the world.

Meanwhile, my daughter was in the other room on my phone. Watching the same cartoon she watches every single day.

I can't describe exactly what I felt standing in that kitchen, but it wasn't good.

It was guilt. And frustration. And something that almost felt like jealousy, which sounds awful to say about a three-year-old. But it wasn't jealousy toward my niece. It was anger at myself.

Because my sister's kid knew Bible stories by name. She could tell you about Noah and David and Goliath and baby Jesus.

My daughter, same age, same church, same Christian parents, couldn't tell you a single one.

And the worst part was I couldn't blame her. She didn't know those stories because I never taught them to her.

I just kept assuming faith would show up on its own.

That night, after all the kids were asleep, I asked my sister about it. I tried to sound casual but I think she could tell it was eating at me.

I asked her when she started doing Bible lessons with her daughter. How she found the time with three kids. What curriculum she used.

She laughed.

She said she didn't do any of that.

She told me she had the exact same problem I did. She wanted her kids growing up knowing Jesus but she could never find a way to make it consistent. The children's Bible lost her daughter's attention after one page. The Bible apps on the iPad led to the kid swiping to something else within minutes. Worship music during dinner just got talked over.

Then a mom at her church told her about something called FaithNest.

She said it was a screen-free Bible storyteller designed for little kids. No iPad. No YouTube. No Wi-Fi. The child just picks which Bible story they want, presses a button, and it reads the whole story to them page by page.

If they can't read yet, it reads for them. If they're starting to learn, they can follow along with the words as they hear them.

It comes with 11 Bible stories. Noah. David and Goliath. Jonah. The birth of Jesus. The Easter story. All told in a way that's gentle enough for a two-year-old to follow without getting overwhelmed.

And it comes with classic Christian songs that every family already knows. Jesus Loves Me. This Little Light of Mine. All the ones you grew up singing at church and Sunday school.

My sister said she bought it not expecting much. She figured it would end up in the toy bin within a week like everything else she'd tried.

But her daughter picked it up the first day. Figured out how to use it in minutes. And then she just kept going back to it.

Every day. Multiple times a day. Without being told. Without being sat down. Without a single lesson plan.

She just chose it on her own.

That's what hit me the hardest.

My sister didn't teach her daughter all those Bible stories. She didn't create a routine or carve out extra time or become some kind of homeschool Bible teacher.

She just put this thing in her daughter's hands and her daughter did the rest.

I ordered one from my sister's couch that same night.

It arrived about a week later. I didn't make a big deal about it. I just set it on the playroom floor next to her other toys and waited.

Within an hour, she picked it up.

By the end of the day, she had listened to three stories.

By the end of the week, she was carrying it around the house the same way my niece was at Thanksgiving.

The first time I heard her singing Jesus Loves Me by herself, I was standing at the kitchen sink and I literally froze.

She was in the bathtub. Singing it like it was the most natural thing in the world. Nobody played it for her. Nobody told her to sing it. She just had it in her head because she'd been pressing that button and listening to it over and over on her own terms.

That was the moment I finally understood what Proverbs 22:6 actually means.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

It doesn't say lecture them. It doesn't say force them. It doesn't say sit them down every night for a structured Bible lesson and make sure they pay attention.

It says train. And training can look like giving them something they reach for on their own. Something that puts faith in their hands in a way that feels like play instead of instruction. Something they choose.

That's what FaithNest did for my daughter. And for me.

We've had it for four months now. She uses it almost every day. She has favorite stories she replays over and over. She knows the characters by name. She sings the songs at random. In the car. At the dinner table. Before bed. At grandma's house.

And it started real conversations between us that I never expected. She'll listen to a story and then come find me and ask questions. "Mama, why did God send the big water?" "Mama, what happened to the giant?"

Those little conversations have become the closest thing we have to Bible time. And they happen naturally because she's already engaged before I ever say a word.

I told three friends at church about it. Two of them bought one that same week. One of them told her mom, who is a grandmother of five, and she bought four as Christmas gifts.

That's what keeps happening. Parents find it. Their kids love it. And then they buy more for every kid in their life.

I keep thinking about that verse.

Train up a child in the way he should go.

The verse doesn't say think about it. It doesn't say plan to do it. It doesn't say feel guilty about not doing it and tell yourself you'll start next week.

It says do it. Now. While they're little. While the ground is still soft. While they're still forming their picture of the world and deciding what feels familiar, comforting, and true.

Because once that window closes, you don't get to reopen it.

Last I checked, FaithNest was running 50% off with free shipping. I don't know how long that lasts. I do know they've sold out multiple times this year because my sister tried to buy another one for a baby shower gift and had to wait for a restock.

They also have a 30-day guarantee. If your child doesn't love it, you get your money back. I didn't even know about that until after I'd already decided we were keeping ours forever.

I don't know what your house looks like right now.

Maybe you're already doing an amazing job with Bible time and your kids are way ahead of where mine were.

But if you're anything like I was, standing in your sister's kitchen watching her three-year-old sing hymns while your kid watches cartoons on your phone, just know this.

The gap isn't as big as it feels. One small thing closed it for us in a week.

And that verse? It stopped keeping me up at night. Because I finally started living it.

bodyText:
My daughter hit me in the face at the grocery store. In front of everyone.

She wanted something off the shelf but she couldn't tell me what it was. And I kept grabbing the wrong thing. 

So she hit me.

I put her in the cart and walked out without buying anything. 

I just sat in the car and cried.

My daughter was 2 years old, and she only had 6 words. 

And it had been like that for months.

Every day was the same thing. She'd want something, she couldn't tell me what it was, and the whole house would fall apart. 

Breakfast. Getting dressed. Bathtime. Bedtime. It didn't matter. 

Any moment where she needed something and couldn't say it turned into a war.

I tried everything people told me to try. 

I made routines. I gave warnings before transitions. I got down on her level and spoke calmly. I did time-outs. I did time-ins. I read every parenting article about managing toddler behavior.

None of it worked. 

And the more I paid attention, the more I realized the tantrums weren't about discipline at all.

Because they always started the same way. 

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I could see it in her face right before the meltdown — she knew what she wanted to say, she just couldn't get it out. She was trapped. 

And the frustration had to go somewhere. So it came out through her body.

I knew that. Deep down I knew that. But I didn't know what to do about it.

So I tried working on her speech. I started narrating everything I did. I read to her every night. 

I bought flashcards and sat on the floor pointing at pictures saying "can you say dog?”

She'd stare at me. I'd wait. She'd stare. I'd try again. Nothing. And then she would start to cry. And then the crying would turn into a full meltdown. 

I would be sitting there on the floor with a stack of flashcards wondering how something that was supposed to help just made everything worse.

It kept happening. Every time I tried to practice with her it ended the same way. I'd put her on the spot, she'd freeze, the frustration would build, and she'd explode. 

The flashcards made her cry. Asking her to repeat words made her cry. Even pausing after I said something and waiting a few extra seconds to see if she'd try — stressed her out.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point. 

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician about the meltdowns. How many we were having. How physical they were getting. How nothing I tried was helping.

She asked about routine and sleep and discipline. She said it could be behavioral. She said some kids just have bigger emotions at this age. 

She told me to stay consistent and gave me a handout on managing toddler behavior.

I sat in the parking lot staring at the handout. It was the same advice I'd been following for months. 

“Stay calm. Give warnings. Be consistent. Redirect.”

I'd been doing all of it. And my daughter was still hitting me in the face at grocery stores.

That night after we put her to sleep I started googling. "Why won't my toddler stop melting down." "2 year old tantrums getting worse." "Toddler aggressive when frustrated."

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

The pediatrician closed her chart. She said we didn't need the behavioral evaluation anymore.

She just wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.

The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words.

Every page has a red start button and icons they can press to hear each word.

There are themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, the house, the park, getting dressed. 

It has all the words they actually need to communicate. 

And each page has its own game that my daughter would play over and over.

The book says a word, she finds the matching picture, she presses it, and then tries to say it.  

She was practicing without it feeling like practice.

And she had free access to all of this whenever she wanted.

Which is the part I didn't understand until I watched that video. 

My daughter needed to be in control. She needed to decide when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.

Because that’s when kids actually learn to talk. When they're the one driving it. Not when we're hovering with flashcards begging them to say a word.

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound. So beyond learning words she's starting to piece together how they're built.

It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

It's safety tested for little hands.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it. 

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying this is a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight because I was skeptical too.

But if your child is melting down every day and you've tried every behavioral strategy in the book and nothing is changing — it might not be a behavior problem. It might be a communication problem. 

And this book might be the thing that finally gives them the words they need so they don't have to scream for them anymore.

I found out yesterday they've been selling out constantly. If it's out of stock when you look, sign up for the restock alert. It usually comes back within a few days.

The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a sale right now.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom whose daughter went from 6 words and daily meltdowns to actually telling me what she needs. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

P.P.S. — I keep getting asked what age this is good for. My daughter started using it at 2 and she's still using it now. I know friends whose kids started as young as 12 months. The book has enough in it that it grows with them. Worth the money either way.
