bodyText:
I’ve owned Dachshunds for 25 years before I realized the advice I’d been giving people for decades was also completely failing my own daughter.

I’d always told people the same things, be patient, be consistent, don’t let them get away with too much, and remember that Dachshunds are stubborn. I believed every word of it because I’d raised 5 of them myself.

Then 1 of my daughters called me 6 months after I gave her a Dachshund puppy and asked if I would take him back.

My name is Ruth. I live in Omaha, Nebraska, and Dachshunds have been part of my life since I was newly married. I’ve raised 5, buried 3 and probably bored hundreds of people talking about them.

I knew about their backs, their barking, their attitude, their obsession with blankets and the way they somehow hear a cheese wrapper from 3 rooms away while being completely deaf when you call their name. 

So when both my adult daughters wanted Dachshunds, I thought I was the perfect person to help.

I found a good litter, same mother, same father. 

Emily took Felix, a male black and tan miniature smooth hair, and Jessica took Hazel, his sister, they looked the same, and were absolutely adorable.

Emily lived with her husband Mark in a townhouse in Papillion. They both worked full-time, had no children yet and had been talking about getting a dog for over a year. Jessica lived across town with her girlfriend in a small house with a yard.

Christmas week I gave them the puppies with matching bows and beds. I felt like a superhero, on top of the world.

For the first few weeks, I thought I’d been proven right. Emily called constantly saying Felix was brilliant, already learning his name, following them everywhere, sleeping under the blankets and had Mark completely wrapped around his little paw.

Jessica said the same about Hazel. Both girls thought they had the best puppy in the litter.

Then the little things started.

Emily mentioned Felix had begun ignoring them when something more interesting was happening. Then there were a few potty accidents after they thought he was toilet trained, barking at the front window, refusing to go outside in the rain and a habit of following Emily from room to room.

Nothing sounded serious, so I gave her the same advice I had given people for years. Be consistent, don’t repeat yourself, reward the good behavior and remember that Dachshunds can be stubborn.

Then the little things stopped being little.

Felix started barking every time somebody walked past the townhouse. The mail carrier barking became a daily problem, then dogs outside, car doors closing and people talking near the front window.

The rain became another battle. If the weather was bad, Felix would stand at the back door, look outside, look at Emily and walk away, then 20 minutes later she’d find a puddle on the hallway runner.

They cleaned it, then replaced it, then replaced it again. Eventually Emily bought a washable mat because she was tired of fighting over the rug.

Leaving the house started changing too.

Felix had always followed her everywhere, which she thought was adorable at first. Then he started whining when she picked up her handbag, pacing when she put her shoes on and howling after the front door closed.

Their neighbor mentioned it once, then again, then came the first noise complaint.

Emily started rushing home from errands. Mark started getting frustrated. Then they got the 2nd complaint.

When I asked how things were going, Emily would say, “Fine,” but as a mother, you know the difference between fine and “fine”.

So she did what responsible dog owners are supposed to do. She paid for training.

The first thing was a 6-week PetSmart obedience course for $119. Felix was excellent inside the training room, sit, stay, down, come, he looked like a little genius.

Then they got home and it was like somebody had wiped the lesson from his memory.

The trainer said they needed to be more consistent, so they became more consistent. When that didn’t fix it, they hired a private trainer for $95 a session, 6 sessions, $570.

He told them Felix needed firmer boundaries and more exercise. Don’t repeat commands, don’t give in, make him work for what he wants and add another walk every day.

So they did.

Felix got very good at sitting before his dinner. He still barked at the mail carrier, still went on the rug when it rained, still howled when they left and now pulled harder on 2 walks instead of 1.

Then came an anti-bark spray collar for around $60.

Felix worked out exactly how much noise he could make before triggering it and developed this low, constant bark like a grunt that Mark said was somehow more irritating than the original one.

They tried Zesty Paws calming bites, a ThunderShirt, puzzle toys, KONGs, a new harness and a Furbo camera so Emily could check on him while they were out. Around another $600 disappeared.

The Furbo might have been the worst purchase because now Emily would sit at dinner watching Felix pace around the townhouse. She would check him under the table, check again 5 minutes later, then tell Mark they should probably head home.

By then they weren’t just training Felix anymore. Their life was starting to bend around him.

They avoided having people over because the barking was embarrassing. Emily checked the weather before making plans because rain usually meant another potty battle, they planned evenings around how long Felix had been alone, and Mark started sleeping with earplugs because Felix sometimes heard something outside at 5am and decided everybody should know about it.

I still thought we were dealing with separate problems. 

Barking, potty training, separation, listening, leash pulling, each one felt like another thing that needed its own fix.

That was my mistake.

At 6 months, Emily called me and I knew in my gut something was wrong before she had even said hello.

She told me the class hadn’t worked, the private trainer hadn’t worked, the calming products hadn’t worked and Felix seemed worse than when they started.

Then she told me how much they had spent.

By the time we added the class, private trainer, bark collar, supplements, Furbo, harnesses, toys and replacing the hallway runner twice, it was around $1,300.

$1,300 and they were still putting down a washable mat when it rained.

But the money wasn’t why she was crying.

Mark had finally said it.

“I can’t keep living like this.”

Emily told me they were fighting about Felix constantly, who had forgotten to take him out, who had responded when he barked, whether Emily was babying him, whether Mark was being too hard on him, whether they should pay for another trainer and whether anything was actually going to change.

Then she said, “Mom, can you just take him?”

This was the puppy I had found and wrapped in a Christmas bow because I thought I was giving my daughter something that would make her home happier. Now that dog was becoming the biggest argument inside it.

I told her we’d talk the next day, then I called Jessica because I needed to hear how Hazel was doing. By then I was starting to wonder whether I had made the same mistake twice.

Jessica picked up and sounded completely different.

She said Hazel was doing really well. The rainy-day accidents had stopped, she was settling when they left, the barking was manageable and she was checking in on walks and coming when called far more reliably.

I remember asking, “What trainer did you use?”

She said, “I didn’t.”

That got my attention.

Jessica told me she’d been awake around midnight about 6 weeks earlier because Hazel had been howling again. She ended up in a Dachshund Facebook group, found a thread from another owner and bought something they recommended.

“What?” I asked. 

She said it was a breed specific training guide made for dachshunds.

She sent me the link and I started reading it that night, and after about 20 minutes I started feeling sick.

Not because I thought the guide was wrong. Because it explained something I should have understood after 25 years with this breed.

I had spent decades calling Dachshunds stubborn like that explained anything.

It didn’t.

“Stubborn” was just the label I had put on what I could see.

The guide explained how a Dachshund was bred for 1 of the most independent jobs you could give a dog. 

Go underground, away from the handler, hunt a badger, make decisions alone, keep going and don’t wait for somebody to tell you what to do next.

Generation after generation, the dogs that trusted their own judgment, persisted and didn’t give up were the dogs people bred forward.

Then we put that same brain in a living room and act surprised when it doesn’t do everything we say.

That was Felix and Hazel. Same litter, same blood, same instincts, but 2 very different outcomes because 1 owner had started understanding the brain she was working with before the other did.

The difference wasn’t that Jessica somehow received the easy puppy.

That small shift changed the way I saw every problem Felix and Emily had.

The barking wasn’t 1 completely separate issue and the toilet refusal wasn’t another. The selective hearing, pulling, following Emily everywhere and struggling when she left weren’t 5 random issues in the same dog.

They were different places where that independent, persistent Dachshund brain was making its own calculation. 

What happens if I bark, is going outside in the rain worth it, why should I leave this smell and come back to you, why should I stay here if following you feels better, what happens when you leave me?

Emily had been trying to overpower those decisions after Felix had already made them.

But Jessica had the guide, and the guide taught her how to change the calculation before anything had happened.

Jessica told me just a few of the protocols she’d started using had already changed everything for her in the first few days.

The Quiet Command gave the barking a clear beginning and end instead of what Emily was doing, which was yelling “quiet” after Felix had already been barking for 5 minutes. 

The Weather-Proof Toilet Routine changed the value of going outside until the warm hallway rug stopped winning every time it rained so Jessica never faced the same potty issues Emily did.

The Confidence Method broke leaving the house into predictable steps so Hazel never worried when Jessica left, because she knew she was always coming back. 

The recall and cooperation work made checking in with Jessica worth choosing, instead of expecting a Dachshund to just abandon whatever interests them simply because their name had been called.

For the first time, it seemed like a training program that actually works because it was written specifically for the dog the owner has. 

I drove over to Emily's house the next evening to tell her everything that Jessica had told me.

I showed Emily the guide and told her I owed her an apology. I had spent 6 months telling her to be more consistent without ever properly explaining what she needed to be consistent with.

I sent her the link to the guide and bought it for her because I felt so bad. We started going through it together while I was there. 

3 weeks later she called me from a walk and the first thing she said was, “He just looked at me.”

I thought she was crying, then I realized she was laughing.

They had passed another dog, Felix noticed it, started moving toward it and then turned back to Emily on his own. She hadn’t pulled him or repeated his name 5 times, he checked in because he chose to.

It sounds tiny until you own a Dachshund who has spent 6 months treating your voice like background noise. Then it feels enormous.

The other things were changing too.

Felix hadn’t gone on the hallway rug in nearly 2 weeks, including 3 rainy days. The mail carrier would still get a bark because Felix was still Felix, but it was done in under 2 minutes instead of becoming a 30-minute headache.

Emily could start leaving without the immediate panic they had been seeing before.

Mark noticed it too, and that mattered more than anything because Felix wasn’t the only thing becoming calmer. Their house was.

A few months earlier, Emily had asked me to take back the puppy I gave her. Now Felix was still there, Mark was still there and the washable mat eventually disappeared from the hallway.

Same dog, different understanding.

That’s why I’m writing this.

I’ve had Dachshunds for 25 years and still confuse experience with understanding. 

I knew what they did, but I didn’t properly understand why they did it.

If you own a Dachshund and you’re dealing with barking, accidents, selective hearing, pulling, following you everywhere, separation problems or the feeling that your dog knows exactly what you’re asking and simply doesn’t care, those problems may not be as separate as they look.

And throwing another generic solution at each one can get expensive very quickly.

Emily spent around $1,300 before she understood that.

The Complete Dachshund Guide is $37.

It includes the cooperation and recall system, Quiet Command, Weather-Proof Toilet Routine, Confidence Method for separation anxiety, leash training, Behavior Reset and IVDD Prevention Blueprint, plus the rest of the complete breed-specific system and free monthly updates.

It’s delivered instantly so you can start training tonight and it comes with a 90-day money-back guarantee if it doesn’t work for you.

I’m not recommending it because every Dachshund becomes perfect.

Felix certainly didn’t.

He still burrows under every blanket he can find, believes rain is personally offensive and has opinions about almost everything. He’s still a Dachshund.

The difference is that Emily finally knows how to work with the dog she actually has instead of spending more money trying to turn him into a dog he was never bred to be.

I thought I was giving my daughter a puppy for Christmas.

What I actually gave her was a working hound in a 10-pound body and a handful of advice that wasn’t nearly good enough.

I can’t change that part.

But if I can stop another Dachshund owner spending $1,000, $2,000 or another 6 months feeling like they’re failing a dog they love, writing this is worth it.

Please get it for yourself and spare yourself the pain.

Ruth, Omaha, Nebraska. Dachshund owner, 25 years

P.S. Emily was around $1,300 in before she called me asking to take Felix back, group classes, private training, bark products, calming chews, equipment, replacement rugs and a camera so she could watch the problem happen while she was away.

3 weeks after she started using the guide, Felix was checking in voluntarily on walks, hadn’t gone on the rug in nearly 2 weeks and the barking that used to take over the townhouse was ending in minutes.

Same dog. Different instructions.

Earlier would have been easier. Today still counts.

bodyText:
Diane is 63 years old.

She drives a Subaru. She's a retired kindergarten teacher. She held everything together for her family for 40 years.

And last Tuesday she stole from my cat boarding facility.

A small glass jar. Wrapped in her cat's towel. Slipped into her tote bag at 6:47 AM before we'd even unlocked the door.

I watched it happen on camera.

When she told me why, I forgave her before she finished the sentence.

In fact, I was the one who ended up apologizing — for not giving her the answer sooner.

Let me start from the beginning. Because this story isn't what you think.

My husband Marcus and I have been running a small cat boarding facility for the past 6 years. Five-star reviews, 28 private rooms, climbing trees, the works. We've boarded hundreds of cats. We've dealt with the picky eaters, the hider-under-the-bed cats, the one who somehow learned to open his room door on the second night, the senior who only ate tuna if I sang to him.

Normal stuff.

But about 8 months ago, something started happening that we'd never experienced in six years.

Clients started asking about the small jar on the feeding station counter.

Not the food bowls. Not the water fountain. Not the treat tin.

The little glass jar next to the food scoops.

See, I keep a small wellness station on the counter for cats — water bowls, a few approved treats, and a glass jar filled with an unflavored powder. There's a handwritten card next to it that says: "Daily taurine sprinkle — one scoop on her food. Great for boarding cats during a stressful stay."

Most clients let us add it to their cat's bowl the way they'd let a hotel add a turndown mint. It's hospitality. Nobody thinks twice about it.

But the pickup conversations started shifting.

"I don't know what you fed her but the smell is gone from her litter box. Like, completely gone. What was in that jar?"

"He hasn't thrown up once since we got him home. Three days. That has NEVER happened. What did you do?"

"She's been playing with toys she's ignored for two years. The vet said it was 'just aging.' What's actually going on?"

Now — I knew what was in that jar. I'll explain why later. But what I didn't expect was clients seeing changes from a four or five-day stay. It took my own cat weeks to show real differences. I figured a few days of taurine wasn't enough time to move the needle for anyone.

I was wrong.

The comments kept clustering around the same things. And they were too specific. Vomiting stopped. Litter box smell gone. Energy that hadn't been there in years. Eating their full bowl without leaving half of it.

That wasn't the boarding stay. That wasn't the climbing trees. That was the same shift I'd seen happen once before — in my own kitchen — happening to strangers' cats whose owners had no idea what they were sprinkling on the food.

One couple — both in their late 50s — booked their 13-year-old back for another stay the following month specifically because the wife said her cat hadn't thrown up in three weeks for the first time in years and she wanted to know what we did.

A retired teacher extended her cat's stay by two days because she said for the first time in months, her cat had eaten a full bowl without backing away from it halfway through. She kept watching her cat eat through the window of her room like she was watching a different animal.

Something was happening. Something real.

Then last month, something happened that still keeps me up at night.

A woman named Diane dropped off her cat Don on a Thursday. Nice couple — her and her husband. Mid-60s. She was warm, chatty, organized — the kind of energy where you could tell she was the one who held everything together. Her husband was quieter. But Don the cat was the one who broke my heart. He was 11 years old. Used to be 14 pounds. Now he was 8. Vomiting almost daily, she told me. Three different prescription foods. Two rounds of dewormers in the past year. The vet kept saying "he's just an old cat."

They left Don with us for four nights.

On pickup morning, Diane was right on time. She paid the invoice. Thanked us. Carried Don out to the car in his carrier.

But when I went to clean the feeding station for the next cat, something was wrong.

The jar was gone.

Not the treats. Not the water bowls. The glass jar of taurine powder that sits on the counter. Gone.

It wasn't in the recycling. Wasn't in the cabinets. Wasn't behind the scale. I checked every drawer, every shelf, every bag in every trash can.

The jar was simply missing.

I pulled up the camera footage from the feeding station — we have a disclosed camera there that clients know about. Standard facility security. Nothing hidden.

And there it was.

6:47 AM on pickup morning, before we'd even unlocked the front door. Diane had come in through the side entrance to grab Don's carrier early. The feeding station was empty. She walked to the counter. Looked over her shoulder. Picked up the jar. Wrapped it in one of her cat's towels. Put it in her tote bag. Walked back to Don's room.

She took the whole jar.

My first reaction was frustration. Not because the powder was expensive — it wasn't, really. But because we had three cats coming in that afternoon and I'd have to drive 30 minutes to my house to grab more from our pantry.

But that frustration lasted about ten seconds.

Because I thought about the retired teacher watching her cat eat through the window. The couple who booked again. Every pickup conversation from every client who'd watched their cat get a scoop of powder on the food and walked out four days later with a cat they barely recognized.

This woman watched her cat for four days. And whatever happened to him — or to her — was enough that she couldn't leave without it.

That's not theft. Not really.

That's someone who found something and was terrified of losing it.

I texted her: "Hi Diane — hope Don settles back in at home. I noticed the jar of powder is missing from the feeding station. Everything okay?"

Forty-five minutes later, my phone rang.

She was crying.

Not the polite kind. The ugly kind. The kind where someone has been holding something in for a long time and it finally comes out.

"I'm so sorry," she said. "I know it was wrong. I'll pay for it. I'll pay you whatever you want. I just —"

She stopped. Took a breath. Started again.

"Don has been on prescription food for almost three years. Hill's i/d. His vet says it's the best thing for his 'sensitive stomach.' Every six months we go in and the vet says 'we're managing it, just keep doing what you're doing.'"

Her voice got harder.

"But he is NOT managed. He hasn't been managed in years."

"The vomiting started slowly. Once a week. Then twice. Then almost every day. Yellow bile in the morning. Undigested food in the afternoon. I've been cleaning vomit off my carpet for three years. I bought a steam cleaner JUST for that."

"Then the weight loss. He went from 14 pounds to 8. I can feel every rib through his fur. But he keeps eating. He BEGS for food. Then throws half of it back up an hour later."

"Then the smell. The litter box was so bad I had to keep the bathroom door closed. My grandkids stopped coming over. They said the house smelled. I cried about it in my car after my daughter brought it up."

"His vet says he has a sensitive stomach. Says some cats are just like that. Prescribed three different foods. The vomiting? 'That's just Don. He's an older cat now. It happens.'"

Her voice broke.

"It's not just aging. I've had cats for 30 years. I know what aging looks like. This isn't aging. This is something else. Something is being taken from him. I've been watching it happen for three years and nobody will listen to me."

I was gripping the phone so hard my knuckles were white.

"That powder on your counter," she said. "I didn't know what it was. I thought it was a probiotic or something. You sprinkled it on his food Thursday evening. He ate the whole bowl. He didn't throw up."

"Friday morning, when I called to check on him, you said he'd eaten his breakfast and was sleeping on the cat tree. He didn't throw up Friday either."

"Saturday I called again. No vomit. Sunday — nothing. By the time I came to pick him up Monday morning, he hadn't thrown up in four days. FOUR DAYS."

She was sobbing now.

"And the smell. I asked you what kind of litter you used because something was different. You told me you used the same brand I do. But the smell wasn't there. It just wasn't there."

"I got him home and I unpacked his stuff and I gave him dinner that night and I waited. I sat on the kitchen floor waiting for him to throw up the way he always does. He didn't. He ate the whole bowl. He cleaned his paws. He jumped on the couch."

"He jumped on the couch. He hasn't done that in over a year."

"And I knew. I KNEW. Whatever was in that jar was the thing that brought him back. And the second it ran out, he was going to go back to throwing up bile at 5 a.m. and disappearing into the same skeleton I've been watching for three years."

"I panicked. I knew it was wrong. I took it anyway. Because I'd watched my cat come back to life over four days and I could not — I could NOT — let that end."

She was crying so hard I could barely hear her.

"I haven't seen him like that in years. I forgot what he sounded like when he was actually hungry instead of starving. I forgot what his fur looked like when his belly wasn't bloated and his spine wasn't sharp. I got him back for four days and then pickup was going to take him away again."

I was crying too.

Sitting on the floor of my own feeding station, tears running down my face, listening to this woman describe my own life back to me.

She could have been telling my story. Word for word.

Because two years ago, I was Diane.

My cat Marigold started vomiting at 9 years old. The vet called it a sensitive stomach. Six months in, she was on prescription food. The vet was thrilled with how she was "managing."

And every morning I sat in my kitchen cleaning bile off my floor.

The details were different but the shape was the same. Don lost his appetite, then started begging — and threw it all back up. Marigold did the same thing. Don's litter box smelled like death. Marigold's did too. Don's vet said "he's just an old cat." Marigold's vet said the same thing. Same script. Same dismissal. Same woman sitting across from a vet knowing in her bones that something else was happening.

What I need to tell you is what I found when I went looking for answers. Because that's the part nobody told me. And it's the reason that powder is on my feeding station counter.

One night — 1 AM, couldn't sleep — I was sitting at the kitchen table with my laptop. Marigold was asleep on a folded towel on the kitchen floor. Not because she wanted to be. Because that's where I'd put her after she'd thrown up there and I'd cleaned the mess and she was too tired to move.

The cat I'd had for nine years used to sleep on my pillow. Now she couldn't make it to the bedroom. Her body gave out wherever she stopped walking. And the vet called it aging.

I started researching. Not "best food for sensitive stomach." I'd already wasted months on that — prescription diet, novel protein, hydrolyzed, hairball formula. None of it touched the vomiting or the weight loss or the smell.

I researched WHY. Why was her stomach failing?

And I found something that changed everything.

It was a long post on a feline health forum. Written by a retired veterinary nutrition researcher. Twenty-eight years of practice. He'd left the field because he said he couldn't keep recommending diets that he now understood were causing the very problem he'd spent his career trying to manage.

I almost scrolled past it. The internet is full of cranks. But his credentials checked out. His writing was precise. Clinical. Not angry — just tired. Like a man who'd spent three decades doing something he'd finally realized was wrong.

He started by explaining what's actually happening inside a chronically vomiting cat.

"Up to 75% of cats are carrying parasites their owners can never see," he wrote. "Indoor or outdoor, premium-fed or not. The eggs are everywhere — on shoes, in dust, on a fly through a screen. Most owners assume their cat is safe because she stays inside. She isn't."

I thought about Marigold throwing up bile at 5 a.m.

"Cats have a built-in defense against this. The liver produces a powerful bile acid that dissolves the protective shells around parasite eggs before they can hatch. Every egg that walks into a cat's body is supposed to be destroyed in her stomach. Before it ever takes hold."

"But that bile acid needs one specific nutrient to be produced: taurine. Cats can't make it on their own. They have to get it from their food. No taurine, no bile acid. No bile acid, no defense. And every parasite egg that walks in walks right through her stomach untouched."

I thought about her shrinking spine.

"Here's what they don't tell you. Commercial cat food destroys 50 to 70% of the naturally occurring taurine through high-heat processing. And if the food is grain-free, the peas and lentils inside bind up whatever taurine survives the heat. So your cat is eating a food that's labeled 'complete and balanced' — and her body is starving for the one nutrient her parasite defense needs to function."

That was exactly what Marigold's vet had done. Switched her to prescription food. Told us she was "managing." Checked the box.

Then this researcher wrote something that made me physically sick.

"But the taurine depletion — as devastating as it is — isn't the part most owners miss. The part they miss is what happens to the cat once the defense collapses."

"With no bile acid to destroy the eggs, parasite larvae hatch in the cat's intestines. They burrow into the gut wall — physically tearing through the lining where food is supposed to be absorbed. The damaged gut becomes chronically inflamed. Food can't pass through properly. Bile that should be killing parasites is instead irritating raw tissue. And the cat throws up."

"This is why chronic vomiting in cats is so often misdiagnosed as 'sensitive stomach.' The cat IS sensitive. But not because of the food itself. Because there are parasites tearing through her gut and the bile defense has been disabled by the very food she's eating."

My hands were shaking.

"This is why dewormers fail. They kill the worms inside today. They do nothing to fix the broken defense. The eggs already in the home — they can live in carpet for years — just wait for the medication to wear off, then walk back into a defenseless gut and start the cycle over."

Then he wrote something I will never forget.

"I had a client. Sixty-two years old. Her cat had been on a prescription GI diet for six years. The vomiting was 'managed.' Twice a week instead of every day. The bloodwork was 'normal.' Every six months they checked the chart and said 'looking great.' She called me one morning crying because her cat had died of intestinal damage from chronic untreated parasitism. The vet had never once tested for the underlying mechanism. The chart had looked fine for six years. And her wife had watched her vet watch it."

I looked across the kitchen at Marigold. Asleep on the towel. Bony. Exhausted.

I've raised Bernedoodles for 14 years and if nobody tells you what I'm about to, you're going to spend the next 6 months watching your dog get worse the same way my daughter did.

I'd always told people the same things, be patient, be consistent, don't let them get away with too much, and remember that Bernedoodles are stubborn. I believed every word of it because I'd raised 3 of them myself.

Then 1 of my daughters called me 6 months after I gave her a Bernedoodle puppy and asked if I would take him back.

My name is Ruth. I live in Omaha, Nebraska, and Bernedoodles have been part of my life since I first discovered the breed over a decade ago. I've raised 3, loved every one of them and probably bored hundreds of people talking about them.

I knew about their stubbornness, their size, their attachment, their obsession with following you into the bathroom and the way they somehow hear a cheese wrapper from 3 rooms away while being completely deaf when you call their name.

So when both my adult daughters wanted Bernedoodles, I thought I was the perfect person to help.

I found a good litter, same mother, same father.

Emily took Felix, a male tri-color standard, and Jessica took Hazel, his sister, same beautiful markings, absolutely adorable.

Emily lived with her husband Mark in a townhouse in Papillion. They both worked full-time, had no children yet and had been talking about getting a dog for over a year. Jessica lived across town with her girlfriend in a small house with a yard.

Christmas week I gave them the puppies with matching bows and beds. I felt like a super mom.

For the first few weeks, I thought I'd been proven right. 

Emily called constantly saying Felix was brilliant, already learning his name, following them everywhere, sleeping pressed against their legs and had Mark completely wrapped around his little paw.

Jessica said the same about Hazel. Both girls thought they had the best puppy in the litter.

Then the little things started.

Emily mentioned Felix had begun ignoring them when something more interesting was happening. Then there was jumping on every guest, pulling on the leash at 35 pounds, pacing the house in the evenings and following Emily from room to room whining whenever she left his sight.

Nothing sounded serious, so I gave her the same advice I had given people for years. Be consistent, don't repeat yourself, reward the good behavior and remember that Bernedoodles can be stubborn.

Then the little things stopped being little.

Felix started jumping on every person who walked through the front door. What was cute at 20 pounds became dangerous at 60. The pulling got so bad that Emily had a sore shoulder after every walk, and with Bernese draft-dog strength behind every pull, it wasn’t getting better.

The selective hearing became worse as well, outside with any distraction, Felix wouldn't even respond to his own name.

Leaving the house changed too. Felix started whining when she picked up her handbag, pacing when she put her shoes on and howling after the front door closed. Then the baseboards near the front door started getting chewed.

Their neighbor mentioned it once, then again, then came the first noise complaint.

Emily started rushing home from errands. Mark started getting frustrated. Then they got the 2nd complaint.

When I asked how things were going, Emily would say, "Fine," but as a mother, you know the difference between fine and "fine."

So she did what responsible dog owners are supposed to do. She paid for training.

6-week PetSmart obedience course. $119. Felix was excellent inside the training room. Then they got home and it was like somebody had wiped the lesson from his memory.

The trainer said they needed to be more consistent. When that didn't fix it, they hired a private trainer for $150 a session, 4 sessions, $600.

He told them Felix needed firmer boundaries and more exercise. They added another walk every day.

Felix got very good at sitting before his dinner. He still jumped on every guest, still pulled with strength Emily couldn't match, still howled when they left, still chewed the baseboards and now pulled harder on 2 walks instead of 1.

They tried calming chews. 3 brands. $280. Felix ate them and still jumped on guests 20 minutes later.

They tried CBD oil, a ThunderShirt, puzzle toys he solved in 6 minutes, a gentle leader he powered through, and a Furbo camera so Emily could check on him while they were out. 

Another $400 disappeared.

The camera might have been the worst purchase because now Emily would sit at dinner watching Felix pace the townhouse and chew baseboards in real time.

By then they weren't just training Felix anymore. Their life was bending around him.

They avoided having people over because the jumping was dangerous. They planned evenings around how long Felix had been alone. Mark started sleeping with earplugs because Felix paced the hardwood at 5am.

I still thought we were dealing with separate problems. Jumping, pulling, selective hearing, pacing, separation anxiety, each one felt like it needed its own fix.

That was my mistake.

At 6 months, Emily called me and I knew something was wrong before she had even said hello.

She told me the class hadn't worked, the private trainer hadn't worked, the calming products hadn't worked and Felix seemed worse than when they started.

By the time we added everything up it was around $1,800.

But the money wasn't why she was crying.

Mark had finally said it.

"I can't keep living like this."

They were fighting about Felix constantly. Then she said, "Mom, can you just take him?"

This was the puppy I had wrapped in a Christmas bow because I thought I was giving my daughter something that would make her home happier.

I told her we'd talk the next day, then I called Jessica because I needed to hear how Hazel was doing.

Jessica picked up and sounded completely different.

She said Hazel was doing really well. The separation anxiety had stopped, she was settling on her mat, the jumping had stopped, she was walking on a loose leash and checking in on walks voluntarily.

"What trainer did you use?"

"I didn't" she said.

Jessica told me she'd been awake around midnight about 6 weeks earlier because Hazel had been howling again. She ended up in a Bernedoodle Facebook group and bought something another owner recommended.

She said it was a breed-specific training guide made for Bernedoodles.

She sent me the link and I started reading it that night, and after about 20 minutes I started feeling sick.

Not because I thought the guide was wrong. Because it explained something I should have understood after 14 years with this breed.

I had spent over a decade calling Bernedoodles stubborn like that explained anything.

It didn't.

The guide explained how a Bernedoodle's brain runs 2 genetic drives simultaneously with zero impulse control.

From the Poodle side, the 2nd most intelligent breed ever measured, a problem-solving brain that treats every blocked path as a puzzle. 

From the Bernese side, one of the most stubborn, powerful working drives in any breed, bred to pull carts and guard farms all day without stopping. Plus the velcro-dog attachment drive that treats separation as an emergency.

Neither parent breed was selected for impulse control.

Then we put that brain in a living room and act surprised when it doesn't do everything we say.

That was Felix and Hazel. Same litter, same drives, but 2 very different outcomes because 1 owner had started understanding the brain she was working with before the other did.

The difference wasn't that Jessica received the easy puppy.

The jumping, pulling, selective hearing, pacing, separation anxiety and destruction weren't 6 random issues. They were just the different places where the same brain was showing the 1 problem. 

Emily had been trying to overpower those drives after Felix’s brain had already fired.

Jessica had the guide, and the guide taught her how to feed both drives and install the off-switch before the chaos started.

Same brains, different approach, reactive vs preventative. 

The Doodle Brain Hack flipped the equation so calmness was the only behavior that paid and chaos became invisible.

The Threshold Pause at every door installed impulse control through the thing they want most, the door opening.

The settling protocol installed the off-switch on a designated mat, rewarding the deep sigh, the hip roll, the chin on the floor.

The separation anxiety protocol was designed specifically for the Bernese velcro-dog drive, teaching the brain that departure always ends the same predictable way.

The Eye-Contact Lottery rewired the value system so checking in with Jessica became the most profitable habit in Hazel's life.

For the first time, it seemed like a training program that actually worked because it was written specifically for the dog the owner has.

I drove over to Emily's house and told her everything. I bought the guide for her because I felt so bad.

3 weeks later she called me from a walk and the first thing she said was, "He just looked at me."

I thought she was crying, then I realized she was laughing.

They had passed another dog, Felix noticed it, started moving toward it and then turned back to Emily on his own. He checked in because he chose to.

It sounds tiny until you own a Bernedoodle who has spent 6 months treating your voice like background noise. Then it feels enormous.

Felix hadn't destroyed a baseboard in nearly 2 weeks. The jumping had stopped entirely. The pacing had decreased by more than half. Emily could leave without the immediate panic and destruction.

Mark noticed it too. Felix wasn't the only thing becoming calmer. Their house was.

A few months earlier, Emily had asked me to take back the puppy I gave her. Now Felix was still there, Mark was still there and the chewed baseboards got repaired and stayed intact.

Same dog, different understanding.

That's why I'm writing this.

I've had Bernedoodles for 14 years and I confused experience with understanding.

If you own a Bernedoodle and you're dealing with jumping, pulling, selective hearing, pacing, separation anxiety, destroyed baseboards or the feeling that your dog knows exactly what you're asking and simply doesn't care, those problems may not be as separate as they look.

Emily spent around $1,800 before she understood that.

The Complete Bernedoodle Guide is $37.

It includes the Doodle Brain Hack system, the Threshold Pause, the brain games, the settling protocol, the Eye-Contact Lottery, the separation anxiety protocol, leash walking, doorbell desensitization, recall training, jumping and biting resets, counter surfing, diet guidance, grooming protocols, plus free monthly updates.

It's delivered instantly so you can start training tonight and it comes with a 90-day money-back guarantee if it doesn't work for you.

I'm not recommending it because every Bernedoodle magically becomes perfect.

Felix still follows Emily into the bathroom, still believes he fits on her lap at 75 pounds and has opinions about almost everything. He's still a Bernedoodle.

The difference is that Emily finally knows how to work with the dog she actually has instead of spending more money trying to turn him into a dog he was never bred to be.

I thought I was giving my daughter a puppy for Christmas.

What I actually gave her was a Poodle-cross brain with Bernese stubbornness in an 80-pound body and a handful of advice that wasn't nearly good enough.

But if I can stop another Bernedoodle owner spending $1,000, $2,000 or another 6 months feeling like they're failing a dog they love, writing this is worth it.

Please get it for yourself and spare yourself the pain.

Regardless of their age, this will help.

👉 https://pawpowa.com/pages/bernedoodle-guide

Ruth, Omaha, Nebraska. Bernedoodle owner, 14 years

P.S. Emily was around $1,800 in before she called me asking to take Felix back. 3 weeks after she started using the guide, Felix was checking in voluntarily on walks, hadn't destroyed a baseboard in 2 weeks, the jumping had stopped and the pacing was half of what it had been. Same dog. Different instructions.

👉 https://pawpowa.com/pages/bernedoodle-guide

P.P.S. If your Bernedoodle is already 2, 4 or 7 years old, don't assume you've missed the window. Older patterns take more work because the dog has practiced them longer, but that doesn't make the Poodle-cross brain unteachable.

Earlier would have been easier, but today still works.

bodyText:
👑 My inheritance returns in one month. That’s why the people who raised me suddenly want me dead.
Training
Traci’s POV

“Traci, you need to rest. You’re pushing too hard.” Corbin’s voice cut through the sharp morning air while I drove my fist into the padded target again. Sweat slid down my spine despite the cool breeze rolling through the clearing behind the old patrol cabins.
“I’m fine,” I muttered, throwing another punch. 
The target jerked backward. Corbin caught it before it toppled over completely and shot me a flat look. “That response right there tells me you are absolutely not fine.”
“Funny. I thought the dark circles and emotional damage gave it away first.”
His mouth twitched like he was fighting a grin. “Traci,” he warned.
“But Corbin, you know how important this is to me.” I stepped back long enough to grab the towel hanging from the fence post beside me. “For my survival. Out of everyone in this pack, you understand that better than anybody.”
“Yes,” he replied calmly, folding his arms over his chest. “And because I understand, I also know you’re useless if you collapse face-first in the dirt.”
“That only happened once,” I huffed out as I continued. 
“It happened yesterday.”
I pointed at him. “Technically, I landed with dignity.”
“You passed out beside a tree and scared three patrol wolves.”
“I call that dramatic flair.”
A laugh escaped him before he shook his head. “You are impossible.”
“And yet here you are. Every morning. Still training me.”
“That’s because somebody has to keep you alive.”
Before I could answer, another voice drifted toward us. “Corbin, honey, I brought you two breakfast and coffee.” Marge appeared through the trees carrying a tray loaded with steaming cups and wrapped sandwiches. The woman had the supernatural ability to look put together at six in the morning while I looked like I’d crawled out of a battlefield.
Honestly, maybe I had.
“Thank the Moon Goddess,” Corbin breathed dramatically. “I was two minutes away from starvation.”
“You ate an hour ago,” Marge said.
“That was emotional support food. Entirely different category.”
She rolled her eyes and handed him a coffee before walking toward me. “Traci, sit down before you fall down.”
“I’m not….” I started to say before I got interrupted. 
“Don’t argue with me. I raised three boys. I survived that. You don’t scare me.”
I smirked despite myself and finally dropped onto the old wooden bench near the training ring.
Before I get ahead of myself, let me explain. I’m Traci Silver. Born into the Silver Clan Pack as the daughter of two alphas. My father ruled this territory with strength. My mother ruled it with intelligence sharp enough to make grown warriors nervous. Together, they were unstoppable. Until the rogues killed them.
I was twelve when everything burned down around me. One night changed my entire life. One night turned me from future alpha into unwanted burden.
I was their only child. The rightful heir to the Silver Clan. Everyone knew it. The laws knew it. The elders knew it.
But laws stopped mattering after funerals.
Ralph stepped in immediately after my parents died. He told everyone he was only taking temporary control until I came of age. Said he wanted stability for the pack.
People believed him. Maybe some genuinely wanted to. Others were simply too afraid not to.
Back then, I still lived on the alpha floor of the packhouse. I still had my own room. My own things. My own future. That lasted less than a week. Ralph moved his family into the alpha wing and shoved me into the attic like unwanted storage.
“There just isn’t enough room,” he’d told me while his sons carried my belongings upstairs in garbage bags.
Funny how there was enough room for his giant ego though.
The attic became my prison after that.
Cold winters.
Leaking ceilings.
Broken windows patched with cardboard.
I lost everything the day my parents died.
Not only them. Everything.
Friends stopped speaking to me. Some out of fear. Others because cruelty spreads fast when powerful people allow it.
I was bullied constantly. Starved when Ralph’s mate decided I “hadn’t earned dinner.” Beaten whenever one of his children blamed me for something. Locked in the dungeon for days at a time over offenses I didn’t commit.
At thirteen, Ralph stripped me of my alpha title publicly and labeled me omega instead.
The humiliation wasn’t accidental. He wanted the pack to see me beneath them.
Weak.
Broken.
Forgettable.
Unfortunately for him, hatred is excellent motivation. I survived five years under that roof. Five years of pretending I wasn’t counting every single day until freedom.
Because my parents planned ahead. That part still makes me smile. My inheritance legally transfers to me at eighteen.
Not Ralph.
Not his children.
Me.

This year, Ralph signed me up himself. That alone told me something was wrong.

So was Marge.
And Sarah…my best friend since childhood. She never left my side even after her parents forbade her from speaking to me.
Corbin started training me in secret when I was twelve. At first, it was simple self-defense.
Then endurance.
Combat.
Weapons.
Strategy.
By fourteen, I was running border patrols with trusted warriors under darkness so nobody would report it back to Ralph.
I fought rogues before most teenagers learned pack politics.
I learned how to survive while everyone else learned how to socialize.

Marge laughed into her cup while I glared at him.
Traitor.

Silence settled over us briefly. The wind rustled through the trees surrounding the clearing. 
My body ached from training. Old scars burned beneath my sleeves.
One month.
Just one more month. Then nobody would ever control me again.
Corbin stood and tossed me my practice blade. “Alright,” he said with a grin. “Enough emotional bonding for today. Try not to stab me this time.”
I caught the blade easily and stood. “No promises.”
Marge sighed dramatically. “If either of you bleed on my breakfast table later, I’m divorcing both of you.”
Corbin blinked. “Pretty sure that’s not how marriage works.”
“It does in my house.”
I laughed for real that time. And for the first time in years, freedom didn’t feel impossible anymore.

A Problem

By the time Calvin and I finished training the sky had barely started turning gray. Dawn stretched across the mountains in thin streaks while cold mist clung to the training field like it refused to let go of the night. Sweat dampened the back of my shirt, my muscles screamed from exhaustion, and my lungs still burned from the drills Calvin insisted would “keep me alive longer.”
Such a comforting statement before sunrise.
Training at four in the morning had become routine months ago. It was the only way I could survive both worlds. Calvin pushed me through combat before anyone woke up, then I rushed back to the pack house to become everybody’s favorite servant by seven.
Lucky me.
Breakfast had to be started before most of the pack even rolled out of bed. Eggs, biscuits, bacon, fruit, coffee. Endless coffee. Wolves acted like caffeine was some sacred gift from the Moon Goddess herself. If the pot went empty for more than thirty seconds people started acting like civilization had collapsed.
After breakfast was served and the kitchen cleaned, I handled the upstairs chores. Darcy’s room first. Always Darcy’s room. Hers looked like a tornado married a shopping addiction and decided to raise children together. Clothes everywhere. Toys under every surface. Half-eaten snacks shoved into drawers like hidden treasure.
Her sons, Edward, Alvin, and Aaron, somehow made even more mess than she did.
Then came the Alpha and Luna’s suite. Bigger room. Bigger ego. Same filth.
By the time I finished scrubbing floors and hauling laundry downstairs my body already felt heavy. Yesterday’s bruises still covered my ribs beneath my shirt, dark purple fading into sickly yellow. Every movement pulled at sore skin that never fully healed anymore.
I thanked Corbin and Marge after training cleanup and hurried outside toward the pack house again. The sun had barely risen over the trees.
I wasn’t late. Not even close. Which was exactly why my stomach dropped the second Beta Travis stepped directly into my path. “Well, well,” he drawled. “Look who finally decided to show up.”
Before I could answer, his hand clamped around my arm hard enough to bruise.
“Traci, where have you been? You haven’t done a damn thing you were supposed to do.” His fingers dug deeper into my skin while he yanked me forward.
“Beta Travis,” I started carefully, “I was only taking a quick walk before chores…”
“You have not cleaned the rooms. Breakfast should’ve already been handled. Maybe you need a lesson.” The smirk on his face made my stomach twist.
I tried explaining again. Told him it wasn’t even time yet. Told him I had been heading there now.
Didn’t matter. Talking to Travis was like arguing with a brick wall if the brick wall had anger issues and smelled like whiskey.
He dragged me across the yard while pack members avoided looking at us. Nobody intervened. Nobody ever intervened.
The second we reached the dungeon entrance cold dread crawled down my spine.
Wonderful. Exactly how I wanted to start my morning.
Stone steps echoed beneath our feet as he hauled me downward. Damp air wrapped around me instantly, thick with mildew, rust, and old blood. Soft lights flickered against the walls casting ugly shadows across iron cages.
I knew better than to fight. I couldn’t reveal my strength.
Not yet.
“You’re going to learn your place one way or another,” Travis sneered. He grabbed a silver-tipped whip from the wall.
My pulse stuttered.
Silver. Of course it had silver. Because apparently basic torture wasn’t dramatic enough.
He chained my wrists above my head before I could brace myself. The metal bit into my skin while icy panic crept through my chest.
Then the first strike landed. Pain exploded across my back so violently my breath vanished. The second cut deeper. The third nearly dropped me.
By the fifth lash my vision blurred. Silver burned through flesh like acid, tearing into skin while agony rippled through my entire body. Blood soaked down my spine. My knees buckled repeatedly but the chains held me upright.
Somewhere during the beating I blacked out. More than once. I remembered waking briefly to another strike before darkness swallowed me again.
Normally wolves healed injuries quickly.
Normally. Except I still didn’t have mine. Double alpha blood should’ve triggered my wolf at fourteen. Regular wolves shifted at sixteen. Yet here I was at seventeen with nothing except silence where my wolf should’ve been.
No healing.
No strength.
No protection.
Just pain.
“Get up, you worthless wench.” His boot slammed into my side.
I gasped sharply while another wave of agony shot through my ribs.
He unchained my wrists roughly and I collapsed onto the floor before forcing myself upward. My arms trembled violently. Blood dripped from the corner of my mouth as I wiped it away with shaky fingers.
“You have chores to finish,” he barked. “Move.”
I stumbled getting to my feet. Honestly, passing out sounded like the better option. When I accidentally looked toward him his expression darkened instantly.
“You piece of trash,” he snarled. “Don’t you dare look at me.”
Funny. Considering he kept demanding my attention every five seconds.
He grabbed my arm again and dragged me back toward the pack house. By the time we reached the kitchen I could barely breathe through the pain.
Wilma turned from the stove and froze. “Oh, sweetheart…” Her face crumpled immediately. “What happened to you?”
I swallowed hard trying not to cry. “I’m sorry I’m late,” I whispered. “Beta Travis stopped me.”
“Oh hush.” Wilma guided me carefully into a chair. “Don’t apologize for somebody else’s cruelty.”
She grabbed a rag and began cleaning blood from my face with gentle hands. Wilma had worked inside the pack house longer than half these people had been alive. She’d patched me together more times than I could count.
“Here.” She pressed herbs into my palm. “Take these. They’ll dull some pain.”
The kitchen door burst open seconds later. “What the hell, Traci?” Sarah stormed inside looking ready to commit several felonies.
I managed a weak smile. “Hey, Sarah. I’m okay.”
“You look half dead.”
“Technically still alive though. So that’s something.”
Her glare sharpened.
“Just one more month,” I whispered quietly. “I can survive one more month.”
Except deep down I wasn’t sure anymore. Each punishment got worse.
Longer.
Crueler.
Sarah crossed her arms. “Sit there and rest. Breakfast is already handled. I’ll help with the rooms.”
“You know they’ll punish you too.”
She rolled her eyes dramatically. “Please. At this point I’m already on their dislike list. Might as well earn it.”
Despite everything, a tiny laugh escaped me. Then her expression hardened. “They’re going to pay for this someday.”
After breakfast I forced myself upstairs. Every step sent pain slicing across my back. By the time I reached Darcy’s room sweat covered my forehead.
I paused outside the partially open door when I heard laughing inside.
“You should’ve seen it,” Darcy giggled. “After I complained about Traci, Dad punished her immediately. Didn’t even bother checking the time.”
Shelby laughed with her. “That stupid bitch deserves it.”
My stomach twisted.
Darcy continued, voice dripping with excitement. “Dad said she’ll finally be finished at the tournament.”
Silence slammed into my chest.
“Omg, seriously?” Shelby gasped.
Darcy laughed again. “Everything’s arranged. Her fights are set up. Fight to the death.”
The world tilted slightly beneath me. Blood rushed loudly through my ears.
I backed away from the doorway too fast and nearly lost my balance. My shoulder slammed against the wall while panic clawed through my chest.
Fight to the death. This wasn’t punishment anymore. They planned to kill me.
I stumbled into the nearby restroom and splashed cold water across my face with trembling hands.
“Sarah,” I mindlinked shakily. “Sarah, I know their plan.”
Fear surged through our bond instantly. Then I reached out again. “Corbin,” I whispered through the link, staring at my pale reflection. “We have a problem.”

Ten.

My Brother

Absolute bullshit.

Tragic.

Me? I preferred chaos. Not reckless chaos. Controlled chaos. There was a difference.
Barely.
Raiden and I took over the Silver Moon Kingdom when we were sixteen after our parents died suddenly in their sleep. Poisoned. Clean. Quiet. Cowardly.
Nobody was ever caught. Trust me, we searched.
Every servant, guard, healer, advisor, elder, and visiting alpha got investigated. Several people disappeared afterward. One traitor lost a hand. Another ended up hanging from the southern border wall as a warning. Still didn’t bring our parents back.
The kingdom nearly tore itself apart after their deaths. Since we were underage, several packs viewed us as weak targets. Rebellions started within days. Challenges followed immediately after.
Nothing says welcome to adulthood like attempted murder. Our childhood disappeared overnight.
Training had prepared us to rule eventually. From the time we could walk, our schedules revolved around combat, leadership studies, diplomacy, history, battle strategy, politics, and survival. Every lesson drilled into us with one purpose. Become kings.
Just preferably not before eighteen. The Moon Goddess apparently had other plans.
While other teenagers snuck out to parties, my brother and I sat in war meetings deciding which packs needed reinforcement and which alphas deserved public humiliation.
Good times.
Some territories still tested us even now. Not openly anymore because that usually ended badly for them, but smaller acts of disrespect still surfaced occasionally. Border violations. Hidden alliances. Quiet resistance.
People loved underestimating younger rulers. Then acted shocked when we crushed them.
I leaned back against the leather chair inside my chambers and stared out the massive window overlooking the kingdom grounds below. Warriors trained across the lower courtyards while staff rushed between buildings carrying supplies for the upcoming tournament.
The event was already turning the palace upside down.
Preparations flooded every hallway. Fighters arriving early. Arena inspections. Merchants setting up shops. Elders pretending they understood combat. Honestly, somebody needed to ban old politicians from giving warrior advice forever. 
One elder suggested “less violent matches” last year. At a fighting tournament. I still questioned how he survived this long.
“You’re brooding again,” Onyx muttered lazily.
I rolled my eyes. “I’m thinking.”
“Dangerous activity for you,” Onyx smirked, clearly proud of himself. 
“Careful. I can replace you.”
“No you can’t. I’m the entertaining one.
Sarcastic little bastard.
Raiden got silence and wisdom from his wolf while mine acted like a drunken comedian trapped inside my skull twenty-four hours a day.
“Besides,” Onyx continued smugly, “you only look dramatic because you’re staring out a window.”
“I hate you,” I rolled my eyes dramatically.
“You adore me.”
Unfortunately, he wasn’t wrong. A knock sounded against my chamber doors before Kael stepped inside carrying several folders beneath one arm.
Unlike most people around the palace, Kael never looked intimidated walking into royal rooms. Probably because he grew up with us. He’d seen Raiden and me bloody, exhausted, furious, reckless, and occasionally unconscious. Real bonding experiences.
“There you are,” Kael said. “The elders are searching for both of you.”
I groaned immediately. “Why.”
He grinned. “Take a wild guess.”
“Heirs,” I groaned as I dropped my head back dramatically against the chair.

Raiden and I turned twenty-five in two weeks which apparently meant the kingdom might implode if we didn’t produce children immediately. Every council meeting somehow circled back toward legacy, bloodlines, succession, or future rulers. As if children magically appeared because elderly wolves nagged aggressively enough.
“They cornered me during breakfast,” Kael continued while laughing. “One asked if you planned on settling down soon.”
“And?”

Reasonable answer honestly. The pressure surrounding mates only worsened with age. Fated bonds were sacred among our kind. 
Unbreakable.
Powerful.
Most wolves found theirs early. Raiden and I hadn’t.
At eighteen I waited patiently, convinced my mate would appear eventually. Nineteen came and went. Then twenty. After that I stopped expecting destiny to work on my schedule. So I enjoyed myself instead.
Unlike my brother. Raiden remained painfully loyal to a woman he hadn’t even met yet. The male refused relationships entirely. No touching. No sleeping around. No interest whatsoever. Honestly concerning behavior.
“You know your brother nearly murdered Elder Vincent yesterday,” Kael said casually.

I barked out a laugh instantly. Yep. That would do it.
The elders selected fifteen women over the last several years and moved them into the palace hoping either Raiden or I would eventually choose one as a mate. They called them Waiting Ladies. Raiden called them whores.
To their faces sometimes.

Couldn’t blame them honestly. Being queen came with luxury, power, influence, wealth, and status beyond imagination.
Still not happening.
I fooled around occasionally. Nothing serious. Nothing emotional. Just temporary distractions with clear boundaries. The women understood exactly what it was.
A… Release. Nothing more. 
Because despite our differences, Raiden and I agreed completely on one thing. We would never accept chosen mates.
Never.
The Moon Goddess created fated bonds for a reason. Our true mate would stand beside us as Luna Queen or nobody would. Simple.
“Well,” Onyx mused thoughtfully, “hopefully she arrives soon because the elders are one conversation away from arranging a breeding schedule.”
I nearly choked.

“Shocking.”

Kael tossed the folders onto the table beside me before crossing his arms. “You and Raiden better survive the next few weeks. Tournament preparations are already chaotic and the elders are acting feral over your birthday.”
“Wonderful combination.”
“No lies there,” he muttered. 
I stood from the chair and grabbed my jacket from nearby. “Where’s Raiden?”
“In his office threatening somebody through email.”
I smirked proudly. “That’s my brother.”

What once started as small raids along distant borders had evolved into organized assaults with strategy behind them. More warriors. Better timing. Stronger fighters. Somebody was building an army in the shadows, and whoever stood behind it had become bold enough to challenge the throne directly.
Ever since Zayden and I became kings after our parents died, enemies had circled us like starving wolves smelling weakness.
Some attacks came from rogues. Others came from packs pretending loyalty while quietly waiting for an opportunity to overthrow us.
Cowards always preferred hiding behind alliances instead of facing us directly.
The elders constantly shoved the same concern down our throats.
Produce an heir.
Secure the bloodline.
Protect the kingdom.
Because if somebody managed defeating both Zayden and me without heirs in place, the throne could fall into anybody’s hands. That alone was enough to make my patience disappear daily.
Still, neither of us could force ourselves into taking chosen mates knowing our true mate existed somewhere in the world. The Moon Goddess created the bond for a reason.
Besides, Zayden and I already knew how our bond would work.
One mate. Shared between us. Twins born from the same bloodline often shared destiny in ways other wolves didn’t understand. Our mate would belong to both of us equally. Hopefully she wouldn’t try killing us after finding that information out.
“You think too much,” Nyx muttered.
“And you don’t think enough,” I bit back.
“Balance,” he chuckled. 
I ignored him while running through the palace corridors toward the southern entrance. The second I cleared the doors, I shifted.
Bones cracked violently beneath my skin while black fur burst across my body in seconds. My massive paws slammed into the ground as Nyx fully took control. As Alpha Kings, our wolves towered over regular alphas in size and strength. Nyx stood nearly double the height of most wolves with dark black fur that blended into the night itself.
Power rolled beneath my skin immediately.
“Zayden,” I linked sharply while sprinting through the forest. “Location.”
Static crackled briefly before my beta answered. “Onyx and I are already here. Damn, brother, they came prepared tonight.”
Trees blurred around us as Nyx pushed faster through the darkness. The scent hit us first.
Blood.
Silver.
Death.
By the time we reached the south border, bodies littered the ground across the battlefield. Torn earth stretched beneath claw marks and blood stains while growls echoed throughout the trees. Warriors fought everywhere beneath the moonlight.
Rogues definitely weren’t playing around tonight.
“Zayden,” I linked quickly. “Try keeping one or two alive. We need answers.”
“Easier said than done,” my brother snapped back while fighting. “These idiots are suicidal.”
A rogue launched toward one of our warriors only to get thrown sideways into a tree hard enough to crack the trunk.
Nyx growled low. “Something smells wrong.”
I slowed slightly. “What do you mean?”
“Wolfsbane.”
My eyes narrowed instantly. “Damn it.”
Wolfsbane weakened wolves dramatically if inhaled or injected. Slowed healing. Suppressed strength. Too much exposure could stop a wolf from shifting entirely. Which meant this attack had planning behind it.
I opened the pack link immediately. “Everyone listen carefully. Nyx smells wolfsbane. Stay alert for silver or other substances.”
Zayden’s voice followed seconds later. “Fight cautiously. If wolfsbane is involved, silver probably is too.”
Warriors answered quickly through the link while battle continued raging around us.
Then three massive wolves stepped from the tree line directly ahead.
“These aren’t normal rogues,” Nyx growled.
He was right. The wolves stood far larger than average rogues with thick builds packed heavily with muscle. One pure brown. One gray. One black with scars stretching across his muzzle.
Ranked fighters. Possibly elite.
“Try capturing one alive,” I warned.
Nyx lunged first.
The brown wolf charged directly toward us with jaws open wide, but Nyx moved faster. Claws ripped across the rogue’s throat before sliding upward violently.
Blood sprayed across the ground. The wolf’s head separated completely from his body.
“Subtle,” Nyx muttered.
Before we could recover, the gray wolf attacked from behind sinking teeth deep into our back leg. Pain exploded sharply through us.
Nyx snarled viciously before twisting around and slamming the wolf sideways. Claws tore through flesh across his chest while ribs cracked beneath the force. One final swipe ripped directly through his chest.
The rogue collapsed instantly.
As Nyx held the wolf’s heart within his claws, the third rogue leaped from behind aiming directly for our neck.
“Move!” Nyx barked.
Too late.
The rogue’s jaws nearly reached us before another massive black wolf collided into him midair.
Onyx.
Zayden’s wolf slammed into the rogue hard enough to send him crashing across the dirt before pinning him beneath massive paws.
“You’re welcome,” Zayden linked smugly.
“You couldn’t resist showing off.”
“Somebody has to carry this family.”
Nyx snorted loudly. “Honestly he might have a point.”
Traitor.
The rogue struggled violently beneath Onyx while snapping his jaws repeatedly.
“Ryker,” Zayden barked through the link. “Silver chains. Now.”
Several warriors rushed forward carrying restraints while the rogue continued fighting.
“Damn,” I muttered while shifting back into human form. “Thanks, brother.”
Zayden smirked while pulling on a pair of black pants handed over by a nearby warrior. “You’d die without me eventually.”
The remaining rogues fell quickly after that. Within minutes the battlefield quieted except for injured warriors groaning nearby and chains rattling around captured rogues.
Smoke drifted through the trees from scattered fires while healers rushed across the border checking injuries.
Ryker approached us covered in blood and dirt. 
“What the hell was this?” I asked immediately. “Any idea who organized the attack?”
“They hit all at once,” Ryker replied grimly. “Too coordinated for random rogues.”
Zayden crossed his arms. “Did you notice anything unusual?”
Ryker nodded once. “A mark. Several of them carried the same tattoo across their upper chest.”
Nyx immediately stiffened. “What kind of mark?” I asked carefully.
“Broken crown.”
Silence settled heavily around us.
Nyx growled low inside my head. “That belongs to the Rogue King.”
My jaw tightened instantly. Every warrior in the kingdom knew stories surrounding the Rogue King. Most believed he was a myth created to scare young wolves into obedience. Unfortunately, myths usually didn’t leave piles of bodies behind.
“They brand their fighters,” Nyx continued darkly. “Loyalty through fear.”
“How many survived?” I asked Ryker.
“Three.”
“Good.” Zayden’s eyes darkened coldly. “Get them into silver restraints immediately.”
Ryker nodded sharply. “We already started moving them toward the dungeons.”
I glanced back toward the battlefield once more while unease settled heavily in my chest. This wasn’t some random border raid. This was a message. And somebody out there wanted the throne badly enough to start a war for it.
“Get the prisoners secured,” I ordered coldly. “We’ll handle interrogations personally.”
