If you've tried ultrasonic flea repellers and decided they don't work, there's something you need to understand about what you bought.

I learned this the hard way.

Last spring, I spent $47 on three ultrasonic repellers from Amazon. Plugged them in, waited three weeks, and watched my two dogs get worse. More fleas. More scratching. More misery.

I left a 1-star review and went back to chemical treatments.

Three months later, my sister Rachel came over with her dog, Coco. No scratching. Shiny coat. Acting like a puppy at nine years old.

"You're still using those drops?" she asked, watching me apply Daisy's monthly treatment.

"The ultrasonic things I tried were garbage," I said.

"You tried the wrong ultrasonic," she corrected me. "That's not the same thing."

She showed me a photo on her phone. Three white devices in her living room. Different brand than what I'd bought.

"Coco hasn't had a flea in four months," she said.

That's when I started paying attention.

I'm not someone who falls for gimmicks. I've spent thousands on flea control over the years. Topical treatments, oral medications, prescription shampoos, fancy collars, fogger bombs.

Nothing worked long-term. And some of it made things worse.

Last spring, my vet told me Daisy's liver enzymes were elevated. When I told her it was just the monthly flea prevention, she got quiet.

"Those medications are hard on the liver," she finally said. "Especially at her age."

Daisy is ten. She's been with me since college. She still tries to chase squirrels but she's terrible at it. She's the best dog I've ever had.

The idea that I was slowly poisoning her just to stop the scratching made me feel sick.

But what was I supposed to do? Watch her suffer?

The fleas were destroying her. Biting her constantly. She'd scratched herself raw in three spots. Her fur was falling out. She wouldn't eat. Wouldn't play. Just laid on her bed and stared at nothing.

I tried everything the vet recommended. Then everything the internet recommended. Then things I found in random Facebook groups for desperate pet owners.

The only thing that sort of worked was the chemical treatments. But they were literally poisoning her.

So when Rachel told me she'd found something different, I wanted to believe her.

I just didn't.

"How much did you spend on yours?" I asked.

"About a hundred and twenty-five for six of them."

Six. I'd only bought three back in March.

"Why six?" I asked.

"Because you need one in every room your dog spends time in. Otherwise it doesn't work."

I felt my stomach drop.

When I'd plugged in those three cheap units, I'd only covered three rooms. Daisy and Max spend time in six different rooms throughout the day.

"So the fleas were just breeding in the other rooms?"

"Exactly," Rachel said. "That's why they kept coming back."

I'd spent $47. Waited three weeks. Watched my dogs get worse. All because I didn't have full coverage.

"But that's not even the main reason yours didn't work," Rachel said.

"There's more?"

"Yeah. The cheap ones you bought weren't designed for fleas."

I stared at her. "What do you mean? They're ultrasonic pest repellers."

"Right. Pest repellers. For roaches, mosquitoes, spiders. They're made for homeowners with general pest problems. Not pet owners fighting fleas."

She pulled up the Repellix website on her phone.

"Repellix is the only ultrasonic repeller engineered specifically for fleas and ticks," she said. "It was designed from the ground up for pet owners."

She explained it like this:

Most ultrasonic devices emit frequencies around 20-22 kilohertz. That works for large pests like roaches, rats, and mosquitoes. But fleas are tiny. Their nervous systems operate at completely different frequencies than larger pests.

"Repellix emits between 25 and 65 kilohertz," she said. "That's the exact range that disrupts flea and tick nervous systems specifically."

She showed me the Amazon listing for the units I'd bought.

"Twenty kilohertz. Fixed frequency. Designed for mosquitoes and general household pests."

"Your units were operating at the wrong frequency for fleas," she continued. "Even if you'd covered every room in your house, they wouldn't have worked. You were using a pest control device to fight a flea problem."

That hit me hard.

I'd blamed ultrasonic technology. Written a 1-star review. Told other pet owners it was a scam.

But I'd been using the wrong tool for the job the entire time.

"There's another problem with cheap ultrasonic," Rachel added. "They emit one constant frequency. Fleas adapt to it in two to three weeks. Their nervous systems adjust. Like living next to train tracks—unbearable at first, then you stop noticing."

That explained everything.

My Amazon units had seemed to work for the first week. Fewer fleas. Less scratching. Then by week three, the fleas were worse than before.

"Repellix doesn't let them adapt," she said. "The frequency shifts constantly through the 25-to-65 kilohertz range. Fleas can never adjust because there's nothing consistent to adjust to."

"And this actually works?"

"Coco hasn't had a single flea in four months," she said. "And I stopped using those chemical drops eight weeks ago."

Eight weeks without treatments.

I was still putting poison on Daisy's skin every thirty days. Watching her liver enzymes climb.

And Rachel's dog was acting like a puppy.

I went home that night and researched Repellix.

Real customer reviews, not the fake 5-star garbage on Amazon. A 60-day money-back guarantee. Over 3,000 verified pet owners with flea-free results.

I read through about twenty reviews. Most had the same story. Tried cheap ultrasonic repellers designed for general pests, they failed, decided to try Repellix as a last resort, pets were flea-free within two weeks.

One woman caught my attention. Linda. Seven cats. At her wits' end. Everyone told her to bomb her house, but she didn't want more chemicals.

She bought three Repellix units. Within a week, she started seeing results. But still had some fleas lingering.

Then she realized the problem: she'd only covered three rooms. Her cats were in more than three.

So she ordered three more units. Put them in the other rooms.

That's when the fleas disappeared completely.

"It takes about a week to see the magic begin," she wrote.

She'd also tried three other ultrasonic brands before Repellix. None of them worked. Repellix was the only one designed specifically for fleas.

I did the math.

I was spending $45/month on treatments for Daisy and Max. That's $540/year.

If these units lasted even one year, I'd save over $400. But according to their website, they last 4-5 years.

Over five years, that's $2,700 saved. And my dogs wouldn't be poisoned every month.

I ordered the 6-pack that night. $125 after some bundle discount they were running.

I didn't tell my husband. I figured I'd quietly return them when they didn't work.

The units arrived on a Wednesday. Little white plugs with blue LED lights. They looked exactly like the cheap ones I'd bought, which made me even more skeptical.

But I plugged them in anyway. Living room, kitchen, both bedrooms, bathroom, laundry room.

Nothing happened.

Thursday, nothing.

Friday morning, Daisy ate her entire breakfast for the first time in weeks.

Friday night, I realized she hadn't scratched herself all evening.

By Sunday, Max's hot spots were starting to heal.

By Wednesday—one week after I'd plugged them in—I couldn't find a single flea on either dog.

I checked everywhere. Flea comb, magnifying glass, the whole routine.

Nothing. No fleas, no flea dirt, no bites.

My husband noticed on day nine.

"They seem different. Happier. Daisy's been playing with her toys again."

I showed him the Repellix units plugged into the walls.

He stared at me. "You spent how much on plug-in air fresheners?"

"They're not air fresheners," I said. "And they worked."

That was six months ago.

Both dogs are completely flea-free. No topical treatments. No pills. No vet visits for flea-related skin infections.

Daisy's fur grew back. Max stopped hiding. They're acting like they did three years ago before the flea problem got bad.

I haven't spent a dollar on flea control since May.

Last Thursday morning I was making coffee and heard Daisy's nails clicking fast on the hardwood. I turned around and she was doing zoomies. Just running in circles for no reason except joy.

My neighbor Karen saw Daisy playing in the yard last week. First time in months Daisy's had the energy to chase anything.

"What did you do differently?" she asked.

When I told her about Repellix, she pulled out her phone and ordered the 6-pack right there. She's got two dogs and a cat.

I got a text from her five days later. "Why didn't you tell me about this sooner?"

Most people don't know the difference.

They're doing what I was doing—spending $50-$60 every month on chemicals that poison their pets. And when those don't work well enough, they try general ultrasonic repellers designed for roaches and mosquitoes.

Not fleas.

The difference with Repellix is it's the only ultrasonic system built specifically for pet owners fighting fleas and ticks.

It treats the environment, not the dog.

Fleas don't just live on your pet. They live in your carpets, couch, and baseboards. That's why they keep coming back even after you treat your dog.

Chemical treatments kill the fleas on your dog right now. But they don't touch the eggs in your carpet. The larvae under your furniture. The pupae waiting to hatch next week.

The Repellix units make your home uninhabitable for fleas at every stage of their life cycle. They can't reproduce. Can't nest. Can't complete their breeding cycle.

So they leave.

Even if a flea hitchhikes in on your dog after a walk, it can't reproduce in a treated space. The infestation stops at the source.

You need coverage in every room your pets spend time in.

That's why Rachel bought six. That's why I bought six. That's why Karen ordered six immediately.

One unit per room minimum. Otherwise you're just creating flea-free zones and the fleas move between them.

If you're still using chemical treatments every month, if your dog is still scratching and uncomfortable and losing fur, if you've tried cheap ultrasonic repellers and written them off as a scam like I did, please give Repellix a try.

It's not the same as what you tried before.

“We Got You Covered.”👑

A fake toy site took $1,100 from a mom I know. I almost used the same one.

She was trying to spend $45.

So was I.

We were both trying to buy the same thing. A squishy advent calendar.

I want to tell you how I got that close, because if you have a kid in elementary school right now, you might be closer than you think.

Ellie is 8. She asked for one thing this Christmas.

One.

A squishy advent calendar.

If you have a kid her age, you know why. Squishies are all anyone in third grade talks about. And the ones she loves most are the dumplings.

Soft little dumplings with faces. You squeeze one flat in your fist, open your hand, and it slowly comes back.

She has two. She got them months apart. She treats them like pets.

So when she heard there was a calendar with a squishy behind every door, that was the whole list. She wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it to the fridge.

I thought, great. One present. Easy year.

It was September.

I went to buy the famous one. The big-brand calendar every kid knows.

Sold out.

There was a button. "Request an invitation."

An invitation. To pay for a toy.

I clicked it on September 16th. I checked my email every morning for two weeks.

Other moms got theirs. I watched them post about it.

I got nothing.

So I tried the stores. A mom told me one of them puts new stock out at opening. I was at the door at 7:00 on a Saturday.

The man at the service desk didn't even look up. "Gone. Sold before seven."

I went back the next Saturday. Gone.

Then I looked at the resale listings.

$110. $125. $140.

For a forty-dollar box of toys.

And the people who beat me to the shelf were the same people selling it back to me.

I wasn't going to pay a scalper triple. I couldn't make myself do it.

That's when I found the site.

It had the famous calendar. In stock. $45.

It looked exactly right. The logo. The photos. The same red box.

It was 11 at night. I had my card out. I'd typed the first eight numbers.

What stopped me was Ellie. She'd come down for water. She looked at my screen and said, "Mom, is that the real one?"

I opened my mouth, and I didn't know.

I shut the laptop and took her back to bed.

Two days later, a mom in my group posted.

Same site.

She'd tried to spend $45. They took $1,100. Nothing ever came.

I read her post standing in my kitchen, and my hands went cold.

Eight numbers. That's how close I was.

I check three things now, before my card goes anywhere near a toy site.

If every store is sold out and one website has the famous brand in stock, I ask why.

I look for a real guarantee, written down, with a number of days on it.

And I look for a way to reach an actual person.

That site had none of the three. I just hadn't looked.

Another mom did get a box from a different site. The squishies inside were hard as rocks.

And then a squishy dumpling toy sold online got recalled.

So those were my choices. Pay a scalper triple. Bet my card on a website. Or look at my eight-year-old and tell her the one thing on her list wasn't coming.

I kept asking myself the same question.

How does a mother stand there with money in her hand and still can't buy her kid a toy?

My neighbor answered it over the fence, in about ten seconds.

She has a daughter a year older than Ellie. I told her everything. The invitation. The store. The site.

She let me finish. Then she said, "Does Ellie want that box? Or does she want dumplings?"

I said she'd take dumplings over anything on earth.

"Then you've been fighting half the country for a logo."

I didn't say anything.

Because that was it. That was the whole reason I couldn't buy it. Every parent, every scalper, every thief with a fake website was lined up around one box with one name on it.

And my kid had never once asked for the name.

My neighbor went inside and came back with a box of her own. It had landed on her porch four days earlier.

An advent calendar. Twenty-four doors.

Behind every one, a squishy dumpling. Each one dressed for Christmas. Santa hats. Reindeer antlers. Little winter beanies.

No stickers. No filler. Only the thing Ellie loves.

She'd already opened one door to check it. I don't blame her.

"Pick it up," she said.

It filled my palm. I squeezed it flat, opened my hand, and counted.

It came back slow and soft, like it was waking up.

I did it six more times. She had to take it off me.

Then I did what that month had taught me to do. I went looking for the catch.

Was it in stock? Yes. No invitation. No line. A plain button that said add to cart.

Was it a pre-order that shows up in January? No. Hers had come in a week.

Was it tested? Safety tested to US toy standards, ages 3 and up.

And if it turned up and it was junk?

Ninety-day money-back guarantee.

I read that twice. Ninety days meant Ellie could open all 24 doors, and I could still send it back after Christmas.

A fake site doesn't give you ninety days. A scalper doesn't give you ninety seconds.

And I was holding the real thing in my hand, in a kitchen I'd been in a hundred times.

I ordered it right there.

It took about ninety seconds. After a month.

It came in a week. A real box, 24 doors, every one shut.

I was going to hide it until December 1st.

I lasted four days.

On Saturday morning I put it on the kitchen table and told her she could open one door. One. The rest wait for December.

Ellie stopped in the doorway.

She's eight. She knows the famous box. She knew right away this wasn't it.

I held my breath.

She opened door one.

A dumpling in a Santa hat dropped into her hand.

She squeezed it flat and watched it come back.

Then she looked at the 23 other doors.

"Wait. Are they ALL dumplings?"

I said every single one.

She screamed. A real scream. The dog left the room.

She has not said the name of the other calendar since.

The box lives on top of the fridge now, where she can see it and can't reach it. She says good night to it.

The dumpling from door one goes to school in her coat pocket. Three girls have asked where she got it.

"I said my mom found it."

I'll take that.

A couple of honest things.

It isn't the famous one. If your kid wants that exact logo on the box, this isn't it.

And you will be asked every single day if it's December yet.

But I spent a month chasing a box she would have liked, and I came eight numbers away from handing my card to a thief.

I spent ninety seconds buying the one she screamed for.

Ellie is eight. I don't know how many more Christmases one box can do that.

Picture December 1st at your house.

The box is already on the table. Nobody stood in a line for it. Nobody's card got stolen.

And somebody small is holding a dumpling in both hands, staring at 23 more doors.

This is the one:

👉 https://trysoothe.shop/products/squishy-dumplings-christmas-special-advent-calendar

Please use that link. Don't search for it and click whatever comes up. I've seen where that goes.

One calendar is $44. No invitation needed.

If you're buying for more than one kid, buy two and the third calendar is free. That's three for $88, which is less than the scalpers wanted for one.

Every order also comes with a bonus mystery dumpling. I'm hiding ours for Christmas morning.

Don't do what I did and think there's time.

I've watched squishy calendars sell out since September, and it gets worse every week closer to December. This one was in stock when I ordered. I can't promise it will be when you read this.

And it takes about a week to arrive, so it has to be ordered before the first.

P.S. To have it for December 1st, order by November 18th.

P.P.S. The guarantee is 90 days from delivery. She can open every door and you're still covered after Christmas.

bodyText:
Please STOP refilling your cat's water bowl.

I know that sounds INSANE coming from a vet.

But after 11 years in emergency animal care, I finally understand something that most vets won't say out loud.

A full water bowl does NOT mean a hydrated cat.

Let me explain.

If your cat's water bowl sits full at the end of the day, please stop what you're doing and read this.

Because what I'm about to tell you could save your cat's life this summer.

Oliver changed everything for me.

Saturday afternoon. 78 degrees outside. My phone rings. 

Emergency call.

I drove to the clinic expecting the usual. Toxic ingestion. 

Trauma. Or hopefully something we could stabilize quickly.

Instead, a man rushes through the doors carrying a carrier with a cat lying limp inside it.

Oliver. 4 years old. Orange tabby. Perfect health his entire life according to his records.

Now lying on his side. Completely unresponsive.

I took one look at his gums. White. Dry. Signs of severe dehydration and heat shock.

We rushed him into the back. Started IV fluids. Began emergency cooling.

When I checked his internal temperature, I felt my stomach drop.

107.4 degrees. Normal for a cat is 101.5. At 106, organs start to shut down.

I walked back to the waiting room where Oliver's owner was sitting.

He stood up before I could say anything.

"Is he going to be okay? Please. He was FINE this morning. I don't understand. I feed him good food. I take him to the vet every year. I put fresh water in his bowl every single morning. Every morning, Doctor."

He was shaking.

"He was just lying in the sunroom. That's his spot. He naps there every afternoon. The window was cracked. His water bowl was right there. It was completely full."

I tried to steady my voice.

"We're doing everything we can. He's critical. His organs are shutting down from the heat."

He shook his head like he was trying to wake up from something.

"That's... no. That's not possible. He was inside. He was in the shade. He had water. His bowl was RIGHT THERE."

I nodded. "I know. That's exactly the problem."

He stared at me like I'd lost my mind.

"What do you mean that's the problem? He had access to water the entire time."

I didn't have time to explain yet. We worked on Oliver for five hours. IV fluids. Cooling blankets. Monitoring every organ. His kidneys were failing. His liver was shutting down.

We saved Oliver. Barely. Two days in the ICU. His kidneys took months to recover.

He was one of the lucky ones.

When his owner came back for the follow-up a week later, I sat down across from him.

I leaned forward.

"Marcus, can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"In the weeks before this happened, had Oliver been drinking less water? Or acting strange around his bowl?"

His face changed.

"Actually... yeah. For the past month or so he kept jumping on the bathroom counter and pawing at the faucet. I thought it was cute. He'd just stare at the sink until I turned it on. But his bowl was full downstairs so I figured he was just being a cat."

I nodded slowly. I've heard this exact story so many times I could recite it from memory.

"Do you have his water bowl with you like I asked?"

He looked confused. "Yeah, I wasn't sure why you wanted it."

He reached into his bag and pulled out a ceramic bowl. Nice one. The expensive kind from the pet store.

From across the room, it looked perfectly clean.

I took it from him and ran my finger along the inside.

Slimy.

Not visible slime. Not the pink stuff you sometimes see after a few days. Just that slight film you feel when you touch it.

I held up my finger.

"Do you feel this?"

He ran his finger along the rim and nodded. "I don't see anything though."

"You can't see it. But you can feel it. And more importantly, Oliver could smell it."

"What is it?"

"It's called biofilm. It's a layer of bacteria that forms on any surface in contact with standing water. Starts forming within hours of pouring fresh water in."

Marcus stared at the bowl in my hands.

"But I rinse it every day when I refill it."

"I know you do. That's the problem."

I put the bowl down on the exam table.

"Here's what nobody tells cat owners. Biofilm doesn't just sit on the surface. It embeds into microscopic scratches in the material. Ceramic has them. Stainless steel has them. Plastic is the worst."

"So when I rinse it..."

"You disturb the surface layer. But the bacteria in those tiny grooves survive. And they repopulate the entire bowl within hours. Within six hours, they form a protective shell around themselves. A fortress. 800 times more resistant to disinfection than free-floating bacteria."

Marcus shook his head slowly.

"So every time I refilled his bowl..."

"He was smelling contamination you couldn't see. Cats have around 200 million scent receptors. Their sense of smell is 14 times stronger than yours. Oliver could detect things in that water you would never see, taste, or know exist. So he barely drank. A few laps here and there. Just enough to survive. Never enough to actually stay hydrated."

"For how long?"

"Probably weeks. Maybe longer. And here's what that means for a cat in summer. Their cooling system is already fragile. Cats can't sweat like humans. They rely on grooming, seeking cool surfaces, and internal hydration to regulate temperature. If Oliver had been running at 60 or 70 percent hydration because the water smelled wrong to him, his cooling system was already compromised before summer even started."

He put his hand over his face.

"So when he was lying in the sunroom that afternoon..."

"78 degrees. Sun coming through the glass. His body tried to cool down and there was nothing left to cool with. Temperature spiked. Organs started cooking from the inside. Kidneys. Liver. Brain. In that order. And the whole time, his bowl was full. Sitting right there. Looking perfectly fine to your eyes."

He was quiet for a long time.

"He was telling me. The faucet thing. He was telling me he wanted different water."

"Yes. He was."

After Marcus left, I sat in my office for a long time.

This case wasn't unusual.

I see this exact pattern every single summer.

Cat stops drinking as much. Owner thinks they're just being finicky. Maybe notices them pawing at the faucet or drinking from the shower floor but doesn't think much of it. Refills the bowl more often. Maybe scrubs it harder.

Weeks go by. The cat gets chronically dehydrated. Not enough to show obvious signs. Just enough to drain their only buffer against the heat completely.

Then one warm afternoon. Not even a particularly hot one. A sunny window. A warm room. A car ride that took ten minutes too long.

And their body tries to cool down but there's nothing left to cool with. Temperature spikes. Organs start shutting down.

And the owner sits across from me saying the exact same words.

"His bowl was full. I had no idea."

I've heard it 47 times in the last three summers. 47 cats through my ER with heatstroke. Most of them didn't make it.

And I'm tired of it.

About 2 years ago, I started doing something different.

Every owner who came in with a heatstroke case, I asked them to bring their cat's water bowl.

Bowl after bowl after bowl.

Every single one had that film.

And every single owner said the same thing.

"But I put fresh water in it every day."

So I started digging into the research.

What I found changed everything.

I collected 87 water bowls from patients' homes over six months. Stainless steel, ceramic, plastic, glass. It didn't matter. 

I sent them to an independent lab for analysis.

And here's the part that made my stomach drop.

81 out of 87 bowls tested positive for significant biofilm contamination. Bowls that looked perfectly clean. Bowls that had been rinsed or scrubbed that same morning. Bowls that owners swore were spotless.

Scrubbing doesn't eliminate it. Biofilm embeds into microscopic scratches in the surface material.

You can kill the top layer, but the colonies in those grooves survive. They repopulate the entire surface within hours.

And scrubbing actually makes it worse. It creates MORE microscopic scratches for biofilm to hide in. Every time you scrub, you're carving tiny grooves into the bowl surface. Those grooves become permanent homes for bacterial colonies.

Bowls are designed for standing water.

Standing water is designed for biofilm.

But here's the part nobody talks about.

That biofilm shell doesn't just protect the bacteria. It traps everything else flowing through your tap water. Chlorine byproducts. Heavy metals. Sediment. All the invisible contaminants in your pipes get captured inside that bacterial fortress.

Building up. Getting stronger. Hour after hour. Refill after refill.

You refill the bowl and think you're giving fresh water. You're actually pouring fresh water on top of a living bacterial fortress that's been building for weeks.

And here's what breaks my heart.

Your cat already knows something is wrong.

Cats have around 200 million scent receptors. They can detect illness in other animals. They can sense changes in atmospheric pressure before a storm.

So what do you think they smell in that contaminated bowl?

Danger.

That's why your cat takes two laps and walks away.

That's why they jump on the counter and paw at the faucet.

That's why they drink from the shower floor or try to lick condensation off windows.

Their instincts are telling them to find moving water. In the wild, standing water meant contamination. Moving water meant safety. That instinct never left them.

But most owners see this and think their cat is just being finicky.

So they refill the bowl and assume their cat will drink when they're thirsty enough.

Meanwhile, the cat drinks less and less.

And the dehydration starts building silently.

Chronic low-grade dehydration drains your cat's only defense against the heat. Their cooling system runs on internal hydration. Every day they under-drink, that buffer gets thinner.

And here's what terrifies me.

Cats can suffer fatal heatstroke indoors. A sunny window. A warm room with poor airflow. A carrier left in a car for five minutes while you run into the vet's office. It doesn't take a hot day. It takes a dehydrated cat on a warm one.

By the time you notice anything wrong, a limp body, unresponsiveness, it's already a life-or-death emergency.

The margin between slightly dehydrated and dead shrinks to nothing once summer arrives.

And you won't know until it's too late. Because the whole time, their bowl was full. Sitting right there. Looking perfectly fine to your eyes.

That's what happened to Oliver.

His owner did everything right.

Fresh water every morning. Clean bowl. Premium food. Regular vet visits.

But for weeks, Oliver was refusing to drink enough because the water smelled wrong to him. His hydration was draining day by day. And his cooling system was running on a tank that was almost empty.

By the time he settled into his sunny spot on an 78-degree afternoon, there was nothing protecting him from what happened next.

Oliver survived. Barely.

But his kidneys took months to recover. He spent two days in the ICU with cooling blankets and IV fluids.

His owner told me at the last checkup: "I think about all those times I saw the full bowl and felt reassured. I can't unsee it now."

That sentence haunts me.

Because I should have known sooner. I'm the vet. I went to school for this. I studied heatstroke and dehydration extensively.

But nobody ever taught me about biofilm in water bowls. 

Nobody ever connected a full water bowl to a cat that isn't drinking. Nobody told me to look at the bowl as the reason, not the solution.

So after Oliver, I started researching everything I could find.

I read veterinary journals. Microbiology studies. Water safety protocols from research universities.

I needed to understand if there was any way to actually prevent biofilm formation.

That's when I found a study from UC Davis that changed everything.

Researchers identified three specific conditions that prevent biofilm from forming in the first place.

Condition one: Water has to move constantly.

Biofilm needs stillness to anchor. If water never stops circulating, bacteria can't build their fortress. They need those first few hours of still water to establish colonies.

Condition two: Active filtration.

Not a passive filter that saturates. But active circulation through material that captures contaminants before they can accumulate. Starve the bacteria of what they need and they can't colonize.

Condition three: Continuous dilution.

Fresh water introduced continuously so bacterial concentration never builds enough to form the protective shell.

All three. Simultaneously. Without interruption.

The problem is, no cat bowl can do any of this.

Bowls are designed for standing water. Standing water is where biofilm thrives.

So I started looking at fountains instead.

And I immediately hit another wall.

I ordered nine different pet fountains. Every brand with good reviews. Every price point from budget to premium.

Within three weeks, every single one had problems.

Mold growing inside the pump housing. Slime building up in crevices I couldn't reach. Plastic parts scratching and harboring bacteria just like bowls do.

The pumps sat submerged in the water, which meant they became contamination sources themselves.

One fountain looked crystal clear on the surface. But when I took apart the pump to inspect it, the inside was coated in black slime.

That slime was being circulated into the water my cats were drinking.

It was no better than a bowl. In some ways it was worse.

And here's what I noticed. My cats would use a new fountain for about a week, maybe two. Then one day they'd just stop. 

Walk past it and go back to pawing at the faucet. The fountain looked fine to my eyes. But their noses had already detected what mine couldn't.

I was about to give up.

The UC Davis study told me what needed to happen. But nothing on the market was designed around those three conditions. Every fountain was designed to look nice on a kitchen floor and move water in a circle. That's it.

Then I started searching for anyone who had actually found something that worked.

I found a Facebook group for cat owners dealing with dehydration and heat-related issues. Over 9,000 members. All dealing with the same worry and confusion.

I scrolled through the posts.

"My cat has water right there. Full bowl. She just won't drink from it."

"The vet says keep her hydrated but she barely touches her water."

"I've tried everything to get her to drink more. She just walks away."

Hundreds of comments. Thousands. All saying the same thing.

Then I found a thread that stopped me cold.

A woman named Patricia had posted about her 7-year-old cat who had collapsed from heatstroke the previous summer after lying near a window. The vet said if it happened again, there was nothing they could do. She was terrified of every summer since.

Two years later. He was still alive. Still healthy. Drinking more water than he ever had in his life.

Everyone was asking what she did differently.

Her answer:

"I stopped buying cheap fountains from Amazon. They all grow biofilm because they use cheap materials. The steel scratches. The plastic holds bacteria. The pumps grow mold inside. And most of them only circulate water on the surface while it sits stagnant in the reservoir. My cat would use them for a week and then stop. Now I know why."

Someone asked what she used instead.

"There's only one fountain I've found that actually stays clean. It's called Selene. Uses food-grade stainless steel. Same grade they use in hospital equipment. Non-porous at the molecular level so bacteria literally can't grip the surface."

I searched for other mentions of Selene in the group.

Post after post after post.

"Finally found a fountain my cat will actually use long term."

"Three months in, still no biofilm. I check every week because I'm paranoid."

"My cat went from barely touching his bowl to emptying this thing throughout the day. Going into summer feeling safe for the first time."

"I wasted $200 on Amazon fountains before finding this. Wish I'd known sooner."

A vet tech had commented on one thread:

"We recommend Selene at our clinic now. It's the only fountain we've seen that actually prevents biofilm instead of just delaying it."

I ordered one that night.

When it arrived, the first thing I noticed was the weight.

Heavy. Solid. Nothing like the flimsy plastic fountains I'd been testing in my office.

I ran my finger along the inside. Smooth. Really smooth. Not the rough texture of cheap steel.

I set it up in my kitchen.

I have two cats. Milo is a 9-year-old Maine Coon who barely drinks. I worry about him every summer. Luna is a 5-year-old domestic shorthair who's always been a faucet drinker. I wanted to test how they'd both respond.

Day one, Luna was drinking from it within an hour. Cats that already seek running water take to it immediately.

Day two, Milo investigated. Watched the water move. Sniffed it carefully.

Day three, Milo drank.

Really drank.

I stood there watching him drink for a solid 20 seconds without stopping. I hadn't seen him do that in years. Usually it was three quick laps and he was gone.

By day five, they were both using it multiple times a day. Luna stopped jumping on the bathroom counter entirely.

Here's what I was waiting for. Day seven. Day ten. Day fourteen.

The point where every other fountain failed. The point where my cats had always walked away.

I ran my finger along the inside.

Smooth. Clean. No film.

Week two, I noticed Milo had more energy. He was following me around the house again. Playing with toys he'd ignored for months.

Week three, his coat started looking different. Shinier. Softer. 

The dull, dry texture he'd had for years was going away.

Week four, I ran my finger along the inside again.

Nothing.

The steel surface stayed clean. The water never stopped moving. Biofilm never had a chance to form.

For the first time in my career, I had something I could actually recommend with confidence.

I started recommending it to the cats I was most worried about heading into summer. The chronic under-drinkers. The cats like Oliver.

Not all of them trusted it immediately. Cats that have learned to avoid contaminated water are suspicious of anything new.

But within a week or two, they all came around.

And then the same pattern I saw with Milo started showing up everywhere.

Week one, owners would tell me their cat was finally drinking. 

Actually going to the fountain multiple times a day instead of taking a few laps from the bowl and walking away.

Week two, the energy came back. Cats that had been sleeping all day were following their owners around again. Playing. 

Getting excited about things.

Week three, the coats improved. Shinier. Softer. One owner told me she thought her cat was "aging backwards."

Week four and beyond, I stopped dreading summer.

Cats that had been chronically under-drinking for months were finally properly hydrated. Their cooling systems had what they needed. Their bodies had a buffer again.

I ran a trial with 22 of my patients who were chronic under-drinkers. Cats their owners described as finicky with water.

Within 60 days, 20 out of 22 showed measurable increases in daily water intake. The average increase was 67 percent.

Sixty-seven percent more water. From cats their owners swore just weren't big drinkers.

One owner sent me a video of her cat sitting at the Selene fountain drinking calmly for over a minute. She was crying. She said she'd never seen him drink like that in eight years.

He wasn't finicky. He was thirsty. For eight years.

One owner called me after a heat wave in July.

"Dr. Mitchell, it hit 98 degrees this weekend. The AC went out for a few hours. I was panicking. But he just kept going back to the fountain and drinking. He was fine. Completely fine. Last summer I would have been rushing to your ER."

"That's what proper hydration looks like."

She was quiet for a moment.

"Last summer I was terrified to even open the blinds on a sunny day."

"I know."

Now I recommend Selene to every client.

Not just the cats I'm worried about.

Every single cat owner who walks into my practice.

Because by the time a cat collapses from heatstroke, most of the damage has already happened. Prevention is the only thing that actually works.

Here's what I tell every owner who sits across from me.

"Go home tonight. Pick up your cat's water bowl. Don't look at it. Touch it. Run your finger along the inside."

"If it feels even slightly slimy, that's biofilm."

"Your cat has been smelling it for days. Maybe weeks. That's why they're drinking less. That's why they sit at the faucet or drink from the shower floor instead."

"They're not being finicky. They're trying to tell you something is wrong."

If your cat has been avoiding their water bowl...

If you've noticed them pawing at the faucet or drinking from the shower floor...

If you've been refilling it every day hoping they'll eventually drink more...

If you've tried fountains that worked for a few days and then got ignored...

If summer is coming and you're not sure your cat is actually drinking enough to stay safe...

Please don't ignore it.

Here's where I got the water fountain:

👉 https://selenepets.com/products/the-kitty-fountain%E2%84%A2

It's what I use for my own cats. It's what I've been recommending for over a year now.

They're running a summer sale right now. $70 off. And they back every fountain with a 1-year guarantee. If your cat doesn't drink more, full refund. No questions asked.

I've never seen another pet company stand behind their product like that.

I've watched 47 cats come through my ER with heatstroke in the last three summers. Most of them didn't make it.

Every single one had a full water bowl at home.

I've had too many conversations that started with "his bowl was right there, Doctor."

I don't want to have that conversation about your cat.

If this reaches one person before their cat collapses on an 78-degree afternoon, then writing this was worth it.

Please don't wait for the emergency to find out.

Dr. Sarah Mitchell, DVM
11 years in emergency veterinary medicine

P.S. I spent over two thousand dollars on nine different fountains over two years before I understood why they all failed. The water moved on the surface but sat stagnant in the reservoir. Biofilm formed in the hidden places. Your cat's nose found it before you ever could. The problem isn't fountains. The problem is fountains that aren't designed to keep ALL the water moving. Cats that collapse in August get dehydrated in May. The countdown is already happening. Every day your cat avoids that bowl, the margin between slightly dehydrated and dead gets thinner. Your cat knows the difference. Their nose doesn't lie.
title: STOP refilling your cat’s water bowl

bodyText:
Wolves don't get allergies.

They roll in the same grass. They breathe the same pollen. They sleep in the same dirt. They don't scratch themselves raw. They don't get hot spots. They don't get an ear infection every six weeks.

Your dog does.

And you've been told that's just how some dogs are. That certain breeds are "prone to allergies." That it's genetic and you manage it.

A shelter vet told me why wild dogs don't get this and our indoor dogs do. The answer had nothing to do with Apoquel, a higher dose, food switches, or medicated shampoo.

And it explained why I spent $8,247 over four years on a dog who was never getting better. Not for one single day of it.

My name is Deborah. I'm sixty-two, retired, and I live outside Raleigh with my husband Ray and our two Golden Retrievers, Cooper and Millie.

Cooper is seven now.

He spent four of the best years of his life scratching.

And I almost let the same thing happen to Millie.

Let me tell you what happened.

Because if your dog is scratching and the medication isn't holding anymore, you need to read this.

It started with Cooper.

He was the sweetest dog I've ever known. The kind who leans his whole body weight against your legs and just stands there being held.

He started scratching at 2.

Paw licking first. Then the rust stains on his front paws. Then the head shaking and that yeasty corn-chip smell coming out of his ears.

It went quiet over the winter and I told myself it was seasonal. It came back in the spring worse. Then it stopped going quiet at all.

I took him in.

First visit was $312. A scrape and a swab.

"Environmental allergies. Common in Goldens. We can manage this."

I asked how long.

"Most likely his whole life."

Read that sentence again.

So we started him on Apoquel. 16mg, half a tablet twice a day. The first bottle was $94.86.

Every morning I wrapped it in a square of cheddar so he'd take it. Then I washed my hands.

And it worked. It was a miracle. The scratching stopped almost completely. He slept through the night, and so did I.

For about 3 months.

Then it crept back. The vet said he just needed a higher dose. So half a tablet twice a day became a full tablet twice a day.

The bottle went from $94.86 to $158.

Six weeks. Then it came back exactly where it had been.

We added Cytopoint. $200 every six weeks.

The scratching would calm down and then return. Calm down and return.

Over the next four years I watched Cooper slowly disappear.

He stopped playing with his toys. He stopped meeting us at the door. He stopped leaning on my legs. Stopped doing the things that made him Cooper.

And the hardest part was how young he was. By two, he should've been running around the house, bringing us his toys, begging to play, and getting excited every time we grabbed the leash.

 Instead, most days he just lay there licking and chewing his paws.

He started pulling away when I put my hand on his back. I thought he was sore.

Then the skin. It got thicker and darker in patches. The medication couldn't keep up anymore. The scratching broke through no matter what we did.

One Tuesday, I walked into the kitchen and there was blood on the rug.

He had chewed his front paw down to the skin in the night. He'd been at himself in the dark for hours while we slept upstairs.

I sat down on the floor next to my dog and cried.

By year four, Cooper was on:

Apoquel. $158 a bottle.

Cytopoint. $200 every six weeks.

Prescription food. $89.

Vet visits. Antibiotics every time his ears flared up again.

$8,247.

And he was still lying on my kitchen floor with a paw he'd chewed open in the night.

He was six years old.

Two to six. That’s the whole young part of a dog’s life. And Cooper spent it scratching, chewing his paws, and dealing with his skin.

No playing fetch in the yard because he’d chew his paw open again. No long walks without worrying he’d come home licking. Half the time, he didn’t even want to get up and play.

I have one video of Cooper running around with a stick, from before any of this started. That’s the only video I have of my dog just being a dog.

Then Millie started scratching at 2.

Same breed. Same age it started.

I panicked.

I was not putting Millie on Apoquel. Not after watching Cooper spend four years on it and still scratch. I wasn't doing that all over again.

So I tried everything the Facebook groups recommended. Fish oil. Grain-free food. Medicated shampoo. Highly rated probiotics from Amazon.

I spent hundreds of dollars over six months.

Nothing worked. The scratching got worse. Hot spots started coming up on her side. Her ears smelled sour every few weeks and I'd catch her shaking her head in the hallway at night.

The vet pushed Apoquel again.

"At this point we need to get the inflammation under control. It's progressing."

I sat in the parking lot after that appointment and cried.

Because I'd heard those exact words before. About Cooper. Right before the four years, $8,247, and a dog who never got better.

A few weeks later, I had to go back to the rescue where I'd adopted Millie to drop off some donations.

While I was in the lobby, Millie started scratching. Hard. That frantic, full-body scratch where her back leg goes so fast it's a blur and you can hear her nails on her skin from across the room.

A woman in scrubs came over.

"How long has she been doing that?"

"About a year. We've tried everything."

Her face changed.

"Come with me."

Her name was Dr. Ellen Barrow. She'd run the medical side of that shelter for eleven years.

I told her all of it. Cooper. The Apoquel. The dose going up. The injections getting closer together. The four years. Millie starting the same way. The probiotics that hadn't changed anything. The vet pushing medication.

She listened without interrupting once.

When I finished, she leaned forward.

"I'm going to tell you something that's going to change how you think about this entirely."

I nodded.

"Wolves don't get allergies."

I blinked.

"What?"

"Have you ever seen a wolf scratching itself raw? A coyote with hot spots? A wild dog with a chronic ear infection?"

I hadn't.

"No. Because it isn't normal. It isn't something dogs just get. It's a sign that something underneath isn't working right."

"And in a dog who's been at it this long, it's never one problem."

"It's THREE. And they're feeding each other."

She pulled a sheet of paper from her desk and drew a quick diagram.

"The first problem is her gut."

She drew a circle at the top of the page.

"About 73% of your dog's immune system lives in her gut. And it's kept calm by specific bacteria whose only job is to tell her body to calm down. That everything is fine."

"In the wild, dogs eat their prey whole. Muscle, organs, all of that is loaded with bacteria. A wolf eating a rabbit is swallowing billions of live bacteria with every single meal. Their immune system stays calm their entire life."

"Your dog eats processed food. Even the premium brands. And there is no live bacteria in processed dog food. It's all been stripped out during manufacturing."

"So your dog never gets the steady supply of bacteria a wild dog gets from its food."

"So nobody is telling the body anything. And the immune system panics."

"At pollen. At dust. At the grass in your own backyard."

"It panics by sending out a signal. That signal is what makes a dog scratch."

"And that signal is the one thing Apoquel is built to stop. It blocks it from getting through, and it's very good at it."

"But it never reaches the gut."

"The bacteria are still missing. The immune system is still panicking. The signal is still being made, every hour of every day."

"Apoquel just stops him from feeling it."

"And a panicking immune system doesn't get quieter over time. It gets louder. So the signal comes harder every month, and the same tablet holds less of it back."

I stopped her there.

"I tried four brands of probiotics with Cooper. Two with Millie. Nothing happened."

"I know. And it isn't the chews. A chew is only how you get it into her."

She tapped the circle again.

"A probiotic works on this. Only this one. And even if it works perfectly, your dog has two more problems, and nothing in that probiotic chew touches either of them."

She drew a second circle underneath the first.

"Her nerves."

"After years of itching and scratching and licking, the nerves in the skin physically change. They start overreacting."

"Picture someone screaming in your ear every day for four years. Eventually a whisper makes you flinch."

"That's what happened to your dog. His nerves had been hearing itch, itch, itch for so long that they stopped waiting for a reason. A breeze would set him off. The carpet. His collar."

"And none of that was an allergy anymore. It was nerves that had got too loud. And nothing you were ever given was aimed at them. Not the Apoquel. Not the injections. Not the elimination diets."

Then she drew a third circle.

"The third problem is her skin."

"Healthy skin is a brick wall. Ceramides are the mortar holding it together."

"Your dog's mortar had been dissolving for years."

"So gaps open."

"And two things move into those gaps. Staph and yeast."

"Once they're through, they start their own itch. A completely different signal. One Apoquel doesn't block at all."

"That's the hot spots. That's the brown gunk in his ears. That's the corn-chip smell on his paws."

Then she drew arrows between the three circles.

"Now look what they do to each other."

"The gaps in her skin let more allergens through. So the gut panics harder."

"The gut panicking harder means more signal. So the nerves fire more."

"More firing means more scratching. And more scratching means bigger gaps."

"And then it starts over, worse than the time before."

She put the pen down.

"And Apoquel is standing in front of one door, holding it shut, while the pressure behind it climbs."

I didn't say anything.

"That's why it worked for three months and then didn't," she said.

"Every dollar you spent was aimed at one problem. Nobody ever touched what was piling up behind it."

I felt like the floor dropped out.

"So for four years he was never actually getting better."

"No."

"I paid eight thousand dollars for three good months."

She didn't correct me.

She didn't have to.

"So what do I do?"

"To stop the loop, you have to do three things at the same time."

She wrote them down.

REFILL THE GUT — Put back the exact bacteria she's missing, alive, so the immune system stops panicking and the signal stops being made in the first place.

CALM THE NERVES — Turn down nerve endings that have grown too sensitive, so a breeze and the carpet and your own hand stop registering as an itch.

REBUILD THE WALL — Close the gaps, so allergens can't get in and the staph and the yeast have nowhere left to live.

"Miss even one of these," she said, "and you're wasting money and time your dog doesn't have."

She grabbed a pouch from the shelf behind her.

"This is what I give every dog that comes through this shelter. It's the only one I found that goes after all three at once."

Floof. Salmon based chews.

I read the label four times.

For the gut — It has ten billion live bacteria, built around the two strains an itchy dog is missing. They move into a gut that's been running without them for years and start calming the immune system down.

And they arrive alive, because the strain it's built around is spore-forming. The bacteria sit sealed inside a natural protective shell, so they survive the heat of manufacturing and the acid in the stomach, and only wake up once they reach the gut.

For the nerves — it uses a compound called PEA. It calms the inflammatory cells surrounding the nerve endings, so they stop keeping those nerves on constant high alert. They stop turning every little thing into an urge to scratch.

For the skin — It uses phytosphingosine, which gives the skin the raw material to remake the fatty mortar between the cells. As that mortar fills back in, the wall closes. Allergens and yeast stay out. And once the wall closes, the gut stops being flooded, and the whole loop stops turning.

I asked, "Why didn't anyone tell me about this?"

"Because there's a lot more money in managing this than there is in fixing what's underneath it. Every flare means another prescription, another injection, another infection to treat, another visit. A simple chew that keeps your dog out of that cycle doesn't make nearly as much money."

I said the number out loud to her. $8,247.

She just nodded. Like she'd heard it before.

She handed me two pouches.

"On the house. Salmon flavoured, she'll love it."

I started them both that night.

For Millie. The first two weeks, nothing changed. She was still scratching. Still getting the occasional hot spot.

I was terrified it wasn't going to work.

Then around week three, I noticed something.

The paw licking had stopped. Completely.

Week four. No new hot spots. The existing ones were drying up.

Week five, her ears were clean. I checked them every morning out of habit, I kept expecting the brown gunk and the sour smell. Pink. Clean. I checked again the next day, and the next.

I called Ray into the bathroom.

"Look at her ears."

He looked. "They're... normal?"

"They're normal."

Week six. I realized I hadn't heard her scratch in days.

She slept through the night. Every night. No collar jingling at 3 AM. No licking. Just breathing.

Cooper took about three weeks longer.

Around week nine, he stopped chewing his paws.

Then his ears cleared. And stayed clear.

A few weeks later, Ray called me to the kitchen window.

Cooper was outside running around with a stick in his mouth.

I hadn't seen him do that since before all of this started.

That was six months ago.

Today Cooper is seven. Millie is three.

Neither of them is spending their days scratching, chewing their paws, or dealing with another ear flare.

No Apoquel. No Cytopoint in my house.

They're playing again. Sleeping through the night. Getting excited when we grab the leash.

They're just dogs again.

I think about the four years Cooper spent scratching.

I think about the $8,247 I spent trying to help him while he kept getting worse.

And I think about how close I came to filling that prescription for Millie.

If I hadn't driven out to that shelter. If Dr. Barrow hadn't been on that morning. If Millie hadn't scratched right there in the lobby.

I never would've figured it out at all. I would've kept filling prescriptions, treating the next flare, and watching her scratch until the day it was time to say goodbye.

So if your dog is scratching and the medication isn't holding, listen to me.

One problem is never the problem.

Every medication is aimed at one problem out of the three your dog has. That's why it works at the start. And that's why it stops.

The other two keep building underneath until they get loud enough to come through anyway.

And don't make the mistake I made and assume a probiotic chew means you're covering all three.

The chew isn't the problem. What's inside it is.

I wasted months on those while Millie kept scratching.

Nothing holds unless all three get fixed at the same time. That's why I use Floof.

Count the nights she doesn't wake you.

They give you the full 60 days to try it, and if you don't see a difference, they'll refund you.

You are risking nothing except another year of invoices while your dog is still suffering.

You're at a crossroads:

One path:

Filling the next prescription. Going up to the higher dose. Moving the injection from six weeks to four. Adding the antibiotics when the ears go again. Accepting managed as the best you're ever going to get, Spending more years and money watching your dog lick her paws instead of play.

The other path:

Going after all three at once. Letting the gut stop sounding the alarm. Letting the nerves come down. Letting the wall close.

And getting your dog back while she's still young enough to enjoy it.

I can't get those four years back.

Cooper is seven and he's comfortable and I'm grateful for that every single day. But comfortable was available to him at two. I bought it at seven, and I paid $8,247 for the delay.

If you're reading this and your dog is still scratching,  you still have time.

Don't wait until it's too late.

P.S. — Wolves don't get this because nothing in them is missing. Your dog is missing the bacteria that keep her immune system calm. The immune system panics, the itch keeps firing, the nerves become hypersensitive, and the skin barrier breaks down. Three problems feeding each other, and every medication you've been handed is aimed at one of them. That's why it works at the start. That's why it stops.

P.P.S. — Don't buy another gut-only chew. It does a third of the job, quits in a few weeks, and you blame yourself again. And don't sit on this one. Every week those three keep running together, the nerves get more sensitive and harder to bring back down, the skin takes longer to close, and the invoice gets bigger. I waited four years with Cooper. It cost me $8,247 and the only four years he was ever going to be young. They’re on $19 a month and they haven't scratched in six months.

bodyText:
My daughter-in-law gave me white nurse clogs the day I agreed to watch the girls. I wore them eight months. Last Sunday I chased a rolling sippy cup across the church parking lot in four seconds flat.

In shoes I picked myself. I wore the clogs because I love her.

My name is Carole. I am 65.

Eight months in those clogs, twenty minutes of limping every morning. The morning after Labor Day, in the new pair, zero. I will get to the new pair. They are called Cloud Walk.

But first, Amber.

Amber is my son Tyler's wife. She remembers your coffee order after hearing it once. She organized the whole family dinner the night I announced I would keep the girls four days a week.

The girls are my daughter Jenna's. A three-year-old and an eight-month-old, while Jenna works. I love it so much it is embarrassing.

Amber handed me a box at that dinner. White clogs, the kind nurses wear. She had tears in her eyes.

"So practical," she said. "You're a full-time GRANDMA now. You'll be on your feet all day!"

"I will," I said. And I meant it.

But here is what I could not say out loud, that night or for a long time after. I was still also me. The clogs did not know that.

Before the girls, I had a shoe situation I was quietly proud of. Nothing fancy. Just mine. Picked by me, for my wide feet and my bunion and nobody else's.

I did not know how much of me was in that closet until it was gone.

The clogs came to Easter. They came to the pediatrician, which is fair. They came to Target, to church, to story time, to my sister's birthday.

Every visit, Amber lit up. "There are the grandma shoes!" It became my name tag.

At the Memorial Day barbecue, one of Tyler's old groomsmen looked at my feet. He is at every barbecue. "Man, remember when your mom used to dance at weddings?"

He was joking. Everyone laughed. I laughed too.

Then I went and stood in the kitchen for a minute, holding a plate of deviled eggs I did not want.

On the Fourth of July, Tyler took a picture of me and the girls on the porch swing. It is a good picture. The baby is grabbing my ear. And there at the bottom, better lit than I am, are the clogs.

Amber made it her phone background. "Look who greets me every morning!" So the shoes I did not choose say hello every time she checks the weather.

Tyler says I was being dramatic. Tyler owns one pair of sneakers. "They're fine," he says. They are.

Here is the part that stung. They were not even good at the job.

Amber had picked the slip-in kind, open at the heel. Every time I bent down for the toddler, the left one stayed behind on the floor. I developed a move for it. Knee down, elbow pinned to my ribs, baby on the other hip, toes clawing the shoe back on.

My sister saw it once on a video call. "You look like you're smuggling poultry." One line. She lives two states away. That was her whole contribution.

Three things happened in August.

My niece's engagement dinner. I got a sitter and blew out my hair. I wore the good slacks for the first time since the baby. I felt fifty walking in.

The hostess sat us on a long bench. Every woman at that table had thin pretty sandals on. Then me. White clogs at the end of the row.

After forty-five minutes I stood up for the ladies' room. I had to hold the back of the bench. Ten seconds before my heel agreed to carry me.

"You okay, Aunt Carole?" my niece asked.

"Just the knee," I said. It was not the knee.

The pediatrician, four days later. I caught my reflection in the glass doors. Baby on the hip, toddler by the hand. Two white blocks at the bottom of the picture.

I want to be honest about this. I think other grandmothers have it too. I could not find myself in that reflection. Everything in it belonged to somebody else. Even the shoes were a message about who I was now.

I did not cry. I got the snack cup out in the parking lot like a professional, because that is the job. But I heard it.

Then church. The last Sunday of August. The sippy cup rolled under a stranger's Honda. I bent for it. The right clog stayed on the asphalt.

Bare foot on hot gravel. The toddler took off toward the Honda. I took six limping steps after her, baby on my arm, in a dress, in front of the greeter.

The greeter picked up my shoe. "Here you go, ma'am. Those things have a mind of their own." Two minutes and one knee on the pavement to get it back on.

Tyler called that night. "Mom. Let me take you shoe shopping." Twice, gently.

"No." Twice, less gently. Because Amber checks. Because Amber lights up. Because you do not retire a gift from a woman who cried handing it to you.

I chose the clogs over my own feet for eight months. I understand exactly how that sentence sounds.

Then one afternoon at preschool pickup, I walked out next to a mom I only knew as Ellie's mom.

Forty, maybe. Baby on the hip, toddler by the hand. Soft knit shoes, wide at the front, that she slid on at the door with the toe of one foot. She never put the baby down. She never looked down.

I said, and I heard how hungry it sounded, "Okay. What are those?"

"Cloud Walk," she said. "My sister and I went in on it together, buy one get one. Neither of us has bent down for a shoe since."

I asked if they pinched. I have a bunion the size of a walnut.

"They stretch," she said. "The knit just gives where your foot pushes. My toes have been in sandals all summer and these are wider."

Then she looked at my clogs and lowered her voice. "Mine's the Lavender. Sold out, my sister tried to reorder last week. The other one is still up. If you want it, don't sit on it like I did."

I did not order that night. I kept seeing Amber's face at that dinner, with the box. I sat on it for two days.

On the third day Ellie's mom caught me at the door again. "Did you do it?"

"Not yet."

"Carole. It is the shoe. It is not your feet." She pulled out her phone and texted me the link right there, baby still on her hip.

I ordered the Multicolor, because the Lavender was gone.

Mine arrived on a Thursday.

That night, after bedtime, I lined the clogs up on the kitchen counter like evidence. Then I slid the Cloud Walk on. Standing. No hands.

My toes spread out. Nothing pressed on the bunion. Nothing rubbed the side. I walked the hallway to the guest room and back four times in my nightgown.

Jenna called to check on the girls. "Mom, you sound different. Did you sleep?"

"No," I said. "I got shoes."

I stood in my kitchen and felt like I had been introduced to myself again. Nice to see you, Carole. You still have toes.

Friday was the first test. The baby was on my hip by seven in the morning. I slid the shoes on at the door one-footed, the way Ellie's mom does. The toddler was still looking for her sandals.

"Grandma, you're already outside!"

"I am," I said. "Find your shoes."

Preschool drop-off, the pharmacy, the park, pickup. I counted the squats out of spite. Forty. Forty times down to a three-year-old, twenty-two pounds of baby on the other hip every time.

Not one shoe stayed on the ground. Not once. The preschool teacher held the door for me at pickup. "You are quick today."

Saturday morning I stood up without holding the dresser. I will come back to that.

Tuesday, Target with both girls. One hour and ten minutes. There are zero benches near the registers at our Target. I have looked.

I pushed the cart the whole lap. Lifted the toddler into the seat, lifted her out. Stood the full line.

My feet swelled by the end, the way they do in the afternoon. The knit swelled with them. Nothing cut in.

The cashier looked over the counter at the toddler. "She's got her hands full with you two." Then at my feet. "Those are cute."

"They're new," I said. Nobody had said that about my feet in eight months.

The week after, the pediatrician again. The nurse called us back. I squatted to pull the toddler's sock off, baby on my arm, and stood back up without touching the wall.

She watched me do it. "What are those?"

"Cloud Walk."

She wrote it on the appointment card, right under the date for the next visit. "My mother is on her feet all day. I cannot get her out of her clogs."

"Tell her they stretch," I said. "Tell her it is the shoe, not her feet."

Then the family barbecue. Labor Day.

Both girls, both sets of needs, the Multicolor on my feet. Amber spotted me across the yard and her face did a little searching thing.

"Where are the grandma shoes?!"

"Retired to the guest-room closet."

Right then the toddler pulled at my hand. I squatted down to her level in the grass. Fruit snacks came out of my pocket. Eye contact maintained. Then I stood up without a hand on anything.

Amber watched the whole thing. "Okay wait, those are really cute. Where are they from?"

"They're mine," I said.

My feet. Not the girls' feet. Mine, that the girls borrow for eight hours a day.

The groomsman was there too. He looked at my feet and kept his jokes to himself.

And then, because she is Amber, and because she is eight months pregnant and already swelling: "I'll send you the link. We could split an order, like Ellie's mom did with her sister."

The next morning was the one I promised to come back to. I put both feet on the bedroom floor and stood up. No limp. No dresser.

Twenty minutes every morning for eight months. Then zero. I checked the bunion. The red mark had faded. I made coffee standing up, which sounds like nothing unless you know.

We did split the order. Hers arrived two weeks before her own baby did. In the hospital photos, there they are at the foot of the bed. No clogs. All business. Kind of beautiful.

Tyler looked at the photo on my phone. "Fine," he said. "They're fine." That is the most he will ever say.

For the record, they are not magic. The full weekend hike with the girls still takes the boots in the trunk. But the daily circuit, preschool, Target, the pediatrician, life, rides on two feet I chose.

Which brings me to last Sunday. Same church. Same parking lot. Same sippy cup, under a different Honda.

I bent down. Both shoes came with me. Four seconds, cup in hand, back on my feet. The greeter nodded. "No rescue needed this time."

Amber wanted the Lavender, the one Ellie's mom wears. It was gone in August and it is still gone. She took the Multicolor like me. Her mother wants one now.

If you have a pair of shoes in your closet that announces someone else's version of you.

If your heel needs ten seconds on the back of a bench before it will carry you to the ladies' room.

If your grandbaby is on your hip and your shoe is still on the church asphalt behind you.

You need these shoes. Not because they are pretty. Though they are. But because somebody who loves you decided who you were now, and your feet were never asked.

Eight months of clogs. One summer's end in Cloud Walk. Forty squats. Zero shoes on the ground.

Ellie's mom texted me the link with a baby on her hip, so here it is for you too: https://nimbao.com/cloudwalk

Your move.
title: Retired The Grandma Clogs
