bodyText:
I locked my keys in the car once, with the engine running, in a supermarket car park in the rain.

It was nearly midnight.

Everyone else I rang would have been lovely about it, and useless.

I rang Jo, because Jo always comes.

She drove forty minutes in her dressing gown, with a coat over the top.

She got the door open with a bit of wire from her shed.

Then she called me an idiot all the way home.

We have been best friends since we were nineteen. She is forty-five now.

She cuts her own hair, keeps chickens, and has never once told me a comforting lie.

Everyone needs one person who says the true thing no matter what.

Mine is Jo.

The thing about Jo is she is right early, and quiet about it after.

When the whole school gate bought those toning trainers, she said they were just trainers with a bigger price.

She said the smoothie maker would end up in the loft.

Mine ended up in the loft.

She said the posh face cream was the cheap cream in a heavier jar.

She said the hot tub on the corner would be a frog hotel by June. It was a frog hotel by June.

She kept her brick of a phone for years while the rest of us upgraded every autumn.

When the cheap airline with the funny name folded, it took our holiday deposits with it.

She had booked the boring one. I had teased her for months.

She has never once said I told you so.

Not once in more than twenty years.

Which is almost worse, if I am honest.

She reads the small print. She keeps her receipts in a biscuit tin.

She buys the boring thing, and the boring thing outlives the exciting thing, every time.

I used to think it was a talent.

Now I think she just never wants anything badly enough to lie to herself about it.

Her house is small and warm, and nothing in it is new.

A dog with one ear up.

A radio that gets one station.

Mugs with chips in them that she will not bin, because they hold the right amount of tea.

A sofa older than my marriage, with a blanket over the bad spring.

Her kettle is older than my children. It has outlived three of mine.

When something breaks, she takes it apart on the table, swears at it softly, and puts it back together.

Her garden is mostly potatoes and a bench her dad made thirty years ago.

There is a drawer of zips and buttons and fuses, all labelled in pencil.

She has a torch that works, and spare batteries, and candles that are not just for show.

When the power went out for a whole day last winter, half the street ended up in her kitchen.

Everything she owns has a story and a scar, and she can tell you both.

Nothing in her house was bought to impress anyone.

Somehow the whole room impresses you anyway.

Now the thing I have never told Jo, or anyone.

I am the careful one.

I book the dentist. I do the birthday lists. I read the school emails to the bottom.

I read reviews for a week before I buy anything.

I follow the care cards. I wash things on the setting the label says.

And still I keep getting taken.

There is a drawer in my house that I cannot open in front of people.

The hair thing that promised a salon blow dry.

The ice roller.

The posture corrector that nearly stopped the blood to my arms.

The jeans that were going to change my life.

I cannot throw them out, because of what they cost.

I cannot look at them, because of what they cost.

Every single time, I had done everything right.

That is the part that stings. Not the money.

The being careful, and still being fooled.

You start to think there is something about you. Some smell the adverts can sense.

My husband thinks I am good with money, and I let him think it.

Shame needs silence. I gave it plenty.

That was me, until a Thursday last month.

Every second Thursday, Jo comes round with the same bottle of red. The eight pound one.

We have done it for years, through babies and funerals and one divorce. Hers.

We sit at my table and solve nothing, and it fixes everything.

When I got my fringe cut in, she looked at me for a long moment.

"You hate it," I said.

"No," she said. "I am deciding how long I have to like it before I am allowed to hate it."

"Twenty minutes," I said.

"Then for nineteen more minutes it is beautiful," she said.

That is us. She will tell me my fringe is a crime, then stay until midnight doing my ironing.

When my dad died, she took my kids for the whole weekend and brought them back with my laundry done.

She knew my husband was a good one before I did.

At the reception she leaned over and said, "This one is a keeper." Then she went back to criticising the DJ.

She was right about both.

I trust her more than I trust most of my own thoughts.

So when Jo goes quiet, the quiet is loud.

Last month, on a Thursday, I was up to my elbows in a chicken.

Jo offered to do the mushrooms, and went looking for something to do them in.

She opened the wrong cupboard.

The end one. The one nobody opens.

I knew it by the quiet. Jo does not do quiet.

I turned round, and she was standing there holding it.

The ceramic pan. The expensive one. The one from the back, behind the cake tins.

She looked at it. She looked at me.

Then she put it back, shut the cupboard, and cooked the mushrooms in a saucepan.

She said nothing. Not one word.

And that was worse than anything she could have said.

We ate. She admired a school drawing. She did baths. Nothing.

So when the kids were down, I got the pan out myself and put it on the table between us.

She turned it over. She ran a thumb across the middle. She read the writing on the bottom.

"How long did it last?" she said.

"It started grabbing at three weeks," I said. "By eleven months it was done."

She nodded like a nurse reading a chart.

"You told me," I said. "When I bought it. You said it was still a coating, whatever they called it."

"And you bought it anyway," she said. "So I shut up. What was I going to say?"

"I am asking you now," I said.

"They did not sell you a pan," she said. "They sold you a coating with a handle on it."

The middle had gone dull, where the heat lives.

There was a brown ring where the eggs welded on.

A grey patch that no amount of soaking would shift.

One scratch, from the one time somebody reached for a metal spoon.

Probably me. I blamed my son anyway.

The outside still looked brand new. That was the insult of it.

It looked like a good pan. It photographed like a good pan.

She had me run a nail across it. Where the shine had gone, it felt like paper.

"You nursed it," Jo said.

I did. I did everything on the card.

Low heat. Soft sponge. Wooden tools.

I hand washed that thing for eleven months like it was a newborn.

First the eggs. Then the pancakes. Then everything.

More oil. Then more oil.

Then so much oil I was shallow frying out of spite.

Then the soaking. The bicarbonate of soda. The special cream cleaner for eleven pounds.

Then the back of the cupboard.

And somewhere in there, I decided it was me.

One hot ring. One wrong spoon. One time I answered the door with it still on.

I found a way to make it my fault. I am good at that.

Jo sat back and asked the question nobody asks.

"Why did you buy it?" she said.

And I told her the true thing, out loud, for the first time.

When my daughter was four, we made pancakes on Sundays.

She stood on a chair with the whisk, in the apron with the ducks on it.

One Sunday I saw a fleck missing from the coating of the old pan.

The size of a fingernail clipping. A little black crater in the grey.

I never found it.

I looked while I flipped. Not on the spoon. Not on the side. Not on the plate.

She ate her pancakes with syrup, and she was four, and she was happy, and I watched every bite.

I binned the pan that week. I told nobody why.

And I bought the ceramic set. The good one. The heavy box.

The box said it was the safe one. The adverts said it was the safe one. I needed somebody to say it.

That was my research. A missing flake and a promise printed on cardboard.

Jo was quiet for a while.

Then she said the thing I had been waiting a year to hear, without knowing I was waiting.

"None of that was your fault," she said. "Not the flake. Not the sticking. Not the money. A layer is a countdown. You were just holding it when it hit zero."

I made my rule that night, at my own table.

I said it out loud, so I could not take it back.

I am never paying for a layer again.

Not the old stuff. Not ceramic. Not the fancy hybrids with the metal dots.

"Different chemistry," Jo said. "Same arrangement. The layer is the product, and the product is the part that wears out."

Once you see it, you cannot unsee it. The whole shelf is the same pan in different costumes.

"What do you cook on, then?" I said.

"Kaizen," she said. "It is one solid piece, 99% pure titanium. The surface you cook on is the metal itself, all the way down. There is nothing on it. That is the whole trick."

"Nothing sprayed. Nothing glued. Nothing painted. So nothing to wear out."

"Metal spatula. Steel wool. The dishwasher. It does not rust, and you never have to season it."

"Mine is older than your fridge, and it cooks better now than the day it came."

"The base stays flat, it works on induction, and they give you a 100 day trial and a lifetime warranty. Nobody offers that on a thing they expect back."

I wrote the name on the back of my hand, because that is where we are now.

"There is a catch," she said, and I braced.

"You give it a minute on the heat before the food goes in. Then a little oil. Then the food."

"It is not Teflon. A cold egg in a cold pan will stick, and you will be furious, and it will be your own fault."

I said I thought I could manage sixty seconds.

Jo looked at my fringe and said nothing.

First morning, I did it my way.

Cold pan. Egg straight from the fridge. A toddler on my leg and eleven years of old habits in my wrist.

It stuck like it had been welded.

I stood there scraping my first egg out of the pan that was supposed to change everything.

I nearly put it straight in the end cupboard, next to its friend.

Instead I sent Jo a photo of the wreckage.

"Did you heat it first?" she wrote.

I looked at the message for a long time.

"No," I said.

"Warm pan, little oil, then the egg," she said. "You gave it no chance at all, you plank."

Next morning I gave it a minute. A swirl of oil.

The egg slid round the pan like it was on ice, and out onto the plate in one piece.

I laughed out loud, alone, at eight in the morning, at a frying pan.

Here is the part I did not expect.

I told my sister. It just fell out of me one Sunday.

I spent a fortune on a ceramic pan, I said. Followed every rule. Killed it in eleven months. Hid it in a cupboard for a year.

She went quiet.

"Mine died in nine months," she said. "I thought it was me."

So we put it in the group chat. The school mums. The old work lot.

Four of us had the same story.

Four dead pans in four cupboards, and every one of us had privately decided she was the idiot.

None of us were. I want to say that twice. None of us were.

My sister bought one that week.

My mum has put it on her birthday list, which is the most Mum sentence ever written.

There is no countdown here.

No code, no timer, no breathless bit at the end.

The pan is called Kaizen, and you now know everything I know.

I checked the small print myself, twice, because of course I did.

I do not know if you need a new pan.

Maybe yours is fine. Maybe you already have a Jo.

But if there is a cupboard at the end of your kitchen with something in it you cannot use and cannot throw out, then this is me, opening it.

It was not you. It was never you. It was the layer.

I am off to do the school run.

There is an egg with my daughter's name on it when she gets in, and I am not thinking about the pan at all.

Jo drove forty minutes in her dressing gown to tell me I was an idiot.

This is the return trip.

bodyText:
I bought this before she was born, and I'm a bit embarrassed it's still in the box.

That's the rainbow stacker on the top shelf of her room.
You can see the dust on the box if you zoom in.

I'd seen it in so many of those calm playroom videos.
I pictured her on a rug with it, in soft afternoon light.

Under it, three puzzles, still in the plastic.

I kept saying she wasn't ready yet.
The truth is I didn't know how to get her started.
So it went up high, out of the way, and I kept buying other things.

It's out of the box now. I'll get to why.

I should say up front, I'm the mom who saves toy rotation reels.

The calm shelves, four things out at a time. I have a whole folder of them.

Our real toy room looks nothing like that. It's plastic, most of it lights up, and a lot of it plays the same song when you step on it in the dark.

Some of it was gifts. A lot of it was me, in a toy aisle at 6pm, thinking this might finally be the one she plays with.

Rosie would press a button, watch it flash, and walk straight back out to find me.

I added it up once in my notes app. Every toy in that room. Then I deleted the note before my husband could see it.

The rainbow stacker I wanted before she was born is still in its box on the top shelf. I kept telling myself she wasn't ready for it.

Then she turned two.

Both sets of grandparents. Two aunties. Half of daycare. By Sunday night the toy room floor was new boxes and torn paper.

On the Monday morning the house went quiet. The kind of quiet that makes you put your coffee down.

I found her in the kitchen. She'd pulled out the bottom drawer, the one with all the container lids, and she was sitting in front of it with her legs stuck straight out. Pushing a lid onto a container. Pulling it off. Trying another one.

Forty minutes. I checked the oven clock twice. She hummed the whole time.

I laughed out loud, alone in my kitchen. Then I looked down the hall at a room full of birthday presents and felt so stupid about the money my face went hot.

That night at 11:40pm I was in bed typing "toddler won't play with toys". Then "why does my toddler get bored of toys so fast".

It was all stuff I'd already tried:

🧺 Toy rotation. A whole afternoon setting up the shelf. It lasted nine days.

💡 The light-up learning toys. She'd watch one for about a minute, like a tiny show, then wander off.

🧩 The "open-ended" toys everyone recommends. I just didn't know how to get her started, and she could tell.

📦 A monthly toy subscription box. Half of every box stayed in the box.

Every fix was me buying another thing. None of it started with what she was actually doing.

So I tried the one idea that was free. For a week I wrote down what she kept going back to.

Here's the list, straight off my phone:
👜 The zip on my handbag
🚪 The latch on the side gate
🥣 The lid of the container
🚗 The buckle on her car seat, which she now insists on doing herself

Everything she dropped did the work for her. Press it and it sings, and her only part is to watch. So she watched for a minute and left.

Everything on my list made her do the work. The zip only moves if she pulls it. The lid only goes on if she lines it up.

And none of it lived in the toy room. It was in the kitchen, the hallway and the car.

I didn't need a better toy. I needed the jobs she'd already picked, all in one spot she was allowed to have.

I typed "toddler toy with buckles zips and latches" into a search bar, half joking, and a soft felt busy board came up. It folds shut like a book and zips closed. Pages of buckles, zips, laces, latches and snaps. Nothing flashes. Nothing sings. The pages come off, so she gets one at a time.

I nearly didn't order it. It looked so plain.

"It's the kitchen drawer, made for her," I told my husband when it came.

The first afternoon she went straight for the buckle. Same click as the car seat. Then the zip, tongue poking out the corner of her mouth, and a very loud "did it!" down the hall.

I sat on the floor with a cup of tea and finished it hot.

That was six weeks ago. She still raids the lids drawer some days. I've stopped closing it.

The rotation shelf has three things on it now. The board. A basket of old lids and containers. And the rainbow stacker, out of its box at last. She actually picks it up now there's nothing singing next to it.

What I got back isn't really the money. It's afternoons on the floor watching her work something out, instead of walking her back to a room she never wanted to be in.

If the toy room's full and she's in the kitchen drawer, it's not you and it's not her. She's already showing you what she likes.

I've written the whole thing out because a few moms asked. The exact board is linked below if you want a look. 👇

Even if you skip it, try this for a week: write down what she goes back to. I'd bet most of it isn't in the toy room. 🤍

bodyText:
For four days I watched a guest's nine-year-old hold things out and wait for somebody to take them off him.

Somebody always did, and everybody carried on talking.

I said nothing. He wasn't mine, and it wasn't my place.

His name was Ollie. Last summer his family had the old farmhouse Mick and I rent out to families in the hills, and on the second morning he picked an apple out of the bowl and asked his mom to cut it up.

I'd better start before that.

My husband Mick and I have run the place for 6 years. Two bedrooms, a woodstove, a garden that's mostly nettles, and a river at the bottom of the hill.

Families, mostly. Big ones, small ones, three generations at Christmas. Wellies by the door and somebody's socks drying on the stove.

For the first few years the reviews said the same three things. "Incredible location." "So clean." "The woodstove was perfect."

Then about a year ago the reviews started saying something else.

Guests started asking about the block.

Not the woodstove. Not the view. Not the coffee.

The little wooden block on the kitchen counter.

I should explain, and I should explain why it's there at all, because it isn't decoration.

It's a small wooden block. About the size of a bar of soap, covered in tiny holds and edges, like somebody shrank a climbing wall down to fit in your palm.

There's a handwritten card next to it. It says: "Hardest one is the yellow. Nobody's done it."

I put it there because of my son. I'll come back to that, because it's the part I find hardest to say.

I put it out for the adults, honestly. I did not expect what happened.

The children never put it down.

"Genuine question — what is the wooden thing on your counter and where do I buy four of them. My two did not look at a screen for an entire afternoon and I want to understand what happened."

"My son spent the week obsessed with a block of wood the size of a soap bar. He has asked about it every day since we got home."

"Had to physically remove the little block from my daughter's hand at checkout. Sorry about the shouting."

I started to notice which children in particular.

It wasn't the sporty ones especially. It was any of them. It was all of them. Under about 12, if that block is on the table, it is in a child's hand within an hour, and there is usually a row about whose turn it is.

I mentioned this to Mick, expecting him to find it funny.

He didn't. He teaches children at the climbing wall in town — has done for 22 years, something like four thousand kids — and he said something that changed the way I've looked at every family who's come through here since.

He said: they're starving for it.

Then last summer, a family checked in that I still can't stop thinking about.

Hannah and Tom, both in their forties. Two children — Ollie, 9, and Rosie, 6.

Nice family. Tired, the way families are on the first night of a holiday.

Ollie was the one I noticed, though it took me a day to work out why.

He was bright as anything. Told me the entire plot of a film. Knew more about sharks than I know about anything.

And he didn't use his hands.

I don't mean he couldn't. I mean he'd stopped offering them. When something needed doing — a packet, a zip, a bottle — he'd hold it out and wait, and somebody would take it off him, and everybody would carry on talking.

It's such a small thing. I wouldn't have registered it at all except for the apple.

Second morning, I put a bowl of apples out. Ollie picked one up, turned it over a couple of times, and asked his mum to cut it up.

Hannah said, "just eat it, love."

And he genuinely didn't know how. He had a go, from the side, like you'd bite a sandwich, and gave up and put it back.

Nine years old. He'd never eaten an apple that hadn't already been in slices.

Nobody made anything of it. Tom laughed, Hannah laughed, I laughed, and it was gone in about four seconds.

Day three it rained.

And Rosie — the 6-year-old — found the block.

She didn't put it down for two hours. Then Ollie wanted it. Then there was a row, a real one, the kind where a parent has to physically separate two children and confiscate the object.

Hannah apologised about six times. I told her the truth, which is that it happens most weeks, and that I'd started to find it interesting rather than annoying.

Because here's what I'd noticed by then, over about a year of watching other people's children in my kitchen.

They don't fight over the tablet. There's no fight, because there's nothing to win.

They fight over the block.

By Thursday they'd worked out a system involving a kitchen timer, which was entirely their idea, and which I want on the record was more negotiation than I've managed with my own family in twenty years.

And Ollie — the boy who didn't offer his hands — sat at that table on and off for four days.

Not because anybody asked him to. Because his little sister could do the blue route and he couldn't, and that was intolerable.

They checked out on the Saturday. Hannah left the place spotless. Beds stripped, dishes done, a thank-you note on the counter.

But when I went to flip the house, something was wrong.

The block was gone.

Not the card. Not the coasters. The little wooden block that lives on the kitchen counter. Gone.

I checked every drawer, every shelf, the recycling, the bin. Nothing.

We have a disclosed camera in the common room. Standard security, guests know about it.

I pulled the footage.

6:50 that morning. Hannah comes down before anyone's up. Crosses to the counter. Picks up the block. Stands there for a moment with it in both hands. Puts it in her bag.

Not the children. Hannah.

My first reaction was annoyance, honestly. The next guests were arriving at two and now I'd have to drive home for the spare.

That lasted about ten seconds.

Because I thought about a nine-year-old boy holding an apple he didn't know how to eat, and then about the same boy at that table for four days, losing to his sister and refusing to stop.

That's not theft. Not really.

That's a mother who saw something work and could not risk it not being there on Monday.

So I texted her. "Hi Hannah — hope you all got home safely. The block's missing from the counter. Everything okay?"

An hour later my phone rang. She was crying before I said hello.

"I'm so sorry," she said. "I'll pay for it. I'll pay you whatever you want. I just — I panicked."

Then it all came out.

"In October I sat in a little plastic chair at a parents' evening," she said, "and his teacher told me Ollie is the only child in his class who still can't tie his shoes."

"She was lovely about it. She wasn't telling me off. She said it in about eleven seconds and then she moved on to the next parent because there were nineteen of them waiting."

"And I've thought about it every single day since October and I have never said it out loud to anybody. Not to Tom. Not to my mum."

I sat down on the edge of the bed.

"Because what do you do?" she said. "He's happy. He's clever. He reads above his age. There's nothing wrong with him. You can't take a child to the doctor because he can't tie his shoes."

"And I've bought the velcro trainers, and I cut up his fruit, and I open his yoghurts in the morning because we've got eleven minutes to get out of the door — and I have started to wonder whether I did this."

Then she said the thing that I've thought about every day since.

"I watched him at your kitchen table using his hands for four days. Four days. And on the Friday he did the blue one, and he stood up on the chair and shouted."

"And I thought — that's the first time in about two years I've seen him want to be good at something he can't already do."

"And then I thought about Monday. Getting home. That thing not being on the table."

She was crying properly by then.

"I know it's a piece of wood. I know how ridiculous this is."

I was crying too.

Sitting on the edge of a bed in my own house, listening to a woman apologise for something I would have done.

Because two years ago, I was Hannah. That's the bit about my son, and I'll get to it.

First I want to tell you what Mick said, because it's the reason any of this is on my counter at all.

Twenty-two years of teaching children. I asked him once whether kids had changed. I expected the usual — no attention span, glued to phones, the standard grumble.

He said: they can't hold on.

He said it's not strength. It's not that they're weak, exactly. It's that their hands don't know what to do. They put a hand on something and it just sits there, flat, like a starfish. He has to teach nine-year-olds things he used to teach four-year-olds.

He said the change has been so gradual he can only see it by looking back a decade at a time.

So one night, after Hannah's phone call, I sat at the kitchen table at 1 in the morning and started reading. Properly reading, not scrolling.

I did not expect what I found, and I want to be careful how I lay it out, because a lot of what's written about children and screens is overheated and I don't want to add to it.

So let me stick to the parts that are hard to argue with.

There's a study out of Essex that measured ten-year-olds in 1998 and then measured ten-year-olds again ten years later.

Same age. Same county. Ten years apart.

Arm strength had fallen by 26%. Grip strength by 7%.

And this is the bit I read four times: in 1998, one child in 20 couldn't hold their own body weight hanging from wall bars.

Ten years later it was one in 10.

Double, in a decade.

The papers that covered it ran a headline I've thought about ever since. Children are getting weaker, they said, because they don't climb trees any more.

Then I read the occupational therapists, who are the people who actually get sent the children when something's wrong.

The head paediatric OT at an NHS trust in England put it about as plainly as it can be put. Children are arriving at school and being handed a pencil, and they can't hold it, because they haven't got the underlying skills yet. And she was explicit about why — it is easier to hand a child a tablet than to set up the kind of play that builds hands.

A survey of teachers found 77% saying children are having more difficulty than they used to with pencils, pens and scissors.

And then I found the thing that actually frightened me, which has nothing to do with primary school at all.

There's a professor of surgery in London who trains surgeons. He has been saying for years that the students arriving at his medical school — top of their year, straight A's, the brightest children in the country — increasingly cannot sew.

They haven't got the hands for it. And his point wasn't that they're lazy. His point was that he can no longer assume that a young adult has spent a childhood doing things with their hands.

That's the bill. It doesn't arrive at 9. It arrives at 25, in a room where somebody's supposed to be learning to stitch a person back together.
