title: A little climbing, every day
linkDescription: Scissors, laces and pencil grip are skills modern life stopped teaching. A climbing game for the table that builds children's hand strength.

bodyText:
The moment I finally walked away from my husband and son, they completely lost it.
They came home to find my room emptied out — every single family photo slashed to pieces, and nothing left behind except the belongings I had originally brought into the marriage.
They assumed I was just overreacting and would eventually come crawling back with an apology.
Instead, divorce papers were delivered straight to their doorstep.
My ex-husband immediately started blowing up my phone, furious at how heartless I was being.
My son chimed in impatiently, saying I was too jealous and that Aunt Katherine felt more like his real mother than I ever did.
I shot back coldly: “When you were all busy taking care of Katherine during her recovery, did it ever occur to you that your real wife and mother was lying alone in the hospital battling gastric cancer? Just focus on looking after your precious Katherine.”
Dead silence followed. I hung up and blocked him right away.
They tried desperately to track me down, but I had already settled into my new penthouse.
With trembling fingers, I dialed a number I had sworn never to call again.
“Brother,” I sobbed, “take me home. I only have three months to live.”
The white lights located on the ceiling in the hospital hallway buzzed silently overhead as I sat in the uncomfortable plastic chai tensed as I clutched my phone tightly in my trembling hands. I had been waiting for nearly forty minutes at this point for my doctor, Dr. Reynolds to call me back with my test results, and the knots in my stomach had tightened with each passing minute as I anticipated the worst.

I couldn't wait any longer. I needed to hear my son's voice.

My fingers moved almost automatically tapping the first number that popped up in my speed dial, which happened to be my husband Logan's, line. I pressed the dial button and watched as the phone rang once, twice, three times before he finally answered.

"Logan, where did you take Nick?" I asked, trying to keep my voice steady even as another wave of nausea rolled through me and I forced myself not to throw up on the floor. 

"I'm not feeling well. Can you please bring him home? I haven't seen him in three days."

There was a pause on the other end, followed by muffled sounds in the background, it sounded like laughter, maybe? Children screaming with delight in the background.

"Sorry, not tonight," Logan said flatly, his voice carrying that detached tone it had held for the past two months whenever he was addressing me.

My heart sank at his words. "Why not?"

He didn't give an answer. I pulled my phone from my ears and saw that the call was still ongoing so I repeated.

"Logan, I asked you a question. Why can't you bring our son home?"

More silence. I could hear the sounds more clearly now, it sounded like carnival music, and I could also hear the distant roar of a roller coaster. My chest tightened at this.

"Are you with Katherine?" The name tasted bitter on my tongue.

"That's none of your business, Sedona."

The line went dead.

I stared at my phone, my hands shaking so badly I nearly dropped it. None of my business? Our son was with them, and it was none of my business?

Before I could process what had just happened, my phone chimed with a new message. My blood ran cold when I saw Katherine's name on the screen.

I shouldn't have opened it. I knew I shouldn't have, Katherine had sworn to be a thorn in my life, a very painful thorn, but I was a masochist and couldn't stop myself as my fingers moved of their own accord, tapping the notification.

The photo loaded slowly, each picture a fresh stab to my heart. There they were—Logan, Katherine, and Nick—standing in front of Cinderella's Castle at Disneyland. 

Logan had his arm around Katherine's waist. Katherine was holding Nick's hand, her perfect smile glowing under the sun. And my baby, nIck was beaming at her with pure adoration, that I hadn't seen in months.

They looked like a family. A complete, happy family.

And I was the outsider.

Shame and fury was fighting for dominance inside me as I pulled up Katherine's number with shaking fingers. She answered on the first ring, as if she'd been waiting for my call.

"Katherine," I said, my teeth gritted with pain as I spat. "I don't care what game you're playing with Logan, but Nick is my son. You can have Logan if that's what you want, but you will never, ever take my child from me."

"Really?" Her voice was light, amused, like I'd just told her a particularly entertaining joke to her. "Why don't you ask Nick about that?"

"What are you—"

"Nick, sweetie, your mother's on the phone. Do you want to talk to her?"

My heart leaped. Yes. Yes, I needed to hear his voice, needed him to tell me that he missed me, that he wanted to come home.

"Mom?" Nick's voice came through, but it wasn't the sweet tone I'd been hoping for. It was annoyed, exasperated. "What do you want?"

"Nick, sweetheart, I—"

"We're having fun. Stop bothering us. You're so annoying."

The line went dead.

I sat there, frozen, the phone pressed against my ear even though there was nothing but silence on the other end. My six-year-old son had just called me annoying. He'd told me to stop bothering them. As if I was a stranger interrupting them and not his mum.

"Mrs. Hayes?"

I looked up to find Dr. Reynolds standing in front of me, a manila folder clutched in his hands. His expression was grave, the kind of look that Immediately told me that he planned on delivering bad news.

"Let's talk in my office," he said gently.

I followed him, on autopilot, my mind still reeling from Nick told me. The office was bigger than I expected, although it had been on autopilot, cramped with medical books and framed diplomas. I sank into the chair across from his desk, waiting for the bad news to drop.

Dr. Reynolds sat down and opened the folder, studying the papers inside for a long moment before looking up at me.

"Sedona, I'm not going to sugarcoat this. Your test results show significant abnormalities. Combined with your symptoms—the persistent pain, the nausea, the weight loss—we ran additional scans."

He paused, for a moment before he continued speaking.

"You have gastric cancer. Stage three. It's already spread to the lymph nodes."

The words didn't make sense at first. They were just sounds, syllables strung together. Cancer. Stage three. Spread.

"What does that mean?" I heard myself ask, my voice sounding distant, like it belonged to someone else.

Dr. Reynolds's expression softened with sympathy. "With aggressive treatment—chemotherapy, possibly surgery—we might be able to extend your life expectancy. But I need to be honest with you. Without treatment, you're looking at three months, maybe four at most. With treatment, perhaps a year, maybe more if you respond well."

Three months. Ninety days.

I thought of Nick's face in that photo, smiling up at Katherine. I thought of Logan's arm around her waist. I thought of my son calling me annoying, telling me to stop bothering them.

"Mrs. Hayes? Sedona? Do you have someone you can call? You shouldn't be alone right now."

I shook my head slowly. Who would I call? My husband who wouldn't answer? My son who found me annoying? I'd cut ties with my family years ago when I ran from that arranged marriage, too proud and too in love to ever go back.

"I'm fine," I whispered, though I was anything but.

Dr. Reynolds scheduled a follow-up appointment, handed me pamphlets about treatment options and support groups, said something about hope and fighting spirit. I nodded mechanically, taking the papers he pressed into my hands.

I walked out of that hospital in a daze, clutching my death sentence in a manila folder. The summer sun was too bright, the Chicago streets too loud. Everything still felt like a dream, and I was watching it happen to someone else.

My phone buzzed with another message. Another photo from Katherine. This time, the picture was of Nick asleep in a hotel bed, Logan sitting beside him, his hand gently stroking our son's hair.

I stood on the sidewalk, people rushing past me in their busy lives, and I felt something inside me finally break.

I had given up everything for them. My family, my career, my entire identity. And for what? To be a replacement for the woman my husband actually loved? To be an annoyance to my own child?

I had three months to live. And I was going to die unloved, unwanted, and completely alone.

Chapter 2 Nothing But A Replacement 

SEDONA

I don't remember the drive home. It was all a blur for me. One moment I was standing on that busy Chicago sidewalk, and the next I was pulling into our driveway, the manila folder was seated on the passenger seat, silently reminding me of my death's countdown..

Our house—Logan's house, really, I'd never felt like it was truly mine—loomed before me, filled with expensive decorations and wall to ceiling windows. A monument to wealth and status that had never brought me any warmth.

It hadn't always been this cold. Once...a long time ago, this was a place that was filled with joy and laughter. I sat in the car for a long moment, remembering when I'd first arrived in Chicago three years ago. I'd been running from my family's expectations, from the arranged marriage they'd planned with some business partner's son I'd never even met and they expected me to give my entire life up, just like that. I was supposed to be the obedient daughter, the perfect heiress who would smile and say "I do" to secure another corporate merger.

But I'd wanted more than that. I'd wanted love. Real love.

The car accident had happened on my second day in the city. I'd been so focused on staying hidden, , that I hadn't been paying attention to the traffic light. The impact had been shocking but not serious, it was just enough to leave me shaken and slightly injured on the side of the road.

And then Logan had appeared, like a knight in shining armour. He'd helped me up, insisted on taking me to the hospital, stayed with me through the examination. When he'd asked about my family, I'd lied and said I was an orphan. It had seemed safer that way, easier than explaining that I was a runaway heiress hiding from one of Seattle's most prominent families.

Logan had been so kind then. So attentive. We'd fallen into a fast romance, and when he'd proposed after just three months, I'd said yes without hesitation. I thought I'd found my fairy tale, my happily ever after.

I'd been so stupid and naive.

A sharp pain in my abdomen pulled me back to the present, reminding me of what I had. I pressed my hand against my stomach, waiting for it to pass, so I could breathe properly. These pains had been getting worse for months, but I'd dismissed them as stress, as anxiety over the fact that my son and husband were growing distant from me, every passing day.

Now I knew better.

I grabbed the folder and made my way inside, each step feeling heavier than the last. The house was quiet, eerily so. Usually, I'd hear Nick's laughter echoing through the halls, or the sound of TV playing his favourite cartoons.

But Nick wasn't here. He was at Disneyland, probably already forgetting I existed.

"Sedona? Is that you?"

I froze. That voice—filled with disdain—could only belong to one person.

Sherry appeared in the hallway, Logan's mother.

"Where's Nick?" she demanded, her eyes scanning the empty space behind me. "Don't tell me you left him somewhere again."

I clutched the folder tighter against my chest as protection. "You should ask your son that question."

She rose an eyebrow at me. "What's that supposed to mean? How does a mother not know where her own child is?"

The accusation stung, especially coming so soon after Nick's cruel words. I felt my composure cracking but forced myself to stay calm.

"Logan took him. Three days ago."

Sherry pulled out her phone, scrolling through her screen. I watched as her expression shifted from annoyance to something almost... pleased.

"Oh, how wonderful!" she exclaimed, looking up at me with a satisfied smile. "He's at Disneyland with Katherine. They're having such a lovely time. I told them not to rush back—Nick deserves a proper vacation."

The casual way she said it, as if it were the most normal thing in the world for my husband to take our son on a trip with another woman, made my blood boil.

"You don't find that inappropriate?" I asked, my voice shaking. "Your son is on a romantic getaway with another woman, with my child with them instead of being home, and you think that's wonderful?"

Sherry's smile didn't waver. Rather, she smiled even more as she shrugged her shoulders.

"Katherine is a tennis star, Sedona. She's accomplished, elegant, successful. Of course it's better for Nick to spend time with someone like her rather than..." She gestured vaguely at me, her meaning clear.

"Rather than his own mother?"

"Rather than someone who has nothing to offer him," she said bluntly. "Katherine can teach him about excellence, about ambition. What can you teach him? How to be mediocre?"

I flinched, but Sherry wasn't done.

"Besides, Katherine is Logan's ex-girlfriend. They have history, a connection. It's natural that he'd want to spend time with her now that she's back in Chicago."

"He's my husband now," I said, hating how weak my voice sounded.

Sherry laughed as if I was a jester performing for her, as she wiped tears from her eyelids and continued speaking.

"Oh, sweetheart. Do you really not know?" She stepped closer, her expensive perfume overwhelming. "Do you honestly not understand why Logan married you in the first place?"

"What are you talking about?"

"You look like her," Sherry said simply. "Katherine. Well, a poor man's version of katherine anyway. When Logan was heartbroken after Katherine left to pursue her tennis career, I pressured him to settle down, to marry and produce an heir. And then there you were—stupid and naive in love and a doppelganger of Katherine. 

Each word was a knife to my heart as I clenched my hands into fists.

"If you didn't have that passing resemblance to Katherine, Logan wouldn't have looked at you twice. A girl with no family, no background, no money, no prospects? Please. You were just... available. And good enough for the time being."

The folder slipped from my hands, scattering papers across the marble floor. Sherry glanced down at them, her eyes catching on the hospital letterhead, but she didn't seem to care enough to ask.

"Now that Katherine is back, things can return to how they should be. Logan can be with the woman he actually loves, and Nick can have a proper mother figure. Someone worthy of the Hayes name."

She stepped over the scattered papers, heading toward the door, not caring one bit about my feelings.

"I'm going to call Logan and tell him to enjoy his time with Katherine and Nick. They'll come back when they're ready. Don't wait up."

The door closed behind her with a soft click that sounded like a prison cell locking.

I stood there in the empty foyer, and came to the shocking realization.

I'd never been Logan's choice. I'd been his consolation prize. Our entire marriage, everything I'd thought we'd built together, had been a lie.

I sank to the floor, my hands shaking as I gathered the papers. The medical reports seemed almost laughable now, as I choked back a sob, covering my mouth to muffled the pain coursing through my body.

Chapter 3 Being Replaced

SEDONA

I don't know how long I sat on the bedroom floor, my back against the bed, staring at nothing. The afternoon light had shifted, getting darker, casting long shadows on the room that I had shared with Logan for three years.

Shared...what a joke. He hadn't touched me in months, finding excuses to sleep at the company or in his study downstairs.

Now I knew why.

The scattered medical papers lay in front of me as I reached out for them again. Stage three gastric cancer. Three months without treatment. Maybe a year with it.

I picked up one of the pamphlets Dr. Reynolds had given me—"Living with Cancer: A Guide for Patients and Families." The smiling faces on the cover, surrounded by loving relatives, seemed to mock me. What family did I have? A husband who wished I was someone else and actively cheating on me with his first love without feeling guilty? A son who found me annoying and a nuisance and wasn't even missing me? A mother-in-law who'd just confirmed I was nothing more than a placeholder in her's son's life and my only usefulness was giving birth to NIck?

My real family was in Seattle. Cameron, my older brother, who'd probably spent the last three years furious with me for running away without an explanation. My parents, who I'd abandoned without explanation.

GodEnzo, the man I was supposed to marry, who'd done nothing to deserve being left at the altar.

I'd been so self-righteous, so convinced that I was choosing love over obligation. So I'd run, determined to find real love, authentic happiness. So I could tell my parents 'I told you so'

Instead, I'd found this.

A fresh wave of nausea hit me, and I barely made it to the bathroom before I was sick. When I finally lifted my head, I caught sight of myself in the mirror and barely recognized the woman staring back. My face was pale, my weight was reduced and the clothes that suited me before months ago, were big on me, basically drowning me in this.

How had I not seen it? How had I dismissed all these signs as stress?

Because you were too busy trying to save a marriage that was already dead, a bitter voice whispered in my mind.

I splashed cold water on my face and returned to the bedroom. My phone was ringing—Logan's name flashing on the screen. My heart skipped a beat as I felt hope bubbling up in me. Maybe he'd realized he needed to come home. Maybe Nick had asked for me. Maybe he realized that Katherine was his past and he wanted to choose me.

I grabbed the phone. "Logan?"

"Mom?"

My breath caught. It was Nick's voice, small and uncertain. For a moment, he sounded like my little boy again, the premature baby I'd held in the NICU, the toddler who'd cried for me in the night.

"Nick, sweetheart—" I started, but a coughing fit interrupted me. I tasted copper in my mouth and pulled the phone away, pressing my hand to my lips. When I looked at my palm, there was blood.

"Mom? Are you sick?"

I closed my eyes, trying to steady my breathing. At least he cared enough to ask. At least some part of my son still loved me.

"I'm okay, baby," I managed, my voice hoarse. "I just miss you so much. When are you coming home?"

There was a pause, and I heard Katherine's voice but her voice was too low, for me to hear what she saod.

"You're lying," Nick said, his tone shifting back to that coldness and disdain. 

"You're just faking being sick so I'll come home. But I'm not stupid, Mom. I know what you're doing."

"Nick, I'm not—"

"Aunt Katherine says you always manipulate people to get what you want. And I'm not falling for it. I don't want to come home. I want to stay here with Dad and Aunt Katherine. Stop pretending to be sick to get me to come back home. It's pathetic."

The line went dead.

I sat there, phone pressed to my ear, blood on my hand, and felt something inside me finally shatter completely. My son just called me pathetic for supposedly faking an illness.

If only he knew.

I set the phone down carefully, as if it might explode, and walked to the dresser. Our wedding photo sat there in a huge golden frame, which had been another gift from Sherry.

I picked it up, studying Logan's face. He wasn't smiling. I'd noticed it on our wedding day but dismissed it as he was simply nervous. Now I saw it for what it was, he looked like a man going to his execution, not his wedding.

And me? I was beaming, completely oblivious to the truth.

I looked like Katherine. Sherry's words echoed in my mind. A poor man's version.

I pulled out my laptop and, for the first time in three years, searched Katherine's name.

Pages about her flooded the screen.. Katherine Rogers—tennis prodigy, Grand Slam winner, Olympic hopeful star. She was beautiful, accomplished, everything I wasn't.

There were a lot of articles praising her talents, her grace, her rise to the top of women's tennis.

Until an injury had sidelined her career eight weeks ago.

Eight weeks. The same time Logan had started staying out late, taking Nick on mysterious "outings," barely speaking to me.

I found photos of Logan and Katherine from five years ago, before I'd ever met him. They looked perfect together., Logan was smiling. Really smiling, with genuine joy in his eyes.

He'd never looked at me that way. Not once.

I scrolled through more recent photos. Katherine returning to Chicago. Katherine at a charity gala—with Logan in the background. Katherine at a children's hospital, reading to sick kids—with Nick sitting adoringly at her feet.

I closed the laptop and looked around the room. Noticing just how insignificant, I was, my clothes were limited to one wardrobe, while Logan's filled every corner, and i had a book bookmarked, left carelessly on the table. I was not even present in a space I assumed was mine, just like I had assumed NIck was mine and Logan.

Until Katherine had come back and shown him what a "proper" mother looked like.

My phone lit up with another notification. Not a message this time—a photo uploaded to social media. Katherine's account, public for all her thousands of followers to see.

The photo showed Nick asleep in what looked like a luxury hotel room, his small hand clutching a Mickey Mouse plush. The caption read: "Best day ever with this little sweetheart. Some people are just meant to be in your life. ❤️ #family #blessed #disneyland"

The comments were already rolling in. "Such a cute kid!" "You'll make an amazing mom someday!" "Beautiful family!"

I stared at that hashtag. #family.

She was claiming my son. Publicly. And Logan was allowing it.

I looked down at my wedding ring, the diamond catching the lamplight. Seven years I'd worn this ring. I had held on tight to the promise it apparently represented.

But it had all been a lie. I twisted the ring off my finger. My hand felt strange without it, lighter somehow.

I picked up my phone and typed out a message to Logan.

"Let's get divorced."

I hit send before I could second-guess myself, then pulled the ring off completely and set it on the nightstand next to our wedding photo.

If I only had three months to live, I wasn't going to spend them begging for scraps of affection from people who'd never wanted me in the first place.

I was done being Katherine's substitute. I was done.

Chapter 4 A Moment Of Doubt

LOGAN

My phone buzzed against my skin in my pocket as I was watching my son squeal with delight while he was being taken for a joyride on the spinning tea cup.

I pulled it out as I took a glance at the phone in my hand, squinting to read screen.

"Let's get divorced."

I stared at the message from Sedona, then shook my head and slipped the phone back into my pocket. She was being dramatic again. There was no way she would mean this, not knowing how much she loved me. She was trying to get me to come home on time thinking I would be affected if she did something drastic like this.

This wasn't the first time, she had pulled something this extreme. Ever since Katherine came back from abroad, she had been calling and texting in the middle of doing important things with her acting possessive and jealous which was exhausting.

"Is everything okay? You look tensed about something" I was pulled away from my thoughts by Katherine's voice who had come to stand by me, linking her hand with me, her face flushed with joy despite ger injuries.

She glowed in the California light looking every bit the star beauty she was in my eyes and much more than that, less petty and vindictive.

"It's fine," I said, watching Nick wave at us from the ride as I shrugged my shoulders and continued speaking. "Just Sedona being Sedona....I guess."

Katherine's expression shifted to something I couldn't quite read, like she was thinking about something as she spoke softly. 

"She's called a lot today, hasn't she? Maybe we should go back and check on her, she might be lonely to have texted this much in the space of hours. I'd hate to think she's upset because of me."

"She's fine," I said, perhaps more sharply than I intended. As I tried dial back the anger in my tone as I continued.

"We're here to keep you company while you recover from your injury. You shouldn't have to cut your rest short because Sedona can't understand that other people have needs too and the world doesn't revolve around her."

"Logan..." Katherine touched my arm lightly. "Maybe she's just feeling left out? Nick has been spending a lot of time with me lately. It's natural for a mother to feel like she is being pushed back to second place in her son's heart."

"It's natural for a child to admire someone who is accomplished and inspiring, regardless of who it is. This is not a bad thing at all, to have a role model that he can look up to" I interrupted. "Nick looks up to you, Katherine. He sees what excellence looks like. Sedona shouldn't be jealous of that. She should be encouraging it. She should want the best for her son at all costs."

The ride slowed to a stop, and Nick came running over, his face red from excitement and joy. But instead of talking about the ride, that he just got drown from, he talked about his mum.

"Dad, Mom called again," he said, rolling his eyes in a way that reminded me of his grand mother. 

"But what she did wasn't cool at all. She was pretending to be sick, trying to trick me into coming home."

I listened to this frowning as I asked him. "What do you mean, pretending?"

"She was coughing and stuff, but Aunt Katherine says people do that when they want attention and trying to get people to want them instead by any means possible." Nick looked up at Katherine with adornment in his eyes seeking validation. "Right?"

Katherine's cheeks turned a bit pink as she spoke. "I... I'm sure your mother wasn't..."

But I wasn't listening anymore. I was staring at my phone, at the divorce text, feeling angry in a way that I hadn't expected. Sedona had always been so understanding, before..she had never once complained about it when I worked late or neither had she questioned my decisions or made demands..she had been then picture poster version of a perfect wife. Quiet, and always supportive.

When had she become this person? This jealous, manipulative woman who would fake illness to guilt our son into coming home?

But deep down I knew, it has started from the moment Katherine walked back into my life and then Sedona changed and started having a lot of opinions about where I went, who I was with and how much time Nick spent with Katherine.

I couldn't help myself but think about our wedding years ago. She had been from a terrible background, having no family friends or joy. I had given her everything a woman could ever need in her life and this was how she chose to repay me.

By throwing tantrums when I tried to help an old friend?

"Dad?" Nick tugged on my sleeve, pulling me from.my thoughts as he pointed with his free hand at another fun machine he wanted us to try. "Can we go on Space Mountain next?"

I looked down at my son, then at Katherine, who was watching me with those warm, understanding eyes. She had never been jealous, even now, she was also thinking of Sedona's feelings.

That was the difference between them. Katherine was selfless, and mature and willing to put others first. Sedona was... well, she was acting like a child.

I typed out a response, my fingers moving quickly across the screen.

"Stop this, Sedona. Why can't you be more tolerant? Katherine is injured and needs time to recover. Stop being so selfish."

I hit send and turned off my phone completely. I wasn't going to let Sedona's dramatics ruin this trip for Nick and me. He deserved to have fun, to spend time with someone who wanted the best for him. One day wouldn't kill Sedona after all.

"Come on," I said, taking Nick's hand. "Space Mountain sounds perfect."

As we walked toward the ride, Katherine walked on the other side of Nick and I watched as Nick casually reached out to hold her other hand, making us look like a family of three.

I pushed away the small voice in the back of my mind that whispered something was wrong. And Sedona was right to remain angry by this but I refused to listen.

It was Sedona, she would apologise to me and then things would go back to normal.

They always did.

Chapter 5 : Taking A Risk

Sedona’s POV

I stared at Logan's response until the words blurred together on the screen. I blinked and felt the hot tears roll down my cheeks. I cleaned it off with my hands as the screen became clearer once more as I reread the text that my soon-to-be ex-husband sent.

"Stop this, Sedona. Why can't you be more tolerant? Katherine is injured and needs time to recover. Stop being so selfish." I laughed at this, a bitter sharp laugh that tore from my throat as tears rolled down again as I battled hard to wipe them, but it kept spilling until I was sobbing.

Selfish. He thought I was being selfish.

I was dying, and my husband thought I was being selfish for wanting to see my son, in what might be my last memories before I would head to the great beyond. He called me selfish for wanting to tell him I had cancer. 

His thoughts were soon unbelievable as I felt the urge to laugh at how cruel and ridiculous it was. I pressed my hand to my mouth, afraid that if I started laughing I might never stop. Or worse, that the laughter would turn to screaming.

Katherine was injured. A tennis injury. Something that would heal in weeks, maybe months. 

I was dying. Three months if I was lucky. Less even, the doctor's gave an estimate, but I have seen people who thought they had more time, only to drop dead a week later.

But Katherine's twisted ankle, or whatever godforsaken minor injury had brought her back to Chicago, and straight into my husband's hand, that was what took priority. That was the kind of heavy and scary injury that demanded both my husband and son, to be at her side 24/7.

My fingers moved across the screen, finally deciding to type what I thought of this entire situation.

"Then take good care of your Katherine."

I hit send and watched the message turn from "delivered" to "read." Then I waited. One minute. Two. Five. Ten minutes, I refreshed again, thinking it was network but there was no response.

Of course not. He'd probably already turned his phone off, to avoid talking to me, so I wouldn't bother him with irrelevant things anymore. Being the kind of man he was, he was too busy being the perfect family with Katherine and Nick to be bothered with his dying wife's dramatics.

I set the phone down on the bed and looked around the room that had been my room...no, not room anymore. It was time that I spelled out the bitter truth, that I had been too blind to see, my prison for years. Everything in it spoke of wealth and privilege, a design that wouldn't be found in over 70% of average family houses.

I could note the silk curtains, the designer furniture, the original artwork commissioned by famous artists on the walls. Logan had given me all of this, as if expensive things could substitute for love. Like he was saying, 'oh here is my wealth, but my heart belongs to Katherine, sorry.'

Maybe to him, he really believed money could substitute for loe. After all, I'd been just another acquisition, hadn't I? Something to be bought off the market, just because I had the unfortunate fate of being a lookalike to Katherine. And not just that, he saw me as a manageable Katherine replacement to satisfy his granmotherr's demands for marriage and an heir.

Mission accomplished, Logan. You got your heir. Now you can have the original back, and discard the used replacement.

My phone sat on the nightstand next to my wedding ring, both of them symbols of promises that had never been real. Next to them was another piece of paper—the one I'd been avoiding looking at for three years.

I picked it up with shaking hands. It was worn from being folded and unfolded countless times in those first few months after I'd run away, before I'd forced myself to stop looking at it.

My brother Cameron's phone number, was scribbled on the back of a business card.

He'd given it to me at a family dinner two weeks before my wedding to Enzo.

"If you ever need anything," he'd said quietly while our parents argued about the seating arrangements and floral arrangements while Enzo was with them trying to pacify both women who had different ideas of what the wedding should be like. "Anything at all, Sedona. Even if you do something crazy. Even if you run. Call me. I'll listen, I wont judge and I will be on your side, no matter what."

I'd run. And I'd never called.

For years, I'd told myself it was because I was happy, because I'd found real love, with someone that I never expected. I convinced myself that I didn't need my family's wealth or connections or arranged marriages to be happy and well fulfilled in life. I'd been so proud of my independence, so sure I'd made the right choice in picking Logan.

But pride was a luxury I could no longer afford.

My hands trembled as I picked up my phone and dialed the number I'd memorized but never used. It rang once. Twice.

What if he didn't answer? What if he'd changed his number? What if he was so angry at me for disappearing that he'd—

"Hello?"

Cameron's voice hit me like a physical blow as I felt my breath cut short as both hope and fear warred inside me, seeking dominance. His voice never changed one bit, it still sounded exactly the same as I remembered. I opened my mouth but no sound came out.

"Hello? Is anyone there?"

"Cam?" My voice broke on his name, and suddenly I was crying—deep, wrenching sobs that I couldn't control. "Cam, it's me."

There was a pause, and then: "Sedona? Sedona, is that you?"

"I'm so sorry," I gasped between sobs, unable to stop crying as everything was hitting me at once: the abandonment, the indifference, the pain, and Cam's concern for me despite the fact that he was justified in leaving me to my fate. "I'm so sorry, Cam. I should have called. I should have—"

Chapter 6: A Brother's Love

Sedona’s POV

"Where are you?" His voice was urgent now, filled with concern, cutting to the point; he didn't appear to blame or say, 'I told you so.'To him. I was just his kid sister, who was hurt, and he was ready to fight whoever had caused some reaction from me.

"Are you hurt? Are you safe?"

"I'm in Chicago. I'm... I'm not hurt. Well, I am, but not physically, there is….’’ 

I couldn't form coherent sentences. Everything I'd been holding in for three years came pouring out in broken words and gasping breaths as I tried to force out the words that I desperately needed him to hear.

"Sedona, breathe. Just breathe, okay? Whatever it is, we'll fix it. Are you alone? Is someone threatening you? Are you being held for ransom?"

"No, I'm—" Another sob cut me off. "Cam, I'm sick. I'm really sick."

The line went silent, he didn't say anything but I could hear the heavy sound of him just breathing, apparently trying to cope with what I told him. I could picture him, standing wherever he was, his face going still the way it always did when he was processing something serious.

"How sick?" he asked quietly like he was afraid of the answer he was going to hear.

"Gastric cancer. Stage three." The words came easier now. "The doctor said three months. Maybe four. Without treatment, anyway."

"Jesus Christ." I heard movement on his end, footsteps, a door closing. 

"Sedona, where exactly are you? Give me an address."

"You don't have to—"

"Give me the address. Now."

I rattled off Logan's address, my voice surprisingly steady now that the initial breakdown had passed, I was starting to feel better, just the fact that Cameron was coming to find me, made me feel better than I was, moments ago.

" Got it. I'm getting on a plane tonight," Cameron said. "Don't make any decisions, don't do anything until I get there. Do you understand?"

"Cam, I left. I ran away from the wedding. I humiliated the family. I—"

"I don't care." His voice was fierce. "Do you hear me? I don't care about any of that. You're my sister. That's all that matters."

Fresh tears spilled down my cheeks, but they were different now—not born of despair but of relief. For relief that I wouldn't be alone anymore.

"You should blame me," I whispered. "I've been so stupid, Cam. I 

thought I was choosing love, but I was just—"

"Stop." His tone softened as he spoke to me in that soothing voice. 

"Sedona, I watched you at those family dinners before the wedding. I saw how miserable you were, how trapped you felt. You wanted a choice, wanted to live your own life. No one should blame you for that. I never did."

"But Enzo—"

"Enzo survived. Actually, he married Rachel about six months after you left."

I blinked in shock. "Rachel? My best friend Rachel?"

"The very same. They have a daughter now. Molly. She's adorable. Looks just like Rachel." Cameron paused. "Rachel was devastated when you disappeared, you know. She thought something terrible had happened to you. We all did."

The guilt threatened to overwhelm me again. Rachel had been my closest friend since childhood, and I'd vanished without a word to her too. I didn't want to tell her anything because I knew my family would ask her questions and she was never good at lying and my location would be discovered.

"I'm sorry," I said again, the words feeling inadequate but it was the only thing that I was capable of saying. "I'm so sorry for everything."

"Save your apologies. Right now, I need you to tell me what's going on. You said you're married?"

"Was married. I sent him divorce papers. Well, a text. I sent him a divorce text." A hysterical laugh bubbled up forcing itself out of my throat as I shook my head in disbelief. "God, that sounds pathetic."

"Who is he? What did he do?"

The whole sorry story came tumbling out, as I gave him a summary of how I met Logan after the accident, the sudden romance that soon got to the point of me being proposed to and then married and then giving birth to NIck, prematurely, I also told him about my dedication in being a good mum and wife, then the return of Katherine and everything else that fell apart the moment she had Nick and Logan wrapped around her fingers.

Cameron listened without interrupting, but I could hear his breathing getting harder, could imagine his jaw clenching the way it did when he was trying to control his anger.

"So let me get this straight," he said when I finally finished. "You've been dying alone in Chicago while your husband takes your son on vacation with his ex-girlfriend?"

"When you say it like that, it sounds—"

"Insane? Cruel? Absolutely unforgivable?" Cameron's voice was ice. 

"Where is he now? Still at Disneyland?"

"Yes. He told me to stop being selfish because Katherine's injured and needs time to recover."

The silence that followed was somehow more frightening than anger would have been.

"I'm going to kill him," Cameron said finally, very calmly. "I'm going to fly to Chicago, pick you up, and then I'm going to find this Logan person and kill him with my own hands."

Despite everything, I almost smiled. "You can't kill him, Cam. He's Nick's father."

"Nick is your son. Your son, who told you you were annoying and accused you of faking illness for attention while you were actually dying." His voice cracked slightly. 

"How did this happen, Sedona? How did you end up here?"

"I wanted to be loved," I said simply. "I wanted someone to choose me for me, not for the family name or the business connections. I thought Logan did. I thought I'd found something real."

"And instead you found a man who married you because you looked like someone else."

"Yeah," I whispered. "Instead I found that. For someone who was so desperate about true love ended up being scammed of it, probably the universe giving me karma I deserved for hurting Enzo who had done nothing wrong to me, and yet I disgraced him, ironic isn't it?"

"I'm getting you out of there," Cameron said firmly. "Tonight if I can manage it, tomorrow morning at the latest. We'll bring you home to Seattle, get you the best doctors, the best treatment. You're not dying alone in that house, do you understand? You're not dying at all if I have anything to say about it."

"Cam, the cancer is stage three. It's already spread—"

"I don't care if it's stage ten. We're fighting this. You're a Preston, Sedona. We don't give up." He paused. "And you're my little sister. I'm not losing you. Not after just getting you back."

I pressed my hand to my mouth, trying to muffle the sob that escaped. 

But I was tired of pretending to be Sedona Hayes, instead of Sedona Preston. I was also very tired of being small and invisible by my own family.

"Okay," I said finally. "Okay, Cam. Come get me. Take me home."

“I will get on our family private jet. Pack whatever matters to you. Leave everything else."

After we hung up, I sat on the bed holding my phone, feeling something I hadn't felt in years: hope.

My phone buzzed with a notification. Another photo from Katherine's Instagram—this time of Logan and Nick on Space Mountain, both of them laughing.

The caption read: "Making memories with my favorite people. ❤️"

I looked at the photo one last time, at my husband and son looking happier without me and felt peace blossoming in my heart. Let them have their perfect little family. I was going home.

Chapter 7: A Brother’s Guilt.

Cameron’s POV

I stared at my phone for a full minute after Sedona's call ended, my hand shaking slightly as I lowered it gently to my desk as I exhaled taking a deep breath and closed my eyes trying to process the bomb that I just received this night.

It had been five years. Five years of searching, of hiring private investigators, of lying awake at night wondering if my little sister was alive or dead. And not getting anything, whatever happened to Sedona, I hadn't been able to discover it and now, just like that, she'd called.

She was sick. Dying.

The words kept repeating in my mind even after the call, I wanted to ask Sedona if this was a cruel joke, but I knew she would never lie about something serious such as cancer.

And her timeline she was given was barely three months. My brilliant, stubborn, beautiful little sister who used to follow me around the tennis courts when we were kids, who'd been destined for greatness before she'd thrown it all away to run from a marriage she didn't want.

And I'd let her go. We all had. We didn't want to force her to do anything that she didn't want to.

"Cameron?" Jennifer's voice pulled me from my thoughts as I jerked back, taken unaware, when had she gotten in here. I looked up to find my mother standing in the doorway of my office, her styled hair catching the late afternoon light. At fifty two, Jennifer Preston was still a remarkable woman, never to be taken for granted, someone who commanded both authority and power no matter where she was, though the years of searching for Sedona had added lines to her face, that no amount of skincare could hide.

"Darling, you look like you've seen a ghost. What's wrong?"

I opened my mouth, then closed it again. How did I tell her? How did I explain that Sedona was alive but dying, that we'd found her only to the possibility that we might lose her again?

"Cameron." My mother's voice got harder as she stepped into my office, closing the door behind her sealing off the background voice as she focused her gaze on me, her eyes searching my face trying to pick out what could possibly make me this worried.

"You're frightening me. What's happened?"

"It's Sedona," I said finally, my voice rough. "She called."

The color drained from my mother's face. She gripped the back of the chair across from my desk, her knuckles turning white as she held on tight, not letting go. "Is she... is she alive?"

"Yes. She's in Chicago. She's been there the whole time, apparently." The words tasted bitter. Chicago. We'd searched everywhere—Europe, Asia, South America. We even searched freaking Africa, thinking she was hiding there. But it had never occurred to us that she might be hiding in plain sight, just a few states away. The best hiding places were as always, the one nearest to us, because we wouldn't assume she would hide so near and yet so..so far.

"Chicago?" My mother's voice rose with a mixture of disbelief and relief. "She's been in Chicago this entire time? Why didn't she call? Why didn't she come home? Is she hurt? Is someone keeping her there against her will?"

"No, nothing like that. She's..." I hesitated, trying to figure out how to explain without revealing the cancer. "She's married. Has a son. But things aren't good, Mom. She wants to come home.

Jennifer's hand flew to her mouth, tears already rolling down her face, happiness or disbelief, I wasn't sure of yet.. "

A son? We have a grandson? Oh my God, Parker!" She turned toward the door, ready to call for my father, but I stood quickly and caught her arm before she could reach the door.

"Mom, wait. Please."

She turned back to me, her eyes searching my face. "What aren't you telling me, Cameron?"

I'd never been good at hiding things from my mother. She had an uncanny ability to read people, but this I had to keep from her, at least for now.

If she knew Sedona was dying, she'd fall apart. And Sedona needed me to be strong for her.

"She's been through a lot," I said carefully. "The marriage isn't good. Her husband has been... let's just say he's not the man she thought he was. She needs space, needs time to process everything before she sees everyone."

"But she's okay? She's safe?"

"She will be. I'm going to bring her home."

"We should all go," Jennifer said immediately, already pulling out her phone. "I'll call Parker, we'll take the jet, we can be there in a few hours—"

"No." My voice was sharper than I intended, and my mother froze. I softened my tone. "Mom, she specifically asked for just me. She's fragile right now, overwhelmed. If we all show up, it might be too much. It might scare her away again."

The fear in my mother's eyes told me she understood. We'd lost Sedona once because we'd pushed too hard, tried to force her into a marriage she didn't want, we couldn't afford to make that same mistake again.

"But I'm her mother," Jennifer whispered. "I need to see her. I need to know she's really okay."

"And you will. I promise. Just... give me a day or two to assess the situation, to see what she is going through then I will talk to her about seeing everyone else. But I have to make sure she's ready. Please, Mom. Trust me on this."

Jennifer looked at me for a long moment, then slowly nodded. "Okay. Okay, but you call me the second you see her. The second, Cameron. I want to know everything."

"I will."

"And Parker needs to know. He's been—" Her voice broke. "He's been so lost without her. We both have."

I knew. My father had thrown himself into work after Sedona disappeared, spending sixteen-hour days at the office because being home reminded him too much of the daughter he'd failed to protect. He blamed himself for the arranged marriage, for pushing too hard, for not seeing how desperate Sedona had been to escape. For letting his daughter assume the worst of him, that he valued the business and company more than her. 

"Tell Dad," I said. "But make him understand that this has to be done carefully. Sedona needs us, but she needs us to be patient."

Jennifer nodded, wiping her eyes. "I'll talk to him. When are you leaving?"

"Tonight. I'm having them prep the jet now."

"Then go. Bring our girl home, Cameron. Whatever it takes."

Chapter 8: Flying To Chicago

Cameron POV

After my mother left, I picked up my phone and called my assistant, Marcus. He answered on the first ring.

"Hello?"

"Marcus, I need the jet ready to go to Chicago within the hour. Take care of this urgently, call the pilot. And I need you to compile a list of the best oncologists in the country—no, in the world. Specialists in gastric cancer specifically. Stage three. I need their names on my screen in a few hours, coupled with their location."

There was a pause on the other end. "Is everything alright, Mr. Preston?"

"Just do it, Marcus. And be discreet. I don't want anyone knowing about this yet."

"Of course, sir. I'll have the information sent to your phone within thirty minutes."

"Thank you."

I hung up and stared at my computer screen, at the stock company reports I'd been reviewing before Sedona's call. Suddenly, none of it mattered. The multi-million deals, the corporate acquisitions- all of it seemed little compared to my sister's life.

Stage three. The words haunted me. I wasn't a doctor, but I knew enough to know that stage three was serious. That it had advanced to a stage where it was life threatening and not many come back from that kind of developed cancer stage. That three months she said she had left was a death sentence.

But I refused to accept it. The Prestons didn't give up, and we sure didn't let our family members die without a fight, we do not forsake family no matter what. If money could buy Sedona more time she needed, I'd spend every penny we had. If experimental treatments that proved to be 80% in saving lives existed anywhere in the world, I'd find them.

I pulled up my contacts and scrolled to Dr. Helena Morrison, a family friend and one of the top oncologists at Seattle Grace Hospital.

She'd known Sedona since she was a child, had even treated her when she'd had pneumonia at fifteen. If anyone would fight for my sister, and make sure that she got what it takes, to survive cancer, it was Helena. 

"Cameron Preston," Helena answered warmly. "To what do I owe the pleasure?"

"Helena, I need your help. It's about Sedona."

The warmth in her voice immediately shifted to concern and worry as I could hear the creak in her chair as she sat upright.

"You found her? Is she alright?"

"She's alive, but she's sick. Gastric cancer, stage three. A doctor in Chicago gave her three months."

"Oh, Cameron." The sympathy in her voice made my chest squeeze. "I'm so sorry. Where is she now?"

"Still in Chicago, but I'm bringing her home tonight. I need you to clear your schedule, Helena. I don't care what it costs or what strings I have to pull. I need the best treatment plan possible, and I need it yesterday."

"Of course. Have her records sent to me as soon as possible. I'll consult with my colleagues at MD Anderson and Mayo Clinic. We'll explore every option, that we have for this kind of cancer, whether it's surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, clinical trials. Everything."

"Thank you."

"Cameron," Helena's voice softened a bit. "You should prepare yourself. Stage three gastric cancer is very serious. Even with a lot of treatment—"

"Don't." I cut her off. "Don't tell me she's going to die. I just got her back. I'm not losing her again."

There was a long pause before she sighed as she said. "I'll do everything I can. You have my word."

After we hung up, I grabbed my go-bag from the closet, I had always kept one packed for emergency trips like this and headed down to the parking garage, where my car was waiting.

My hands shook a bit as I unlocked the car and got in. I had to take a moment to steady myself before driving to the airport.

The private jet was ready when I arrived at Boeing Field. The crew greeted me professionally, without making room for small talk, sensing this trip was time sensitive. I had barely settled down in the chair when I felt my phone buzz and I checked it. Marcus had sent me the list I asked for and I saw a missed call from my father and a text message as well.

"Your mother told me. I'm coming with you."

I called him back immediately trying to stop him before he would do anything drastic. "Dad, I need to do this alone."

"Cameron—"

"Dad, please. She asked for just me. If we both show up, it's going to overwhelm her. You know how she gets when she feels cornered. I don't want her to run away again, not at this point when she needs us."

My father was quiet for a moment. Parker Preston wasn't a man who liked being told no, especially when it came to his children. But he had also learned the hard way what happened when he pushed too hard.

"Fine," he said finally. "But I want updates. Every hour, Cameron. And if she needs anything—anything at all—you call me immediately."

"I will."

"And Cameron? Tell her..." His voice cracked slightly. "Tell her we love her. Tell her we're sorry. Tell her we never should have—"

"I will, Dad. I promise."

As the plane began its descent into Chicago, I called Sedona's number. She answered on the second ring.

"Cam?"

"Hey. We're landing in about twenty minutes. You said you'd be at the Hilton on South Michigan Avenue?"

"Yes. Room 1847. I... I couldn't stay at the house anymore. Too many memories."

"That's fine. I'll be there soon. Have you eaten anything?"

"I'm not really hungry."

"Sedona, you need to keep your strength up. Order room service. I'll pay for it when I get there."

"Okay." Her voice was small, exhausted. "Cam? Thank you. For coming. For not hating me."

"I could never hate you. You're my sister who I've missed every single day for five years." My voice thickened. "I'm bringing you home, Sedona. And we're going to fight this. Together."

"What if there's nothing to fight? What if it's too late?"

"Then we make whatever time you have left count. But I'm not giving up on you. I need you to promise me you won't give up either."

There was a long pause, and then: "I promise."

"Good. I'll see you soon. Stay put, okay? Don't go anywhere."

"I won't. I'm not running anymore, Cam. I'm too tired to run."

After we hung up, I looked out the window at the Chicago skyline coming into view. Somewhere down there was my sister, alone in a hotel room, dying because the family she'd married into cared more about a tennis player's bruised ankle than her actual life.

A cold fury settled over me. I'd deal with Logan Hayes eventually. Right now, my priority was Sedona.

Hang in there, Sedona, I thought.

"Your brother is here now. And I'm not letting you go ever again."

Chapter 9: Past Memories

Sedona's POV 

The silence in the house was deafening as I stood in the bedroom staring at the open suitcase on the bed.

My brother was coming soon and I had to get my things out of here before he touched down.

I moved aimlessly through the closet, pulling out only the clothes I'd brought with me three years ago or had bought with my own money, the little that I had with me.

Most of my wardrobe stayed on the hangers because they were echoes of a life that I pretended to fit in. The designer dresses Logan had bought me for charity galas where I'd stood beside him like a prop, instead of a wife, where my job was to smile at old men that Logan had introduced me to, saying it made his company look good.

Not just that, I left behind the expensive shoes Sherry had insisted I needed to "look the part" of a Hayes wife.

The jewelry Logan had given me on birthdays and anniversaries, each piece chosen by his personal shopper because he couldn't be bothered to pick them out himself. 

I left it all.

Let Katherine have it. If she was so desperate to be the catching eye candy hanging off Logan's arms then she was free to do so. He might probably treat her better than he treated me, that was evident already, he can have her and let me go.

Besides she certainly wanted the part more than I ever had.

My hands trembled as I folded a simple cotton dress as my brain supplied the memory of how I had gotten it. This was the very first gown, that I had worn on my date with Logan, when I'd still believed in fairy tales. 

I remembered how he'd looked at me that night, like I had hung the stars in his world, I liked how attentive he'd been to me, reminding me of things that I had said days ago, or how he'd listened to me talk about my dreams of maybe teaching tennis someday, of having a quiet, happy life, with the one I want, raising the family that I wanted, finding true love.

But now, I could see it for what it was. All lies. Or maybe not lies, exactly. Maybe he'd just been seeing Katherine's face instead of mine, hearing what he wanted to hear instead of what I was actually saying. And pretending all along that I was the woman he actually wished me to be. That was probably how he got through with sleeping with me. The thought alone, made me want to throw up as bile rose in my throat but I forced it down, taking deep breaths to calm myself down.

I moved to the dresser, pulling open drawers and sorting through their contents as I browsed through it, taking what was important and leaving the ones that can be thrown away. I was reaching for a stack of shirts when my hand brushed against something small and hard in the back of the drawer.

My heart stopped for a moment as I recognized what it was.

The small wooden box was exactly where I'd left it, hidden behind my winter sweaters. With shaking hands, I pulled it out and opened the lid.

Nick's baby teeth.

Seven tiny white pearls, each one carefully wrapped in tissue paper with the date written on it in my handwriting. I'd saved them all, had planned to give them to Nick when he was older, maybe when he had children of his own. It was a foolish hope that I had, keeping evidences that his mum loved him.

I picked up the first tooth, dated two years ago. Nick had been so brave when it had fallen out, so excited to put it under his pillow for the tooth fairy. I'd stayed up until midnight to sneak into his room and replace it with a dollar bill and a note from the "tooth fairy" telling him how proud she was of his courage.

The memory felt like a knife to my chest.

Nick had been such a difficult baby. Born at thirty-two weeks, barely four pounds, his tiny body fighting for every breath in the NICU. I'd spent six weeks living in that hospital, sitting beside his incubator, talking to him, singing to him, willing him to live. That was the only time that Logan was present, all the time, we both wanted nick to survive. He was the glue holding us together.

bodyText:
I spent more of my best friend's visit under this table than at it.

This is the café floor, taken from my knees.
A squashed bit of banana.
A crayon, the third one to go over the edge.
The teaspoon, which I'd picked up twice already.
And the wheel of the stroller she climbed in and out of the whole time.
My best friend had flown in for one day to see me.
Every time I came back up, I'd lost the thread of what she was saying.
I don't think she ever got to finish a story either.

Jess has been my best friend since we were fourteen. She lives a flight away now, and two months ago she flew in for one day, just to see me.

We met at the café near my house at 10am. Me, Jess, and Mila, who is two.

We were there for 90 minutes. I did not finish one sentence.

Not one. Every time I got halfway, Mila needed something. Down from the chair. Back up. The sugar sachets. My spoon. My face, turned towards her with both her hands.

Jess was lovely about it. She'd start telling me about her new job and I'd say "sorry, keep going" and she'd say "no, it's fine," and neither of us ever found where she'd stopped.

My latte went cold with the heart still on top.

At the door I hugged her and said "sorry, next time properly."

She said "of course, love you."

It was the kindest thing she could have said. That's why I cried at the first red light.

On the drive home I worked it out. I hadn't finished a conversation with another adult in two years. Not with anyone.

And the invitations had quietly stopped. Nobody fell out with me. The group chat just started making plans I found out about afterwards, from photos.

I didn't blame them. For two years I'd been the friend who says "next time properly."

That night I was in bed by 8:30 with my phone, typing "toddler interrupts every conversation" and then "how to have a coffee with a toddler".

Every answer said to teach her to wait her turn. She's two.

And I'd already tried everything I could think of:

🌳 The park instead of a café. Mila runs, I chase, my friend stands by the swings holding both coffees. We talk in twelve-second pieces.

📱 My phone propped against the sugar jar. Twenty quiet minutes, with me half-listening over a cartoon. I still do this in the car sometimes. Screens aren't the enemy. But I wasn't really at that table either.

🌙 Meeting after her bedtime. I'm asleep by 9. I tried twice and yawned through the second one.

🥛 Babycinos. Gone in two minutes. Then she wants mine.

Every fix bought me a few minutes. None of them bought me a conversation.

At 8:52 Jess texted. She's been a nanny for ten years, and I'd honestly forgotten, because to me she's just Jess.

"She's not being difficult. She's two, there's nothing for her hands, and we were doing the one thing she can't join."

I read it about six times.

Talking was the one thing at that table Mila couldn't be part of. Jess and I each had a cup to hold while we talked. Mila had nothing.

Of course she climbed into the middle of it. It was the only way in.

She wasn't interrupting us. She was trying to join.

Jess sent one more message. Give her something of her own to work on, right next to your cup. Lots of steps. Silent. She's busy with her thing while you do yours.

I thought it sounded nice and wouldn't last five minutes in a café. Mila gets bored of new toys before I've got the packaging in the bin.

Then Jess sent a photo of the one she takes to work. A soft felt busy board that zips shut like a book. Buckles, a zip, laces, snaps, little velcro pieces. No sound. The pages come off, so you can hand over one at a time.

I ordered one before I put my phone down.

The first test was a Thursday, with Claire, a friend from my old work I hadn't seen in over a year. I texted her "coffee? warning, Mila's coming."

Our drinks came. I unzipped the board and put one page next to my cup. The buckle page.

Mila clicked it shut. Opened it. Clicked it shut. Then the zip, then the laces, frowning at it like it was very important work.

Claire told me about her sister's wedding. The whole thing, start to finish.

I heard the ending.

Then I told her something, and I finished it. Then I drank my latte, and it was still warm, and I nearly cried into it.

That was seven Thursdays ago. It's our standing coffee now. We share a slice of cake. Mila asks for "my work" when she sees me pick up my keys.

Jess is coming back next month. For the first time in two years, I'm not dreading the goodbye.

I don't think friends stop inviting you because they stop loving you. I think they stop because every visit ends with "next time properly."

Next time properly turned out to be a Thursday.

I've written the whole thing out because a few friends have asked since. 👇 The exact board is linked below if you want a look.

Even if you don't get this one, next time you meet a friend, put something on the table that's hers before the coffees come. You might hear the end of a story. ❤️
