bodyText:
Contract Rule #1: No Intimacy.
The moment he found out his brother was my ex, the hockey superstar staked his claim. He f*cked me eight times that night—hard, raw, and bareback.😱🔥

****************************
Chapter 1
APRIL

Apparently, winning a national hockey championship turns my boyfriend into a colorblind idiot.

I stand in the front row of the roaring, chaotic arena, screaming until my throat is sore, completely drowning in a sea of team colors.

The buzzer just went off. Cole’s team won the cup. Everyone around me is crying, spilling beer, and hugging complete strangers like the apocalypse just got canceled.

Great, right?

But not for me.

I look down at the oversized, sweaty jersey swallowing me whole.

Number 14.

Vance.

I’ve spent the last eight months washing this exact jersey, listening to him complain about his coach, and pretending I understand what a "power play" actually is.

He did it, I think, a proud, goofy smile plastered across my face.

I push my way through the crowd, maneuvering past security guards who are too busy celebrating to care, and make it right down to the ice barrier.

Cole is skating toward the boards, his helmet off, hair perfectly tousled despite the sweat.

I lean over the glass, extending my arms, ready to welcome him into a huge, breathless hug.

He looks right past me like I’m a piece of transparent plexiglass.

In my brain, all this is happening in slow motion like in the movies.

Before I can even blink, Cole skates right past my outstretched arms, ignoring me entirely. He targets a gorgeous, platinum-blonde girl standing three feet to my right.

Chloe—no relation to him, just a high-profile influencer with five million followers and a waist smaller than my thigh.

He goes over the barrier, scoops her entirely into his arms.

Even lifts her off her feet and kisses her.

Right on cue, the stadium's jumbotrons flash their faces across the screen for twenty thousand people to see. The entire arena lets out a collective, synchronized "Awww."

While all I hear is my ears ringing.

My arms are still hovering in mid-air. The smile freezes so hard on my face it feels like it might crack and bleed.

Instantly, a swarm of aggressive reporters and flashing cameras surround the two of them. A woman with a microphone shoves it right into Cole’s face.

"Cole Vance! An unbelievable win tonight! Tell us, is this gorgeous girl the secret muse behind your championship victory?"

Cole beams, wrapping his arm around Chloe’s waist, pulling her flush against his side.

"Always has been," Cole says into the microphone, flashing his signature, dimpled smile. "She’s my lucky charm. Couldn't have done any of this without her."

Bruh, we just fucked hours ago before the game started!

The crowd goes feral.

I can't move; I can't even breathe.

Cole promised.

He promised he'll announce our relationship if he wins the championship.

He made me keep a low profile, sneaking around sketchy hotels whenever he needed to empty his balls, swearing it was all "for the sake of his career."

What was I to him all this time? Just another slut?

Is that what he sees me as?

I thought we had something special. He told me he loved me. I even thought we were getting married.

I’ve fantasized about the ring, the house, the future. I gave him everything, supported him through every stressful game, and believed every single piece of bullshit that came out of his trashy mouth.

Instead, I’m just the nameless shadow he left behind in dark hotel rooms while he takes his victory lap in front of millions with someone else.

The ringing in my ears only gets louder.

I need to get home.

*************

Shock is a funny thing. It doesn't make you scream, and it doesn't make you cry. It just makes your brain function with the terrifying, robotic clarity of an outdated computer.

I don't remember taking the subway back to my apartment. I don't remember walking up the stairs. All I know is that I’m standing in front of my door, still wearing Cole's jersey, operating on numbness.

I turn the key and step inside our cramped, drafty apartment. The place is quiet, except for a very specific squeaking sound coming from the end of the short hallway.

My bedroom.

I frown, walking down the hall. My roomie, Sarah, and I have exactly one sacred, unbreakable rule written on our kitchen whiteboard: Do not bring your boyfriends into our tiny apartment, and under no circumstances do you have sex on our shared furniture.

I push my bedroom door open.

And there they are.

Sarah is on my bed, her back arched, and the guy currently burying his face in her neck is some new guy I've never seen. They are actively tearing up my bed sheets in their sweat and cum.

Sarah looks up, her eyes widening for a split second before her expression settles into something unbothered.

She sighs. “Oops. Sorry, April,"

She didn't even attempt to pull the blanket over herself.

"But we are completely in the middle of something, and the vibe is just way too good to stop. Can you go find a motel or something for the night? Thanks. Love you."

Like, the fuck …

Without even waiting for my answer, she pulls the guy back down by his hair, and they continue right where they left off.

I don't shout. I don't throw a tantrum. I don't even have the physical strength to form a sentence. The shock inside my chest is just too much to let out.

Slowly, I reach down, unclip my apartment keys from my belt loop, and drop them onto the floor. I turn around, walk out the front door, and step directly into the pouring rain.

Because, of course, it’s pouring. God forbid the universe misses an opportunity for a cinematic cliché. Apparently, my life has been officially hijacked by a low-budget director who thinks a woman's soul shattering requires a high-production-value thunderstorm.

God, what am I even saying?

I need to cool off.

The rain is coming down in sheets, soaking through the jersey until it weighs a thousand pounds.

I walk blindly, my sneakers splashing through deep puddles as I approach an intersection just a few blocks away from the arena.

I step off the curb, entirely numb to the horns blaring around me.

Screeech!

The squeal sound slams into my ear. So loud, I flinch, freezing in place.

Some multimillion-dollar black sports car had almost hit me. It literally stopped two inches away from my shins. Like, two inches. One more millimeter, and my kneecaps would have been hood ornaments.

He was about to hit a pedestrian on a fucking crosswalk. You know, the place where drivers are legally required to not vehicular-homicide people?

But I guess when your car costs more than the average human lifespan, traffic laws become mere suggestions, fuckface!!!

I can't even scream that out of my head.

I stare at the car, then the sky.

God, I'm exhausted.

I'm done with the universe; I have no more survival instincts.

“Ah, fuck it.“ I groan and collapse, letting myself fall flat onto the asphalt. I spread my arms out face-up to the sky.

I hear the door fly open. A man in a suit jacks his umbrella open, sprinting over to me in panic.

"Oh my god! Miss! Miss, are you alright?!" the driver begs, hovering over me. "Please, get up! We can settle this; my boss will pay you whatever you want, just please don't lie there! Get off the road!"

I don't move a muscle. I can't. I can't even close my eyes. I'm too weak to do anything right now.

"Just run me over, sir," I say. "Clearly, your billionaire boss doesn't know how to watch the road anyway. Honestly, it's a great night to die. Just put it in drive and finish the fucking job."

Chapter 2
APRIL

The back door of the car opens.

Another man steps out. He doesn't have an umbrella. Can't see his face because I don't care, but only the pants scream money. He can go to hell for all I care.

He doesn't argue with his driver, and he doesn't yell at me. He walks over, stepping right into a puddle next to my head, and bends down calmly.

"Get up."

"No." I pop the 'p', keeping my arms spread out like a dead starfish.

"I said, get up." Still calm.

"Hell to the no."

"Miss—" that's the driver's. But still.

"Hell to the fucking no."

I don't respond. I stare up at the sky, letting the rain wash over my face, pretending I’m a piece of the city infrastructure.

By now, people on the sidewalks are stopping under their umbrellas, whispering and pulling out their phones. A giant, rich-looking suit and a random girl having a crosswalk standoff is prime tabloid material.

Heh.

The guy rubs his temples with two fingers, looking too frustrated for someone who almost killed me.

But what he does next? I don't know whether to feel happy or concerned.

He scoops me off the ground like a sack of potatoes.

My eyes widen instantly, my breath catches in my throat.

I'm too stunned to speak or even scream.

My jaw freezes open as he takes two strides, throws me into the back seat, and slams the door shut.

The interior smells expensive.

I sit up straight. “Huh… excuse me?“

He slides into the seat next to me, wiping the water from his face.

He looks familiar.

"Where are we dropping you off?" he asks.

I can't even look at him. I turn my head, staring blankly out the window, completely paralyzed by everything that has happened tonight. My energy is completely drained.

"Just find an abandoned building and dump me there."

"Got it." He looks up at the rearview mirror, meeting his driver's gaze. “Find the next abandoned building.“

My eyes go wide again. “What?“

“Sir, there aren't any abandoned buildings close by," the driver stammers, looking stressed. "But there's an old church a few blocks away.”

“Perfect. Drop her there.”

“What the fuck!” I scream. Finally, my voice works. “You’re seriously gonna dump me at some creepy-ass church in this weather?”

My whole tough-girl act completely flies out the window. “What kind of serial killer behavior is this?”

He doesn’t even turn his head. “The kind who respects a lady’s wishes. You asked for an abandoned structure. I’m simply providing luxury roadside assistance.”

“I was being sarcastic, you psycho!”

“Could've fooled me. You sounded pretty serious,” he says. His voice is deep, smooth, and honestly? It's annoying as hell.

“Oh yeah? I wonder what serious sounds like to you,” I fire back, rolling my eyes so hard it hurts. “Do I need to spell it out for you, or are you just naturally this dense not to recognize sarcasm?”

"Keep your sarcasm in your throat, young lady!" he yells, jaw clenched.

The raw intensity of him snapping at me makes my breath seize.

The car suddenly feels twenty degrees hotter, and for the first time tonight, my mouth is actually shut.

“Sir,” the driver cuts in, breaking the tension. “We’re at the old church.”

“Good.” He says calmly this time. “Now get out!”

I freeze. The rain hits the roof; it sounds like bullets. The reality of the last three hours finally crashes down on me all at once—Cole's betrayal, Sarah throwing me out like garbage, almost getting killed, and now being dumped in the dark by a psycho.

I snivel once. Twice.

I try to hold it back, biting my lip until it bleeds. It's taking everything in me not to break down. I can't hold it back anymore.

I burst out in tears, burying my face in my hands. My whole body is shaking.

Beside me, the guy goes completely stiff. The asshole who was just screaming at me a second ago is suddenly paralyzed. I can feel him staring at me, totally stunned and out of his depth.

His hands twitch at his sides like he has absolutely no clue how to handle a crying girl.

I really want a hug right now. Even if it's from a stranger, but this guy is too dense to help a poor crying lady.

He slowly starts to reach out; his hand hovers just an inch away from my shoulder, like he's thinking about comforting me, but then he reconsiders. He pulls right back like the air burned him.

"Shit," he curses under his breath, sighs, and runs a hand through his hair.

I completely broke him with the waterworks, and he knows it.

"Arthur," he says, sounding completely drained. "Just... take us home."

I stay completely quiet for the rest of the ride. The only sound in the car is the hum of the engine and my occasional, pathetic sniffling. I just stare out the window at the blurred city lights, hugging myself.

The car finally pulls into the private, underground garage. The driver kills the engine.

I wipe my eyes with the back of my hand, glare over at the man next to me, and break the silence.

"You are seriously so nonchalant and insensitive," I huff, my voice still cracking from crying. "Didn't your mother ever teach you how to placate a crying lady?"

The guy lets out a sigh so hard his chest rumbles. He turns his head slowly, giving me a look that could literally freeze hell over.

"Shut your mouth before I change my mind and throw you back on the street. You are annoying as fuck."

Before I can even process the insult, he clicks his door open, steps out into the garage, and rips my door open. He grabs my arm and drags me straight out of the car.

I stumble, my wet sneakers squeaking on the concrete, but he doesn't care.

He keeps dragging me inside the elevator, up to the penthouse, and straight through the front door.

A middle-aged female butler in a uniform appears, her eyes widening slightly when she sees me.

He shoves me gently toward her. "Take care of this."

This? The emphasis on the 'this' has me losing my damn mind.

Like I was a bag of wet garbage he just picked up from the curb or a stray dog that tracked mud onto his expensive floors.

I open my mouth, ready to unleash a whole storm of curse words and tell him exactly where he can shove his penthouse, but I force myself to hold it back. I bite my tongue so hard I taste copper.

No, April. Shut up. Look at yourself. You're shivering, you have nowhere to go, and you almost died tonight. Do not get yourself kicked out over your big mouth.

I roll my eyes and clamp my lips tightly together as I watch him go.

I glare at the back of his head and stick up my middle fingers.

That should suffice.

Chapter 3
APRIL

I wake up the next morning because the mattress beneath me is entirely too soft to exist in my shitty reality.

Everything comes rushing back: my dramatics, the screaming, the "dead starfish" routine on the asphalt, and worst of all, the pathetic crying in his backseat.

Gosh.

A wave of heat hits my face, and I pull the blanket over my head, groaning into the pillow.

I feel so embarrassed. I was being a little unreasonable last night, honestly.

Wait. No. Screw that.

It was still 100% his fault for trying to run me over, so I ain't apologizing. No way in hell.

My eyes snap open again, then I realize I'm still at his house.

I glance at the time.

10 AM.

April, you have a fucking job.

Panic hits me like a bucket of ice water. I need to get the fuck out of here.

I throw the covers off, slip out of bed, and creep toward the front door, planning a quiet escape.

I reach out, my fingers inches from the handle—

"Going somewhere?"

I gasp, spinning around so fast my spine pops.

Standing by the kitchen island, blocking my path to freedom, is the shirtless, fiercely intimidating giant from last night, calmly drinking coffee.

The morning sun highlights a ridiculous set of abs and sprawling tattoos across his shoulders. He’s watching me like a damn hawk.

I back up a step, my heart drumming in my ribs.

Damn, he’s huge.

And he’s blocking the door, and he brought me to his secluded penthouse. I still don't even know his name. But he's familiar. I think he's some hockey player too. I'm not too into hockey, so… yeah, Cole basically enforced my support for the sport.

But now that he's blocking me, does he want something sketchy from me for saving me last night?

I swallow hard, forcing my face into a deadpan.

"Look," I say, crossing my arms. "You don't want me. I have Hepatitis C, severe infectious rashes, and multiple undisclosed medical conditions. If you touch me, you're going to catch something."

The stranger doesn't blink. He just takes a slow sip of his coffee.

Then he rolls his eyes with a tiny smirk tugging at the corner of his lips, clearly entertained by my garbage lying skills.

"I want a name and an explanation for the chaos you caused last night," he says. "Not a medical chart."

“Okay… um… yeah. I used my weak, frail body and ran into your car," I fire back, dropping my arms and gesturing wildly to myself. "Your car almost died, so forgive me, Your Highness. Is that the explanation you wanted?”

He sets his mug down on the counter. "You forgot the part where you cried like a baby in my backseat," he says smoothly, taking a step toward me. "But sure. Let's start with your name, frail body."

“Kim Kardashian.“

He rolls his eyes, annoyed now.

“Your name, Bitch.“

“Cardi B.“

He stares at me for a long, silent three seconds.

“Have you ever been to a psychiatric hospital before?“ he deadpans, staring at me like I’m a fascinating psychological experiment.

"No, but I'm thinking about it after dealing with a serial killer like you."

He runs a hand over his face, letting out a dry laugh. "Right. Well, 'Cardi', your clothes are in the laundry room down the hall. Get changed and get out. I have practice in an hour, and I don't need a crazy girl haunting my penthouse."

"Gladly," I snap, already marching past him. But as I pass the kitchen counter, my eyes catch on the framed photo resting by the keys. It’s him and—

My heart drops into my stomach.

Cole.

I freeze in my tracks, my eyes darting from the photo to the shirtless giant watching me.

Oh, my god. The familiar face, the hockey, the luxury. This isn't just some random rich athlete.

This is Asher, Cole’s older brother and the captain of the NHL team Cole plays for.

Holy shit. I am standing in the kitchen of the one guy who could ruin Cole’s entire life with a single phone call.

I whip my head around.

“Are you—”

“Keep whatever you want to say in your throat.“ He spits and walks out.

I book it down the hall to the laundry room, yank my warm clothes out of the dryer, and scramble into them. My hands are shaking.

Asher Vance. Cole’s older brother and team captain. Nah, I need to get out of here; I need nothing to do with Cole ever again.

I tie my sneakers in a messy knot and rush back to the living room, desperate to hit the elevator and escape.

But his irritated voice stops me.

"Mom, for the last time, I am not hiring an actress," Asher groans into his phone, pacing the floor. "I don't care if Cole is bringing a new girl home. Let him."

He rubs his temples, his voice rising. "Your petty competition with his mom is getting out of hand. I can't just manifest a girlfriend by tonight so you can brag... Jesus, Mom, stop crying.

Fine… I'll figure something out."

He hangs up with a sigh and throws his phone on the counter.

Then, he spins around and locks eyes with me.

Oh fuck.

I look away, freaked out by his glare. My sassy mouth completely shuts down. Keeping my eyes glued to the floor, I start shuffling backward toward the front door, trying to sneak out.

My hand finally grips the cold door handle. One second to freedom.

"Wait."

Asher's voice cuts through the room.

I slowly look back, still holding the handle. "What?"

"I need a favor."

“…you wanna empty your balls..?“ I shrink, lifting a brow.

Asher’s face twists in pure disgust. He actually flinches, staring at me like I’m completely insane.

“God no...what the fuck…what's going on in your fucking brain? Jesus..“

"Hey, you're the one cornering me shirtless in a penthouse, asking for mystery 'favors'!" I shoot back, gripping the door handle tighter. "Can you blame me for thinking the worst?"

"Yes! Yes, I can," he snaps, pinching the bridge of his nose. "I need a date, you psycho. A warm body to sit next to me at a family dinner tonight so my mom stops crying."

“A warm body? I'm dead ass cold.“

“Will you do it, yes or no?“

I blink, and the gears start turning. A date. To his family dinner.

Where Cole is gonna be. With his new girl.

My heart does a massive flip. If I walk into that dinner on the arm of the team captain—Cole’s older, way more successful brother—Cole will absolutely lose his mind. It is the ultimate petty revenge.

Hmmm.

But then reality hits. Asher has no clue who I am yet. If he finds out I'm his brother's freshly dumped ex, this whole thing blows up.

"Hire an actress," I say flatly, cracking the door open. "I told you, I have a fucking job. And unlike you, Your Highness, I actually get fired if I don't show up."

Asher scoffs, crossing his arms. "I'll pay—”

“How much are we talking about?“ My eyes are popping out of my socket.

"Two grand. For three hours of sitting there and pretending you're normal."

Two thousand dollars. That covers my part of rent and my overdue bills. I look at his smug face, then back at the door.

"Three grand," I counter, lifting my chin. "And you tell your driver to stop offering to dump my corpse at old churches."

He rolls his eyes, irritated. "Deal, Cardi. Deal."

Chapter 4
APRIL

HOLY MOLY.

Have I ever even seen a nice place before? I didn't even know what "nice place" meant until today. 'Cause, fuck. Here I thought Asher's place was killing it, but their family home is something else.

It’s not even a house; it’s a straight-up castle. The wrought-iron gates opened up to a driveway so long I thought we were road-tripping to another state. There are fountains, perfectly trimmed hedges, and enough outdoor lighting to guide a Boeing 747 to a safe landing.

I look down at the dress Asher had delivered a few hours ago. It fits perfectly, which is honestly annoying because it means his creepy scanning skills from this morning are incredibly accurate.

"Stop fidgeting," Asher says from the driver's seat, effortlessly steering his black SUV up to the front entrance. He looks ridiculously… good in the suit and all.

"I'm not fidgeting," I say, crossing my arms to stop them from shaking. "I'm just mentally preparing myself to secure my three grand. Remember the rules, Vance. Three hours, no touching, and I get to eat my weight in expensive food."

Asher pulls up to the valet, kills the engine, and turns to look at me. His eyes trace my face for a little but long.

"Just don't mention the Hepatitis C and we'll get through this fine."

“Dude, I was just joking.”

He steps out of the car and drags me out. Again.

We walk up the massive steps, and the giant double doors swing open before we can even knock.

And right there, standing at the bottom of the stairs with his arm wrapped around a blonde girl in a tight pink dress, is Cole.

He scans his older brother, confident at first, but then his gaze shifts to me.

Cole freezes. The smirk completely wipes off his face.

“Apr—”

“Honey, I'm feeling dizzy.” I interrupt, dropping my body against Asher.

He leans in, whispering. “What the fuck is wrong with you? We haven't even started dinner yet.”

“I panicked, okay.” I blurt out.

He frowns. “Panicked? Why?”

Oh boy.

Shit.

Before I can invent another medical condition, the click of heels saves my life.

A gorgeous woman walks in, smiling warmly at us. She looks like an actual angel, totally dressed up and radiating pure sweetness.

"Oh, welcome! You must be the lovely girl Asher mentioned," she says, her voice smooth as honey. "It's so great to finally meet you. We're so happy to have you tonight."

Wow. She’s stunning. And so nice!

I immediately pull away from Asher, putting on my best fake-girlfriend smile. Time to secure the bag and impress the mom.

I step forward, opening my arms to give her a huge hug.

"Oh, thank you so much for having me—"

Asher yanks me back. I stumble against his chest.

“Bitch, she’s not my mother.”

“Oh, sorry. She's the stepmom, and we’re snubbing her, got it.”

Seems stepmother notices our shenanigans.

The fake sweetness drains from her face. She sneers at us, shuts us out, and walks right past us over to the blonde girl.

"Oh, sweetie, your dress is just beautiful! Come, let's go eat," she gushes, grabbing the blonde's hand.

Cole is still standing there, staring at me like he's seen a ghost.

I give him a petty little blink, keeping close to his giant older brother.

Asher sighs, his hand still on my waist, nudging me forward. "Move, dinner's this way."

We follow them into the dining room. The table is huge, loaded with shiny silverware and fancy glasses. Everyone sits down, and the tension is so thick it's crazy.

I sit next to Asher, ready to eat my weight in expensive food and get my three grand, while Cole glares at me from across the table like he's about to explode.

The food gets served, and it's so incredibly good that I zone out. I'm so engrossed in shoving this five-star meal down my throat that I completely forget to notice the father. Like, that he actually exists and is sitting right there.

Suddenly, the clinking of silverware stops.

I look up, chewing a massive piece of steak, only to realize the entire table is dead silent.

Everyone is staring at me like I'm some kind of creep.

Including Asher.

I chew slowly, the steak suddenly feeling like a rock in my mouth.

I look around the table.

The stepmom looks like she just swallowed a whole lemon—her face is twisted in disgust as she stares at my full cheeks.

But then my eyes shift to the older woman sitting next to Mr. Vance. I think that's Asher's mom.

I don't even know what to make of her expression; she looks like she's witnessing a train wreck in slow motion.

Meanwhile, Blondie leans over to Cole, whispering something in his ear. Cole doesn't even blink; his eyes are locked onto me like lasers, burning holes through my face.

The silence is so loud I can hear my own heartbeat.

I swallow the steak with a loud gulp.

I’m fully expecting Asher to drag me out by my hair, but suddenly, the old man at the head of the table bursts out laughing.

Mr. Vance throws his head back. "God, I love her!" he says, slapping the table. "She’s such a cutie! Finally, someone who actually eats the damn food instead of picking at it like a bird."

Uh… okay.

He gestures to one of the maids standing nearby. "Hey, get over here. Put some more of that prime rib on her plate. Keep it coming!"

Beside me, Asher looks completely thrown off.

I grin with my confidence instantly rushing back. Boom. Three grand and extra steak.

But before I can dig back in, the doors of the dining room swing open, and a guy walks in late.

"Sorry I'm late, Dad, traffic was—"

The guy stops dead in his tracks. I turn my head, and my fork slips right out of my fingers, clattering loudly against my plate.

It’s Sarah's fuck buddy. The exact guy I saw fucking Sarah yesterday.

And he’s wearing a tailored suit, looking around the room like he owns the place.

Jace blinks, his eyes landing straight on me in my fancy dress. His jaw drops. "April? What the hell are you doing here?"

Chapter 5
APRIL

Mr. Vance frowns, looking between us. "You two know each other?"

"Yeah," Jace says, crossing his arms and looking completely baffled. "I know her bestie."

Bestie?

"You mean roommate," I mutter under my breath, correcting him. Because let's be real, Sarah is barely a roommate right now, let alone a bestie.

The stepmom instantly clears her throat, shifting the attention away from Jace to clear the awkward air. She turns to Blondie with a huge smile. "So, tell us, how are things going with you two? The chemistry is just sparking between you and Cole, I can just feel it."

That comment immediately triggers Asher's mom. She sits up straighter, her eyes narrowing as she glares at the stepmom before turning her gaze to us. "And what about you, Asher? How did you and April meet? Your relationship seems so... sudden."

Asher’s body goes rigid next to me. I can practically feel his annoyance growing by the second.

Alright, time to earn my three grand and help this guy out. Plus, Cole is still staring a hole through my head, and I really want to make him suffer.

I put on my best sweet face and slide closer to Asher. I wrap both of my arms around his bicep, leaning my head against his shoulder.

"Oh, it was totally like a movie," I gush, looking up at Asher with heart-eyes, squeezing his arm. "My big, strong bear here swept me off my feet. I honestly don't know what I'd do without him."

That's cringe. I know.

Asher freezes under my touch.

Across the table, Cole’s fork clatters against his plate.

“Aww wonderful.” His mom coos, clapping her hands like some middle school kid watching her first romance. “So when are you guys getting married?”

Cole almost choked on his food.

Asher warns, “Mom st—”

“Soon.” I say way too fast.

Asher freezes, giving me the most bombastic side-eye. His eyebrows are practically in his hairline, and his face literally says, Are you fucking insane?

But I don't care. I beam at his mom, squeezing his arm even tighter.

"Soon?" Cole chokes out, slamming his water glass down so hard the table shakes. He looks like he's about to pop a vein in his neck. "Are you serious right now?"

"Oh, absolutely!" the stepmom chimes in as she pats Blondie’s hand. "Well, Cole and sweetie here have been talking about a summer wedding themselves. It’s just so beautiful when things work out organically."

Asher’s mom glares across the table like she wants to launch her wine glass at the woman’s head. "Well, Asher and April don't need a massive, gaudy summer wedding to prove their love."

Okay. Is this some kind of competition?

The passive-aggressive back-and-forth keeps going, the two moms parading us around like prize ponies. The stepmom keeps pushing Cole and Blondie, and Asher's mom keeps pushing us.

No wonder Asher is always grumpy.

"I mean, we already talked about the venue," the stepmom boasts, preening. "The Hamptons would be perfect for Cole."

"Asher prefers something more intimate," his mom fires right back with a fake smile. "A private island, maybe. Somewhere exclusive."

"A wedding seems a bit fast, don't you think?" Cole chimes in, looking right past Asher and locking his eyes onto me. "I mean, Asher... do you even know anything about this girl? Did you actually do a background check on her, or did you just pick her up off the street?"

"Huh... excuse me."

The whole table goes quiet. I feel the bicep under my hands turn to steel.

I glance at Asher. Why is he getting worked up? That insult was directed at me, not him.

Cole tilts his head, his eyes scanning my dress with pure disrespect. "Who knows what kind of history she has. You should be careful who you let into this house. Some girls will do absolutely anything for a quick buck."

What the fuck.

He doesn't say the actual word out loud, but the implication hangs in the air like a foul smell. He’s basically calling me a whore right in front of his entire family.

"Cole!" Mr. Vance snaps, slamming his hand on the table. "That is enough. Watch your mouth at this table."

Cole just shrugs, leaning back, totally smug. But the damage is done.

Beside me, Asher has checked out. The tension radiating off him is suffocating. Finally, he pushes his chair back.

"Excuse me."

He walks straight out of the dining room.

The table goes a bit quiet, and I realize I’m sitting here alone with three people who want to murder me. Yeah, nope.

"Uh, excuse me too," I say, quickly standing up. "I'm gonna go check on my... big, strong bear."

I hustle out of the dining room before anyone can stop me. The hallway is massive, and I honestly have no idea where he went. I start walking down a long, winding corridor, completely lost in this giant castle. I’m about to turn a corner when a hand shoots out from the shadows.

A grip locks onto my arm, yanking me backward. Before I can even gasp, I'm pushed up against the wall, trapped.

Asher is looming over me with his eyes drilling into mine.

"You're getting knee-deep in this, Cardi," he warns. "Marriage? What the hell is wrong with you?"

"I didn't suggest it. Your mother did. Besides, I was trying to help!" I squeak. My heart's doing triple-time, and it definitely isn't from fear. Up close, he smells ridiculously good—like expensive cologne and pure trouble. "Your stepmom was totally baiting your mom. I couldn't just let them win."

"I don't need your help," he snaps, leaning in a fraction closer. His gaze drops to my lips for a split second—or maybe I'm just imagining it—but the proximity is killing me. "And I definitely don't need you making promises we can't keep. Do you have any idea what my mother is going to do with that? She's probably looking up caterers right now."

"Then tell her we broke up tomorrow!" I huff, putting my hands on his chest to push him back a little, but it's like pushing a brick wall.

My heart is thumping so hard I could faint.

"You paid me three grand to be a distraction. I distracted them."

"You're a menace," he says with his face like he's trying to figure out a riddle. "A chaotic menace."

Menaces are supposed to be chaotic, but okay.

"Hey, you're the one who picked me up. Remember? You could have just run me over."

“Is everything alright?”

Cole. That's Cole's voice.

Asher pulls away. I see him shut his eyes a bit before turning back.

“You need something?”

"No, I'm just curious," Cole says, his smirk getting wider as he looks between the two of us. "You guys are already fighting out here? For a supposedly strong relationship that's ripe for marriage, that's pretty strange."

He steps a little closer, his eyes sliding down my body again with that same nasty look from the dinner table. "But hey, I get it. When you buy something cheap, you can't really expect it to last. Right, April? Just let me know when he's done with you; maybe I can find a use for you too."

My jaw drops. The sheer nerve of this guy is unbelievable.

“Are you fucking insane—”

Beside me, Asher chuckles, cutting me off.

Then, out of nowhere, Asher’s arm blurs.

BAM!

I see a rock-solid fist connect right with Cole's jaw. The sound of the punch echoing through the hallway is sickening.

Cole flies backward, his legs tangling up as he crashes hard onto the floor, clutching his bleeding face.

Asher stands over him, totally calm, shaking out his knuckles like he just swatted a fly. He looks down at his brother with venom in his eyes.

"That's for calling her a whore."

Chapter 6
APRIL

I’m pretty sure my jaw is somewhere down on the floor.

Before I know it, footsteps echo down the hallway.

"What in the hell was that?"

Jace strolls around the corner first, hands shoved lazily into his pockets. He chuckle when he sees Cole.

"Damn, didn't know the house tour came with live entertainment."

"What happened?! I heard a crash!"

Stepmom’s voice pierces through the air like a siren. She hustles down the hall, Asher’s mom and Blondie trailing right behind her.

"Oh my God! Cole!" Chloe shrieks, dropping to her knees beside him. "Babe! What happened to your face?"

"Cole! Sweetie!" Stepmom gasps, clutching her pearls so hard I think the string might snap. She whips her head toward Asher. "Asher, did you do this?!"

"Do what?" Asher’s voice is smoother than butter, completely unbothered.

Asher’s mom pushes her way to the front, looking between her two sons. She doesn't even look upset—if anything, there's a subtle glint of pride in her eyes, though she tries to mask it with fake concern. "What is the meaning of this commotion, Asher?"

"Good thing Dad went to take a call," Jace chimes in. “Old man would’ve had a stroke seeing his golden boy tasting the floorboards."

“Shut up,” Chloe spits.

"He is bleeding! Look at his nose! Asher, explain yourself right now!"

Cole lets out a muffled groan from the floor, trying to push himself up with Chloe's help. "He... he fucking—"

"He tripped," Asher cuts in smoothly.

"He tripped?" the stepmother echoes, her voice hitting an octave only dogs can hear. "His whole jaw is swelling up!"

"Yeah. Tragic, really," Asher says flatly.

Without breaking eye contact with his stepmother, Asher grabs Cole by the collar and yanks him straight off the floor.

Cole winces, clutching his bloody nose.

Asher doesn't even flinch. He leans in and casually pats Cole’s shoulder three times.

"Good boy. Watch your step next time, hmm?"

Cole freezes, but before he can choke out a response, Jace wheezes with laughter.

"Watch his step," he snorts. "Classic. Invite me to dinner more often."

"This is insane!" Stepmom snatches Cole away like a bruised toddler. "He assaulted him!"

"He said he tripped, Sandra," Asher’s mom cuts in, a little too aggressively. "Maybe your son should spend less time running his mouth and more time watching his feet."

"You—"

"Anyway," Asher’s mom turns to us, beaming wildly. "Since Cole can't talk venues tonight, April dear... we start wedding planning first thing tomorrow morning."

My stomach drops through the floor. Oh, God. She's already looking up caterers, as Asher said.

Asher grabs my wrist and tugs me past the madness. "Come on, Cardi. We're out."

Behind us, Jace calls out over the shouting, "Hey, April! Tell your roommate I said hi!"

I grimace, clinging to Asher's arm as we hit the cool night air. The bag is secured, my ex is bleeding, but at what cost?

A fake wedding with a ticking time bomb.

*******

In the car, there’s this much-needed silence after all that madness. But after a few minutes, the quiet starts driving me nuts. I shift in my seat and throw him a casual look.

"So, um... come to think of it, is it your driver's day off or something? Because you driving yourself is definitely not the first impression I had of you. I figured a guy like you had a guy for that."

"Shut up," Asher says flatly, not even bothering to look at me.

Ouch.

The quick shutdown stings, and the hurt instantly turns into irritation. I cross my arms and roll my eyes.

"Right. My bad," I scoff, leaning back. "I thought since you stood up for me back there, you were actually starting to be nice. But nah. Cole calling me a whore just bruised your precious ego."

Asher’s jaw clenches hard.

"He was your ex, wasn't he?"

I freeze. "I—how did you...?"

"You think I'm blind?" he cuts in, swerving into the fast lane. "The tension was obvious the second you walked in. You think I don't know how he operates? What he does to every woman he calls a toy or a slut?"

I open my mouth to fire back, but the words die in my throat.

Damn.

He's right, and it hits like a splash of ice water. A gross memory flashes in my head—all those late nights where Cole demanded wild, degrading stuff.

How he’d force me to kneel on the floor to pull his boots off the second he walked in, making me beg just to get a basic text back, or how he'd record videos of us in bed "for his eyes only" and threaten to leak them to his frat boys whenever I tried to call him out on his shit.

He made me feel like an insecure dog dancing for scraps, framing it like some passionate test of loyalty. And the worst part? I went along with it, begging for his approval and convincing myself it was "love."

How I've been so stupid.

I was never special to Cole. I was just another project he broke down for fun. And Asher just made me realize just how badly I messed up.

"Stupid. Stupid, naive bitch," I whisper under my breath, smacking myself in the face.

"What the hell are you doing?" Asher snaps.

I violently shake my head, blinking fast to force back the tears burning behind my eyes.

No stranger had ever treated me like absolute shit before. Cole was the first outsider who made me realize that all the "character development" and tough-girl growth I thought I had after everything with my mom... was just pure child's play. I thought I was strong. I thought I was untouchable. But I had let a snake tear me down to nothing and call it affection.

“Hey... are you even listening?"

"I'm fine," I choke out…

“I said let's break…“ He sighs. “Never mind.“

“What were you saying—”

"Forget it," Asher mutters, slapping his forehead. "Shit, I forgot."

He takes a sharp turn onto the main road. "Where am I dropping you off? Give me your address."

My stomach flips. Going back to my apartment to face my roommate right now? No way.

"Can I... stay over at your place tonight?" I ask, my voice small. "I can't deal with my roommate right now."

He frowns, starting to grumble. "What? No—"

"Please," I beg. "Just for tonight. I promise I'll be gone before you wake up."

Asher opens his mouth to say no, but then he actually looks at my face—the tear-streaked eyes and my red cheek.

"Fine," he grunts. "One night. I don't want to see you when I wake up."

"Thank you," I whisper.

Twenty minutes later, we’re inside his high-rise penthouse.

"If you need anything, call Margaret," he says, tossing his keys on the counter.

"Thanks."

I head into the bathroom and shut the door to wash off the night. I step up to the mirror, pulling out my phone to set an alarm so I can leave as early as possible to face my asshole boss. But then my heart stops at the notification from an unknown number.

"Hi April, how have you been? I know you blocked me, but blocking me can't get rid of me. Come home quick, I'm here waiting with your roommate."

My blood turns to ice.

bodyText:
I run an Airbnb — a big old farmhouse in the hills that families book for the summer. Last month a guest sent me a message that made me sit down on the kitchen floor.

Not a complaint. Not a question about the lockbox. Not a request for a late checkout.

A photo. And five words I haven't been able to stop reading.

Let me start at the beginning, because this goes somewhere I never saw coming.

My husband Mick and I have run the place for 6 years. Two bedrooms, a woodstove, a garden that's mostly nettles, and a river at the bottom of the hill.

Families, mostly. Big ones, small ones, three generations at Christmas. Wellies by the door and somebody's socks drying on the stove.

For the first few years the reviews said the same three things. "Incredible location." "So clean." "The woodstove was perfect."

Then about a year ago the reviews started saying something else.

Guests started asking about the block.

Not the woodstove. Not the view. Not the coffee.

The little wooden block on the kitchen counter.

I should explain, and I should explain why it's there at all, because it isn't decoration.

It's a small wooden block. About the size of a bar of soap, covered in tiny holds and edges, like somebody shrank a climbing wall down to fit in your palm.

There's a handwritten card next to it. It says: "Hardest one is the yellow. Nobody's done it."

I put it there because of my son. I'll come back to that, because it's the part I find hardest to say.

I put it out for the adults, honestly. I did not expect what happened.

The children never put it down.

"Genuine question — what is the wooden thing on your counter and where do I buy four of them. My two did not look at a screen for an entire afternoon and I want to understand what happened."

"My son spent the week obsessed with a block of wood the size of a soap bar. He has asked about it every day since we got home."

"Had to physically remove the little block from my daughter's hand at checkout. Sorry about the shouting."

I started to notice which children in particular.

It wasn't the sporty ones especially. It was any of them. It was all of them. Under about 12, if that block is on the table, it is in a child's hand within an hour, and there is usually a row about whose turn it is.

I mentioned this to Mick, expecting him to find it funny.

He didn't. He teaches children at the climbing wall in town — has done for 22 years, something like four thousand kids — and he said something that changed the way I've looked at every family who's come through here since.

He said: they're starving for it.

Then last summer, a family checked in that I still can't stop thinking about.

Hannah and Tom, both in their forties. Two children — Ollie, 9, and Rosie, 6.

Nice family. Tired, the way families are on the first night of a holiday.

Ollie was the one I noticed, though it took me a day to work out why.

He was bright as anything. Told me the entire plot of a film. Knew more about sharks than I know about anything.

And he didn't use his hands.

I don't mean he couldn't. I mean he'd stopped offering them. When something needed doing — a packet, a zip, a bottle — he'd hold it out and wait, and somebody would take it off him, and everybody would carry on talking.

It's such a small thing. I wouldn't have registered it at all except for the apple.

Second morning, I put a bowl of apples out. Ollie picked one up, turned it over a couple of times, and asked his mum to cut it up.

Hannah said, "just eat it, love."

And he genuinely didn't know how. He had a go, from the side, like you'd bite a sandwich, and gave up and put it back.

Nine years old. He'd never eaten an apple that hadn't already been in slices.

Nobody made anything of it. Tom laughed, Hannah laughed, I laughed, and it was gone in about four seconds.

Day three it rained.

And Rosie — the 6-year-old — found the block.

She didn't put it down for two hours. Then Ollie wanted it. Then there was a row, a real one, the kind where a parent has to physically separate two children and confiscate the object.

Hannah apologised about six times. I told her the truth, which is that it happens most weeks, and that I'd started to find it interesting rather than annoying.

Because here's what I'd noticed by then, over about a year of watching other people's children in my kitchen.

They don't fight over the tablet. There's no fight, because there's nothing to win.

They fight over the block.

By Thursday they'd worked out a system involving a kitchen timer, which was entirely their idea, and which I want on the record was more negotiation than I've managed with my own family in twenty years.

And Ollie — the boy who didn't offer his hands — sat at that table on and off for four days.

Not because anybody asked him to. Because his little sister could do the blue route and he couldn't, and that was intolerable.

They checked out on the Saturday. Hannah left the place spotless. Beds stripped, dishes done, a thank-you note on the counter.

But when I went to flip the house, something was wrong.

The block was gone.

Not the card. Not the coasters. The little wooden block that lives on the kitchen counter. Gone.

I checked every drawer, every shelf, the recycling, the bin. Nothing.

We have a disclosed camera in the common room. Standard security, guests know about it.

I pulled the footage.

6:50 that morning. Hannah comes down before anyone's up. Crosses to the counter. Picks up the block. Stands there for a moment with it in both hands. Puts it in her bag.

Not the children. Hannah.

My first reaction was annoyance, honestly. The next guests were arriving at two and now I'd have to drive home for the spare.

That lasted about ten seconds.

Because I thought about a nine-year-old boy holding an apple he didn't know how to eat, and then about the same boy at that table for four days, losing to his sister and refusing to stop.

That's not theft. Not really.

That's a mother who saw something work and could not risk it not being there on Monday.

So I texted her. "Hi Hannah — hope you all got home safely. The block's missing from the counter. Everything okay?"

An hour later my phone rang. She was crying before I said hello.

"I'm so sorry," she said. "I'll pay for it. I'll pay you whatever you want. I just — I panicked."

Then it all came out.

"In October I sat in a little plastic chair at a parents' evening," she said, "and his teacher told me Ollie is the only child in his class who still can't tie his shoes."

"She was lovely about it. She wasn't telling me off. She said it in about eleven seconds and then she moved on to the next parent because there were nineteen of them waiting."

"And I've thought about it every single day since October and I have never said it out loud to anybody. Not to Tom. Not to my mum."

I sat down on the edge of the bed.

"Because what do you do?" she said. "He's happy. He's clever. He reads above his age. There's nothing wrong with him. You can't take a child to the doctor because he can't tie his shoes."

"And I've bought the velcro trainers, and I cut up his fruit, and I open his yoghurts in the morning because we've got eleven minutes to get out of the door — and I have started to wonder whether I did this."

Then she said the thing that I've thought about every day since.

"I watched him at your kitchen table using his hands for four days. Four days. And on the Friday he did the blue one, and he stood up on the chair and shouted."

"And I thought — that's the first time in about two years I've seen him want to be good at something he can't already do."

"And then I thought about Monday. Getting home. That thing not being on the table."

She was crying properly by then.

"I know it's a piece of wood. I know how ridiculous this is."

I was crying too.

Sitting on the edge of a bed in my own house, listening to a woman apologise for something I would have done.

Because two years ago, I was Hannah. That's the bit about my son, and I'll get to it.

First I want to tell you what Mick said, because it's the reason any of this is on my counter at all.

Twenty-two years of teaching children. I asked him once whether kids had changed. I expected the usual — no attention span, glued to phones, the standard grumble.

He said: they can't hold on.

He said it's not strength. It's not that they're weak, exactly. It's that their hands don't know what to do. They put a hand on something and it just sits there, flat, like a starfish. He has to teach nine-year-olds things he used to teach four-year-olds.

He said the change has been so gradual he can only see it by looking back a decade at a time.

So one night, after Hannah's phone call, I sat at the kitchen table at 1 in the morning and started reading. Properly reading, not scrolling.

I did not expect what I found, and I want to be careful how I lay it out, because a lot of what's written about children and screens is overheated and I don't want to add to it.

So let me stick to the parts that are hard to argue with.

There's a study out of Essex that measured ten-year-olds in 1998 and then measured ten-year-olds again ten years later.

Same age. Same county. Ten years apart.

Arm strength had fallen by 26%. Grip strength by 7%.

And this is the bit I read four times: in 1998, one child in 20 couldn't hold their own body weight hanging from wall bars.

Ten years later it was one in 10.

Double, in a decade.

The papers that covered it ran a headline I've thought about ever since. Children are getting weaker, they said, because they don't climb trees any more.

Then I read the occupational therapists, who are the people who actually get sent the children when something's wrong.

The head paediatric OT at an NHS trust in England put it about as plainly as it can be put. Children are arriving at school and being handed a pencil, and they can't hold it, because they haven't got the underlying skills yet. And she was explicit about why — it is easier to hand a child a tablet than to set up the kind of play that builds hands.

A survey of teachers found 77% saying children are having more difficulty than they used to with pencils, pens and scissors.

And then I found the thing that actually frightened me, which has nothing to do with primary school at all.

There's a professor of surgery in London who trains surgeons. He has been saying for years that the students arriving at his medical school — top of their year, straight A's, the brightest children in the country — increasingly cannot sew.

They haven't got the hands for it. And his point wasn't that they're lazy. His point was that he can no longer assume that a young adult has spent a childhood doing things with their hands.

That's the bill. It doesn't arrive at 9. It arrives at 25, in a room where somebody's supposed to be learning to stitch a person back together.

And then I sat there and worked out what had actually happened, and it isn't screens, or at least it isn't only screens. It's much less dramatic than that, and I think that's why nobody notices it.

A child's hand isn't given to them. It gets built.

And for the whole of human history it got built by accident — by a thousand tiny jobs a day that nobody ever called training.

Laces. Buttons. Zips. Peeling an orange. Opening a packet that didn't want to open. Scissors. Tin openers. Getting a jar lid off. Doing up a coat with cold fingers. Climbing a tree, a fence, a wall, a drainpipe.

Nobody scheduled any of it. Nobody called it anything. It was just what a day contained.

Now go through that list.

Velcro instead of laces. Elastic laces instead of laces. Fruit that arrives in slices. Pouches instead of packets. Bottles with sports caps. Screw tops that a toddler can open. Everything cut up, opened, unwrapped and handed over — often by me, at seven in the morning, because we have eleven minutes to get out of the door.

Not one of those decisions is wrong. I made every single one of them. They're all sensible. They all save a small amount of time on a difficult morning.

But nobody was keeping score, and together they cancelled the entire apprenticeship.

And nothing replaced it. That's the whole thing. Nothing replaced it, because nobody ever knew it was a curriculum in the first place.

I want to be fair about this, because parents get enough. This is not a story about lazy parents. The shops genuinely don't sell laced shoes in small sizes any more — I went looking. Schools have quietly cut back on scissors and craft because the timetable went to academics and screens. It isn't one villain. It's a thousand reasonable decisions, all pointing the same way.

Then there's the last part, and it's the reason I bothered writing any of this down.

Hands are built on a clock.

The research calls the years from about 6 to 12 a golden age for motor learning — a window where the nervous system is laying this down fast and takes to it easily.

It doesn't slam shut. Adults learn things. But it never again costs as little as it costs at 8.

So a child who spends that window not using their hands isn't behind. They're building a different pair of hands, and they'll have those hands for sixty years.

Then I understood why everything I'd have suggested to Hannah was useless.

Screen time limits — I've watched a hundred families try. It's a war you have to win again every single evening, and it puts you against your own child. And it doesn't put anything into his hands, it just takes something out.

LEGO, blocks, play-doh — all completely right, and all of it now sits in a box, because a nine-year-old thinks play-doh is for babies and there's something better in the next room.

The handwriting packets, the exercises off the internet — correct, and refused. Even the occupational therapists have this problem. There's a whole thread of them somewhere asking each other for hand exercises that don't feel childish, because their own patients won't do the childish ones.

And "just make him do it" is the same war as the screens, every night, forever.

Which brings you to the actual problem, and once you see it you can't unsee it.

The most-asked question I found from parents, over and over, was not "how do I limit screens."

It was: what will my child pick up instead?

That's the whole thing. That's the only question. Hand-work only counts if the child chooses it, because anything you have to enforce, you have to enforce forever, and you will lose one Tuesday when you're tired.

So it has to beat the tablet on the tablet's own terms. It has to be a thing a child wants to win.

The thing on my counter is called the Boulder Block.

A tiny company makes them out of solid wood — real climbing holds you reposition into 32 different routes, made by hand. There's a 60-day money-back guarantee.

I'm not going to pretend it's magic, and I'd rather be straight with you than sell you something.

It doesn't teach a child to tie a lace. It won't fix handwriting on its own. Anybody who tells you a wooden toy will do that is lying to you.

What it does is one thing, and the one thing happens to be the thing that went missing.

It gives a child's hands something difficult and interesting to do, in thirty-two increasing steps, for as long as they want — and children want to. That's it. That's the entire pitch.

And the reason it works where the play-doh didn't is embarrassingly simple. There's a hardest route on it that they can't do yet. So it's a game with a top, and there's a sibling who might get there first.

Mick says it's the same reason the wall works on kids that nothing else works on. It isn't exercise. It's a problem with a summit, at a size a child can hold.

Now — the part I promised, about my son.

Two years ago I was Hannah, and my version was worse, because I had less excuse.

Sam is 12. My husband spends his evenings teaching other people's children to use their hands, and I still managed to raise a boy whose hands didn't get much to do, because I am the one who opens things. I'm quick and he's slow and the bus comes at eight.

I noticed the same way Hannah did — someone else said it, kindly, in passing, and I carried it around for months.

We didn't do anything dramatic about it. I put the block on the table where he eats his cereal and I stopped opening things.

That's genuinely all.

The first fortnight, he ignored it. Then he could do four routes and I couldn't, which was the day it became interesting to him.

By about two months in, the thing I noticed wasn't his hands. It was that he'd started having a go at things before handing them to me. The jar first, then me. Which had been the other way round his whole life.

His hands did change, over months, not days — I'd be lying if I said otherwise. But that wasn't the bit that got me.

The bit that got me is that he stopped waiting for somebody else's hands.

So that's why there's a block on the counter of a holiday cottage, which is a strange thing for a holiday cottage to have.

And those reviews I mentioned at the start? Now you know why they don't sound like reviews about a woodstove.

Here's what I told Hannah on the phone that day.

"Keep it. But let me send you a link, because you've got two children and one block, and you already know how that ends."

She laughed, which was a relief. "We had to use a timer."

I sent her the link that afternoon. She ordered three — one for Ollie, one for Rosie, and one she said was "for the car," which I think we both knew meant it was for her.

Last month — about nine months after they left — she sent me a photo.

It's Ollie's school book, open, one page of his handwriting.

I don't know what it looked like in October. I never saw it. She just wanted somebody to see this one.

Five words underneath it.

"His teacher asked what changed."

That's the message that made me sit down on the kitchen floor.

Not the theft. Not the confession. A page of a nine-year-old's handwriting, sent by a woman who spent nine months carrying a sentence from a plastic chair at a parents' evening and never told anybody.

I printed it. It's on the fridge next to the thank-you note she left on the counter.

If you're reading this, I think I know exactly where you are.

Your child is fine.

That's the honest truth of it. Bright, funny, doing well, no problems anybody's named.

And somewhere at the back of your head is a small collection of things you've noticed and never said out loud. The apple. The packet handed to you across the table. The shoes you bought in velcro without really deciding to.

You're not going to take a child to a doctor for that. There's nothing to take them for.

One path: carry on. Everything is reasonable, nothing is urgent, and it costs you nothing this week or next. The window is quiet on the way past, and one day you'll have a young adult whose hands were never taught, and neither of you will connect it to anything.

Another path: put something on the table that is hard, and interesting, and has a top — and let them fight over it.

That's all this is. It's not therapy and it isn't school. It's the apprenticeship that used to be free, in a lump of wood, because the world stopped handing it out.

And here's the part that matters most to me.

Ollie is 9. Rosie is 6.

Whatever their hands are going to be, they're being built right now, this year, while everybody's busy.

They'll never know it happened. That's rather the point.

— Bea

bodyText:
The moment I finally walked away from my husband and son, they completely lost it.
They came home to find my room emptied out — every single family photo slashed to pieces, and nothing left behind except the belongings I had originally brought into the marriage.
They assumed I was just overreacting and would eventually come crawling back with an apology.
Instead, divorce papers were delivered straight to their doorstep.
My ex-husband immediately started blowing up my phone, furious at how heartless I was being.
My son chimed in impatiently, saying I was too jealous and that Aunt Katherine felt more like his real mother than I ever did.
I shot back coldly: “When you were all busy taking care of Katherine during her recovery, did it ever occur to you that your real wife and mother was lying alone in the hospital battling gastric cancer? Just focus on looking after your precious Katherine.”
Dead silence followed. I hung up and blocked him right away.
They tried desperately to track me down, but I had already settled into my new penthouse.
With trembling fingers, I dialed a number I had sworn never to call again.
“Brother,” I sobbed, “take me home. I only have three months to live.”
The white lights located on the ceiling in the hospital hallway buzzed silently overhead as I sat in the uncomfortable plastic chai tensed as I clutched my phone tightly in my trembling hands. I had been waiting for nearly forty minutes at this point for my doctor, Dr. Reynolds to call me back with my test results, and the knots in my stomach had tightened with each passing minute as I anticipated the worst.

I couldn't wait any longer. I needed to hear my son's voice.

My fingers moved almost automatically tapping the first number that popped up in my speed dial, which happened to be my husband Logan's, line. I pressed the dial button and watched as the phone rang once, twice, three times before he finally answered.

"Logan, where did you take Nick?" I asked, trying to keep my voice steady even as another wave of nausea rolled through me and I forced myself not to throw up on the floor. 

"I'm not feeling well. Can you please bring him home? I haven't seen him in three days."

There was a pause on the other end, followed by muffled sounds in the background, it sounded like laughter, maybe? Children screaming with delight in the background.

"Sorry, not tonight," Logan said flatly, his voice carrying that detached tone it had held for the past two months whenever he was addressing me.

My heart sank at his words. "Why not?"

He didn't give an answer. I pulled my phone from my ears and saw that the call was still ongoing so I repeated.

"Logan, I asked you a question. Why can't you bring our son home?"

More silence. I could hear the sounds more clearly now, it sounded like carnival music, and I could also hear the distant roar of a roller coaster. My chest tightened at this.

"Are you with Katherine?" The name tasted bitter on my tongue.

"That's none of your business, Sedona."

The line went dead.

I stared at my phone, my hands shaking so badly I nearly dropped it. None of my business? Our son was with them, and it was none of my business?

Before I could process what had just happened, my phone chimed with a new message. My blood ran cold when I saw Katherine's name on the screen.

I shouldn't have opened it. I knew I shouldn't have, Katherine had sworn to be a thorn in my life, a very painful thorn, but I was a masochist and couldn't stop myself as my fingers moved of their own accord, tapping the notification.

The photo loaded slowly, each picture a fresh stab to my heart. There they were—Logan, Katherine, and Nick—standing in front of Cinderella's Castle at Disneyland. 

Logan had his arm around Katherine's waist. Katherine was holding Nick's hand, her perfect smile glowing under the sun. And my baby, nIck was beaming at her with pure adoration, that I hadn't seen in months.

They looked like a family. A complete, happy family.

And I was the outsider.

Shame and fury was fighting for dominance inside me as I pulled up Katherine's number with shaking fingers. She answered on the first ring, as if she'd been waiting for my call.

"Katherine," I said, my teeth gritted with pain as I spat. "I don't care what game you're playing with Logan, but Nick is my son. You can have Logan if that's what you want, but you will never, ever take my child from me."

"Really?" Her voice was light, amused, like I'd just told her a particularly entertaining joke to her. "Why don't you ask Nick about that?"

"What are you—"

"Nick, sweetie, your mother's on the phone. Do you want to talk to her?"

My heart leaped. Yes. Yes, I needed to hear his voice, needed him to tell me that he missed me, that he wanted to come home.

"Mom?" Nick's voice came through, but it wasn't the sweet tone I'd been hoping for. It was annoyed, exasperated. "What do you want?"

"Nick, sweetheart, I—"

"We're having fun. Stop bothering us. You're so annoying."

The line went dead.

I sat there, frozen, the phone pressed against my ear even though there was nothing but silence on the other end. My six-year-old son had just called me annoying. He'd told me to stop bothering them. As if I was a stranger interrupting them and not his mum.

"Mrs. Hayes?"

I looked up to find Dr. Reynolds standing in front of me, a manila folder clutched in his hands. His expression was grave, the kind of look that Immediately told me that he planned on delivering bad news.

"Let's talk in my office," he said gently.

I followed him, on autopilot, my mind still reeling from Nick told me. The office was bigger than I expected, although it had been on autopilot, cramped with medical books and framed diplomas. I sank into the chair across from his desk, waiting for the bad news to drop.

Dr. Reynolds sat down and opened the folder, studying the papers inside for a long moment before looking up at me.

"Sedona, I'm not going to sugarcoat this. Your test results show significant abnormalities. Combined with your symptoms—the persistent pain, the nausea, the weight loss—we ran additional scans."

He paused, for a moment before he continued speaking.

"You have gastric cancer. Stage three. It's already spread to the lymph nodes."

The words didn't make sense at first. They were just sounds, syllables strung together. Cancer. Stage three. Spread.

"What does that mean?" I heard myself ask, my voice sounding distant, like it belonged to someone else.

Dr. Reynolds's expression softened with sympathy. "With aggressive treatment—chemotherapy, possibly surgery—we might be able to extend your life expectancy. But I need to be honest with you. Without treatment, you're looking at three months, maybe four at most. With treatment, perhaps a year, maybe more if you respond well."

Three months. Ninety days.

I thought of Nick's face in that photo, smiling up at Katherine. I thought of Logan's arm around her waist. I thought of my son calling me annoying, telling me to stop bothering them.

"Mrs. Hayes? Sedona? Do you have someone you can call? You shouldn't be alone right now."

I shook my head slowly. Who would I call? My husband who wouldn't answer? My son who found me annoying? I'd cut ties with my family years ago when I ran from that arranged marriage, too proud and too in love to ever go back.

"I'm fine," I whispered, though I was anything but.

Dr. Reynolds scheduled a follow-up appointment, handed me pamphlets about treatment options and support groups, said something about hope and fighting spirit. I nodded mechanically, taking the papers he pressed into my hands.

I walked out of that hospital in a daze, clutching my death sentence in a manila folder. The summer sun was too bright, the Chicago streets too loud. Everything still felt like a dream, and I was watching it happen to someone else.

My phone buzzed with another message. Another photo from Katherine. This time, the picture was of Nick asleep in a hotel bed, Logan sitting beside him, his hand gently stroking our son's hair.

I stood on the sidewalk, people rushing past me in their busy lives, and I felt something inside me finally break.

I had given up everything for them. My family, my career, my entire identity. And for what? To be a replacement for the woman my husband actually loved? To be an annoyance to my own child?

I had three months to live. And I was going to die unloved, unwanted, and completely alone.

Chapter 2 Nothing But A Replacement 

SEDONA

I don't remember the drive home. It was all a blur for me. One moment I was standing on that busy Chicago sidewalk, and the next I was pulling into our driveway, the manila folder was seated on the passenger seat, silently reminding me of my death's countdown..

Our house—Logan's house, really, I'd never felt like it was truly mine—loomed before me, filled with expensive decorations and wall to ceiling windows. A monument to wealth and status that had never brought me any warmth.

It hadn't always been this cold. Once...a long time ago, this was a place that was filled with joy and laughter. I sat in the car for a long moment, remembering when I'd first arrived in Chicago three years ago. I'd been running from my family's expectations, from the arranged marriage they'd planned with some business partner's son I'd never even met and they expected me to give my entire life up, just like that. I was supposed to be the obedient daughter, the perfect heiress who would smile and say "I do" to secure another corporate merger.

But I'd wanted more than that. I'd wanted love. Real love.

The car accident had happened on my second day in the city. I'd been so focused on staying hidden, , that I hadn't been paying attention to the traffic light. The impact had been shocking but not serious, it was just enough to leave me shaken and slightly injured on the side of the road.

And then Logan had appeared, like a knight in shining armour. He'd helped me up, insisted on taking me to the hospital, stayed with me through the examination. When he'd asked about my family, I'd lied and said I was an orphan. It had seemed safer that way, easier than explaining that I was a runaway heiress hiding from one of Seattle's most prominent families.

Logan had been so kind then. So attentive. We'd fallen into a fast romance, and when he'd proposed after just three months, I'd said yes without hesitation. I thought I'd found my fairy tale, my happily ever after.

I'd been so stupid and naive.

A sharp pain in my abdomen pulled me back to the present, reminding me of what I had. I pressed my hand against my stomach, waiting for it to pass, so I could breathe properly. These pains had been getting worse for months, but I'd dismissed them as stress, as anxiety over the fact that my son and husband were growing distant from me, every passing day.

Now I knew better.

I grabbed the folder and made my way inside, each step feeling heavier than the last. The house was quiet, eerily so. Usually, I'd hear Nick's laughter echoing through the halls, or the sound of TV playing his favourite cartoons.

But Nick wasn't here. He was at Disneyland, probably already forgetting I existed.

"Sedona? Is that you?"

I froze. That voice—filled with disdain—could only belong to one person.

And then there you were—stupid and naive in love and a doppelganger of Katherine.

Chapter 3 Being Replaced
