The table goes a bit quiet, and I realize I’m sitting here alone with three people who want to murder me. Yeah, nope.

"Uh, excuse me too," I say, quickly standing up. "I'm gonna go check on my... big, strong bear."

I hustle out of the dining room before anyone can stop me. The hallway is massive, and I honestly have no idea where he went. I start walking down a long, winding corridor, completely lost in this giant castle. I’m about to turn a corner when a hand shoots out from the shadows.

A grip locks onto my arm, yanking me backward. Before I can even gasp, I'm pushed up against the wall, trapped.

Asher is looming over me with his eyes drilling into mine.

"You're getting knee-deep in this, Cardi," he warns. "Marriage? What the hell is wrong with you?"

"I didn't suggest it. Your mother did. Besides, I was trying to help!" I squeak. My heart's doing triple-time, and it definitely isn't from fear. Up close, he smells ridiculously good—like expensive cologne and pure trouble. "Your stepmom was totally baiting your mom. I couldn't just let them win."

"I don't need your help," he snaps, leaning in a fraction closer. His gaze drops to my lips for a split second—or maybe I'm just imagining it—but the proximity is killing me. "And I definitely don't need you making promises we can't keep. Do you have any idea what my mother is going to do with that? She's probably looking up caterers right now."

"Then tell her we broke up tomorrow!" I huff, putting my hands on his chest to push him back a little, but it's like pushing a brick wall.

My heart is thumping so hard I could faint.

"You paid me three grand to be a distraction. I distracted them."

"You're a menace," he says with his face like he's trying to figure out a riddle. "A chaotic menace."

Menaces are supposed to be chaotic, but okay.

"Hey, you're the one who picked me up. Remember? You could have just run me over."

“Is everything alright?”

Cole. That's Cole's voice.

Asher pulls away. I see him shut his eyes a bit before turning back.

“You need something?”

"No, I'm just curious," Cole says, his smirk getting wider as he looks between the two of us. "You guys are already fighting out here? For a supposedly strong relationship that's ripe for marriage, that's pretty strange."

He steps a little closer, his eyes sliding down my body again with that same nasty look from the dinner table. "But hey, I get it. When you buy something cheap, you can't really expect it to last. Right, April? Just let me know when he's done with you; maybe I can find a use for you too."

My jaw drops. The sheer nerve of this guy is unbelievable.

“Are you fucking insane—”

Beside me, Asher chuckles, cutting me off.

Then, out of nowhere, Asher’s arm blurs.

BAM!

I see a rock-solid fist connect right with Cole's jaw. The sound of the punch echoing through the hallway is sickening.

Cole flies backward, his legs tangling up as he crashes hard onto the floor, clutching his bleeding face.

Asher stands over him, totally calm, shaking out his knuckles like he just swatted a fly. He looks down at his brother with venom in his eyes.

"That's for calling her a whore."

Chapter 6
APRIL

I’m pretty sure my jaw is somewhere down on the floor.

Before I know it, footsteps echo down the hallway.

"What in the hell was that?"

Jace strolls around the corner first, hands shoved lazily into his pockets. He chuckle when he sees Cole.

"Damn, didn't know the house tour came with live entertainment."

"What happened?! I heard a crash!"

Stepmom’s voice pierces through the air like a siren. She hustles down the hall, Asher’s mom and Blondie trailing right behind her.

"Oh my God! Cole!" Chloe shrieks, dropping to her knees beside him. "Babe! What happened to your face?"

"Cole! Sweetie!" Stepmom gasps, clutching her pearls so hard I think the string might snap. She whips her head toward Asher. "Asher, did you do this?!"

"Do what?" Asher’s voice is smoother than butter, completely unbothered.

Asher’s mom pushes her way to the front, looking between her two sons. She doesn't even look upset—if anything, there's a subtle glint of pride in her eyes, though she tries to mask it with fake concern. "What is the meaning of this commotion, Asher?"

"Good thing Dad went to take a call," Jace chimes in. “Old man would’ve had a stroke seeing his golden boy tasting the floorboards."

“Shut up,” Chloe spits.

"He is bleeding! Look at his nose! Asher, explain yourself right now!"

Cole lets out a muffled groan from the floor, trying to push himself up with Chloe's help. "He... he fucking—"

"He tripped," Asher cuts in smoothly.

"He tripped?" the stepmother echoes, her voice hitting an octave only dogs can hear. "His whole jaw is swelling up!"

"Yeah. Tragic, really," Asher says flatly.

Without breaking eye contact with his stepmother, Asher grabs Cole by the collar and yanks him straight off the floor.

Cole winces, clutching his bloody nose.

Asher doesn't even flinch. He leans in and casually pats Cole’s shoulder three times.

"Good boy. Watch your step next time, hmm?"

Cole freezes, but before he can choke out a response, Jace wheezes with laughter.

"Watch his step," he snorts. "Classic. Invite me to dinner more often."

"This is insane!" Stepmom snatches Cole away like a bruised toddler. "He assaulted him!"

"He said he tripped, Sandra," Asher’s mom cuts in, a little too aggressively. "Maybe your son should spend less time running his mouth and more time watching his feet."

"You—"

"Anyway," Asher’s mom turns to us, beaming wildly. "Since Cole can't talk venues tonight, April dear... we start wedding planning first thing tomorrow morning."

My stomach drops through the floor. Oh, God. She's already looking up caterers, as Asher said.

Asher grabs my wrist and tugs me past the madness. "Come on, Cardi. We're out."

Behind us, Jace calls out over the shouting, "Hey, April! Tell your roommate I said hi!"

I grimace, clinging to Asher's arm as we hit the cool night air. The bag is secured, my ex is bleeding, but at what cost?

A fake wedding with a ticking time bomb.

*******

In the car, there’s this much-needed silence after all that madness. But after a few minutes, the quiet starts driving me nuts. I shift in my seat and throw him a casual look.

"So, um... come to think of it, is it your driver's day off or something? Because you driving yourself is definitely not the first impression I had of you. I figured a guy like you had a guy for that."

"Shut up," Asher says flatly, not even bothering to look at me.

Ouch.

The quick shutdown stings, and the hurt instantly turns into irritation. I cross my arms and roll my eyes.

"Right. My bad," I scoff, leaning back. "I thought since you stood up for me back there, you were actually starting to be nice. But nah. Cole calling me a whore just bruised your precious ego."

Asher’s jaw clenches hard.

"He was your ex, wasn't he?"

I freeze. "I—how did you...?"

"You think I'm blind?" he cuts in, swerving into the fast lane. "The tension was obvious the second you walked in. You think I don't know how he operates? What he does to every woman he calls a toy or a slut?"

I open my mouth to fire back, but the words die in my throat.

Damn.

He's right, and it hits like a splash of ice water. A gross memory flashes in my head—all those late nights where Cole demanded wild, degrading stuff.

How he’d force me to kneel on the floor to pull his boots off the second he walked in, making me beg just to get a basic text back, or how he'd record videos of us in bed "for his eyes only" and threaten to leak them to his frat boys whenever I tried to call him out on his shit.

He made me feel like an insecure dog dancing for scraps, framing it like some passionate test of loyalty. And the worst part? I went along with it, begging for his approval and convincing myself it was "love."

How I've been so stupid.

I was never special to Cole. I was just another project he broke down for fun. And Asher just made me realize just how badly I messed up.

"Stupid. Stupid, naive bitch," I whisper under my breath, smacking myself in the face.

"What the hell are you doing?" Asher snaps.

I violently shake my head, blinking fast to force back the tears burning behind my eyes.

No stranger had ever treated me like absolute shit before. Cole was the first outsider who made me realize that all the "character development" and tough-girl growth I thought I had after everything with my mom... was just pure child's play. I thought I was strong. I thought I was untouchable. But I had let a snake tear me down to nothing and call it affection.

“Hey... are you even listening?"

"I'm fine," I choke out…

“I said let's break…“ He sighs. “Never mind.“

“What were you saying—”

"Forget it," Asher mutters, slapping his forehead. "Shit, I forgot."

He takes a sharp turn onto the main road. "Where am I dropping you off? Give me your address."

My stomach flips. Going back to my apartment to face my roommate right now? No way.

"Can I... stay over at your place tonight?" I ask, my voice small. "I can't deal with my roommate right now."

He frowns, starting to grumble. "What? No—"

"Please," I beg. "Just for tonight. I promise I'll be gone before you wake up."

Asher opens his mouth to say no, but then he actually looks at my face—the tear-streaked eyes and my red cheek.

"Fine," he grunts. "One night. I don't want to see you when I wake up."

"Thank you," I whisper.

Twenty minutes later, we’re inside his high-rise penthouse.

"If you need anything, call Margaret," he says, tossing his keys on the counter.

"Thanks."

I head into the bathroom and shut the door to wash off the night. I step up to the mirror, pulling out my phone to set an alarm so I can leave as early as possible to face my asshole boss. But then my heart stops at the notification from an unknown number.

"Hi April, how have you been? I know you blocked me, but blocking me can't get rid of me. Come home quick, I'm here waiting with your roommate."

My blood turns to ice.

bodyText:
At sixteen I turned eighty pounds into a six figure brand from my bedroom. Then I spent nine years forgetting how I did it.
I am Gregory Cooke. I am 27. I live in the UK, and I have spent most of my life building things online, which sounds glamorous until you see the receipts.
Here are the receipts. I built a Shopify web design agency from 2018 to 2021. Over three thousand clients. Forty two people on the payroll at the peak. It was the first Fiverr account to pass a million dollars in revenue. I sold it at twenty two and moved to Dubai. Then I spent 2022 as a CMO inside eight and nine figure companies, sitting in rooms where the marketing budget for one quarter was larger than everything my agency ever earned.
I have also registered ninety seven domains on GoDaddy for businesses that never worked. That account still exists. Scrolling it is not a pleasant experience.
If you have a business that already earns money and you still cannot buy a stranger's attention at a profit, read the rest of this. It is the only thing I actually know how to fix, and it took me nine years and a lot of expensive detours to notice I had already solved it once, badly, with almost no money, before I could legally drink.
So let me start there, because the eighty pounds matters more than the million.
I was sixteen. I was supposed to be revising. My mum thought I was revising. What I was actually doing was sitting on the floor of my bedroom with a laptop that ran hot enough to leave a mark on the carpet, building an ecommerce store for a product I had found on a supplier site at about two pounds a unit.
The eighty pounds was everything I had. It was birthday money and a bit of cash from helping in a shop. It was not seed capital, it was eighty pounds, and I remember the exact feeling of putting a card number into an ad platform for the first time and understanding that if this did not work by Friday there was no Saturday version of the plan.
I did not have a strategy. I had arithmetic. I could not afford to be clever, because clever costs time and time costs money you have not got. So I did the only thing the arithmetic allowed.
I sold something cheap at the front. Not because cheap is a philosophy, but because at sixteen with eighty pounds I could not pay to introduce myself to anybody. The product had to pay for the click on the same day the click happened. That was the entire constraint and it shaped everything.
Then I added a second thing at the checkout, a small extra item, a couple of pounds, ticked or unticked in a box. I did that because the first thing on its own did not quite cover the ads, and I could see the gap in the numbers, and the box closed the gap.
Then I put a bigger thing after the sale, on the page that said thank you. A bundle. More units, better price. Half the people ignored it. Enough people did not.
That was it. That was the whole business. Cheap thing at the front, small bump at the checkout, bigger offer after the sale. Eighty pounds became a six figure brand inside about a year, run by a dyslexic teenager who was hiding a laptop under a duvet when he heard footsteps on the stairs.
It fell over eventually, and it deserved to. I was sixteen. The supplier changed, the shipping times went stupid, I had inventory I could not sell and a spreadsheet I did not understand, and the whole thing folded the way most first businesses do. I want to be honest about that because the version of this story where the teenager wins forever is a lie and you would smell it.
But here is the part that took me nine years to see. The business failing had nothing at all to do with the structure. The structure was correct. The structure was the most correct thing I have ever built. What failed was everything around it, the stock, the supplier, the sixteen year old.
I threw out the structure with the failure. That is the mistake. That is the whole story.
Because what happened next is that I got good. Properly good. I learned design, then teams, then delivery, then hiring, then sales, and every single one of those skills quietly moved me further away from the arithmetic I had worked out on a bedroom floor.
The agency had three thousand clients and not one of them arrived by accident. Somebody pitched. Somebody replied. Somebody got on a call. Somebody delivered so well that the client told a friend. It was a very successful business and it was also a business with exactly one engine, and the engine was human effort, and the only way to make it bigger was to hire more humans.
Forty two people means forty two people's rent. It means Monday is not yours, it means a designer in one time zone and a developer in another and a client in a third, it means a phone that goes at 6am and again at 11pm, and a permanent hum in your chest that stops only when you are asleep, and not always then.
I got out in 2021. Seven figures, wired, done, twenty two years old, standing in a Dubai apartment I could not have imagined at thirteen.
Six weeks later I was bored and quietly panicking, because the money was a number in an account and I had absolutely no idea how to make another one without building the same heavy thing again.
So I went and worked inside other people's companies instead. Eight figures. Nine figures. Three thousand employees in one of them. And I learned something that genuinely shocked me, which is that most large companies are slower and more fragile than the small agency I had just sold. Bigger is not better. Bigger is just bigger, and it costs more to hold up.
By the time I came home I had a very expensive instinct. Every time something did not work I concluded that I needed a bigger version of it. More people. More offers. Another tool. A second brand. I have a spreadsheet from that period where I costed out hiring a copywriter, a designer, a funnel builder and a media buyer for a single quarter, and the total came to more than most people spend on a car, and the truthful thing to say about it is that it would not have fixed anything, because I would have been paying four talented people to make the same structural mistake faster.
I should tell you that I am dyslexic. Severely. There is a ninety four page educational psychologist report about me from when I was ten that also mentions dyscalculia, dyspraxia and ADD. I spent eighteen months in and out of hospital at twelve with my legs not working properly and nobody able to explain why to my parents. I do not say that for sympathy. I say it because I am not a naturally gifted operator running on horsepower. I am somebody who has to find a model simple enough that I can personally run it or the whole thing collapses. At sixteen that constraint made me build the right thing. At twenty five that constraint was being buried under complexity I had acquired on purpose.
By 2023 the complexity looked like success from the outside. I had an ad campaign running that made over three hundred and fifty thousand dollars a month in profit. That is my result, in my account, and I am not telling you it is normal. I had a free Skool community with two thousand six hundred and ninety two people in it. I had consulting clients who paid properly. I had thirty six thousand students who had been through my free material.
And I still could not do the one thing I actually wanted, which was put a total stranger in front of what I knew and have that transaction pay for itself on the day it happened.
Everything I had was heavy. The community needed me in it. The campaign needed the team who ran it. The consulting needed my calendar. I had swapped an engine made of forty two people for an engine made of three people and me. Better. Same shape.
Then the turn, and it was not a business event.
My son Romeo was born.
I am not going to write the sentimental version, because you have read it a hundred times and it is usually written by somebody selling a course. Here is the unsentimental version.
I was sitting in the corner of a room at a stupid hour holding him, and I did an honest audit of everything I had built, and the answer was that if I stopped for two weeks all of it stopped. The community would go quiet. The campaign would need decisions nobody else could make. The consulting would simply not happen, because the consulting was me.
I had exited a company at twenty two and I had somehow rebuilt myself a job. A well paid one with a good view.
And the thing about a job is that it takes the years while you are busy defending it. Romeo is not going to be four months old again. My dad is not getting younger. There is no version of that time that gets refunded later because the quarter went well. Money you can make again. That, you cannot.
That was the moment. Not the money. The structure.
So I tore it down, on purpose, faster than any sensible person would.
I deleted the Skool community. Two thousand six hundred and ninety two people, gone, by choice. I switched off the campaign making over three hundred and fifty thousand dollars a month in profit. That is my result and I turned it off, which is either brave or stupid depending on the week you ask me. I shut down a YouTube channel that was growing. I let most of the team go and kept three people.
Everybody I told thought I had lost my mind, and several of them said it out loud.
Then I tried to rebuild something simple, and I failed at that for a long while, and this is the part I want to itemise properly, because you have probably tried most of it and I do not want to insult you by pretending these things are stupid. They are not stupid. I ran them all. They all have the same flaw and it took me an embarrassing amount of money to see it.
The live webinar. Weekly, ninety minutes, registration page, reminder emails, the whole apparatus. It converted people who already knew who I was. To a cold stranger it is a request for ninety minutes of their evening before I have earned ninety seconds of their attention, and no amount of slide polishing fixes a bad trade.
The VSL to a booked call. The same problem wearing a better suit. The very first thing I ask a stranger for is a slot in their diary and a conversation about thousands of dollars, on the first click, from somebody who has known I exist for forty seconds. Warm buyers close somewhere in the region of twenty to thirty five percent. Cold traffic closes at five to ten. I was not being outsold. I was asking the wrong people for the wrong thing at the wrong moment.
The lead magnet. I have built more of these than I can count. They build a list of people who have proved exactly one thing, which is that they will trade an email address for a PDF, and then you spend six weeks nurturing that list into permission to sell. Lead generation costs are up about twenty percent year on year, and a free lead is the precise objective that funnel is built on, so it gets structurally worse every quarter rather than better.
Buying leads outright. Forty dollars a lead, nothing coming back on day one, a small single digit percentage of them ever buying anything at all. That is not an acquisition model, it is a charity model. You are funding strangers' education and hoping a few of them tip on the way out.
Setters and closers on the phone. It works. I will not pretend it does not work, because it does. It also means the size of your business is the size of your payroll, and the day you want to double you hire, and now you are back to forty two mortgages, only this time with a dialler.
Posting daily. I did it for years and I was good at it. The problem is not that content does not work. The problem is that content is rent. You pay it every day forever, and on the day you stop paying it the traffic leaves, and there is nothing on the balance sheet at the end. You cannot decide on a Monday that organic reach will double this week. A business needs to be able to decide things.
The tool stack. I counted mine once on a Sunday night, the way you count things you are avoiding. Email platform, page builder, scheduler, webinar software, CRM, video hosting, two AI tools, a form thing, a survey thing and a Zapier account holding half of it together with tape. That week I was not running a business. I was doing unpaid IT with a customer list attached.
Affiliates and referrals. Real, valuable, worth having, and completely outside your control. Referrals arrive when they arrive. You cannot open the tap.
The agency model itself, which I had already done at scale. It is a rental agreement with extra steps, because every client can leave you on thirty days notice, and the better you are the more of your week belongs to whoever is unhappiest.
And a bigger, better course. I taught thousands of people and I am proud of the teaching. But making the course better does not change the moment when a stranger who has never heard of you is asked to care.
Every single one of those things is either a way of getting attention or a way of converting attention with human labour.
Not one of them changed what happens in the ninety seconds after a stranger sees you for the first time.
And I want to name the thing that keeps competent people stuck longer than anything else, because it kept me stuck for years. It is not laziness and it is not fear of hard work. It is that the next obvious step in front of you always earns money today, and the thing that would actually change the structure earns nothing for weeks. So you take the call. You always take the call. And a year goes past made entirely of reasonable decisions.
The discovery, when it came, was humiliating in the way that useful things usually are.
I was in an office in early 2024 trying to explain the problem to somebody, drawing boxes on a whiteboard, and I heard myself describe what I wanted. I said I want somebody who does not know me to be able to buy something today, cheap enough that they do not have to think about it, and I want that transaction to pay for the advert that brought them, so I never have to fund the introduction.
And I stopped, because I had described the bedroom.
Not a strategy from a book. Not something I learned at an eight figure company. My own arithmetic, from when I was sixteen, worked out with eighty pounds and no other options, and then abandoned for nine years because I got successful enough to afford worse ideas.
Cheap thing at the front. Small bump at the checkout. Bigger offer after the sale.
The teenager was right. The teenager was right because he was poor, and being poor meant he could not build anything that required patience, or payroll, or a nurture sequence, or a call. He needed the first transaction to fund the next click, that day, or the business ended on Friday.
Everything I built after that was an attempt to buy my way out of that constraint using labour, and every single one of those attempts eventually needed me inside it.
So I went and looked at my own numbers, honestly, for the first time in a while. The campaign I had switched off had one obvious property. It had a cheap front end and a path underneath it. The things that had not worked all had one obvious property in common too. They asked for something expensive, or something free, first.
Free builds a list of people who like free. Expensive builds a queue you have to staff. Cheap builds a buyer, and a buyer is a completely different species to a lead. Somebody who has handed over card details and received something genuinely good has crossed a line that no amount of email nurture gets a free subscriber across.
That is the whole insight and it is not sophisticated. It is the arithmetic of somebody with eighty pounds who cannot afford to be introduced.
So I rebuilt it deliberately, as an adult, with the things I had learned at scale bolted onto the structure a sixteen year old had worked out on a carpet.
There are four parts and they are physical. You could point at each of them on a screen.
The first part is the front door. A low ticket digital product built out of what you already know. Mine is twenty seven dollars. It is not a teaser and it is not a lead magnet with a price on it. It is a genuinely useful finished thing, priced so that a stranger who has never heard your name can buy it today, without a phone call, without a webinar, without knowing anything about you except that the page in front of them makes sense. Twenty seven dollars is not a decision. It is a reflex.
The second part is the path underneath it, and this is where almost everybody gets it wrong. One product at one price cannot survive paid traffic. It just cannot. Meta CPMs sit around eleven dollars and fifty four cents and they never came back down after the iOS changes. So under my twenty seven dollar product there are two order bumps, ticked at the checkout, and three upsells after the purchase. My average order value across all of it is a hundred and sixty eight dollars and forty two cents. That is my number, in my business, and it is the only reason the maths works. The bump and the upsell are what turn a twenty seven dollar product from a hobby into an acquisition engine.
The third part is the traffic, and the honest bit about traffic is volume. A static ad now fatigues in about eight and a bit days. Roughly six or seven out of every hundred ad variants you make ever become performers. That is not a reason to be discouraged, it is a production instruction. You cannot make four ads a quarter and expect a machine. You need a system that keeps producing them, week after week, so that when the winner dies, and it will die, there is another one behind it. This is where the AI actually lives in what I do. Not as a promise, not as a headline, just as the thing that lets three people produce the volume of creative that used to need a department.
The fourth part is the back end, and this is the part that makes everybody's eyebrows go up. The back end is what you already sell. The consulting, the programme, the service, the retainer, the thing that costs thousands. Those buyers are already inside your world because they paid you twenty seven dollars and you did not waste their money. Last year we closed five hundred and fifty two deals between three thousand and ten thousand dollars with nobody on a phone. No setter, no closer, no discovery call. That is my result, in my business, and I am telling you the mechanism, not promising you the outcome.
The line that makes it click is this. You stop paying to introduce yourself.
I want to give you the honest version of the numbers, including the parts that are not flattering, because I am not going to sit here and imply this is a normal Tuesday.
On the thirty first of March I spent fourteen thousand four hundred and fifteen dollars on ads and did fifty seven thousand four hundred and twenty five dollars in sales, which is just under four times the spend, and about forty three thousand dollars net in one day. That is my result, in my account, on my offer, after a decade of building this kind of thing badly and then well.
Very few people ever have a fifty thousand dollar day. I mean that. Most people who build a front door properly will never see one, and I am not going to stand here and promise you a number, because I do not know your offer, your market, your traffic or your work rate, and anybody who does promise you a number is selling you something they cannot deliver.
Also, in that same month, three hundred and thirty thousand dollars came in and seven hundred and twenty four thousand went out. Cash in a business like this is a wave, not a line, and I would rather you knew that now.
Twenty two thousand sales. A hundred and fifty three refunds. Zero point six percent, which tells me the front door product is not junk, and if yours is junk none of the rest of this saves you.
Now the part I actually wanted, which had nothing to do with the money.
The first fortnight after the front door went live, the change was small and strange. I woke up and there were orders from people I had never spoken to, in countries I have never visited, at three in the morning, while I was asleep in a house with a baby in it. Nothing about my day had been spent on any of them.
By week three I noticed I had stopped checking my phone at breakfast. That sounds trivial. It was not trivial. For nine years my first waking thought had been a status check, because everything I had ever built could go wrong in the night and needed me to catch it.
By week five I took a Tuesday off. Not a holiday, not an announcement, just an ordinary Tuesday with nothing in the calendar, spent on the floor of a living room with a very small person who does not care about ROAS. The campaign kept running. In six weeks we had gone from zero to fifteen thousand dollars a day in ad spend, which is my number and my risk tolerance, and the day that was happening I was mostly thinking about lunch.
By week six something else changed that I only noticed later, looking at the calendar. The nature of the work had inverted. For nine years my working week had been a list of people waiting on me, and the good days were the days I cleared it. Now my working week was a list of things I was testing, and the good days were the days something surprised me. Nobody was waiting on me for anything. I sat down on a Thursday, wrote three new adverts, changed two headlines, and closed the laptop before the school run traffic started, and the business did not notice I had gone.
By week eight the sensation had changed shape completely. Before, growth meant hire, and hire meant interview, onboard, manage, worry, pay. Now growth meant change a number in a box and see what came back. That is a different job. It is a job I can do with dyslexia and a toddler and a normal amount of sleep.
And the quietest one, the one I did not expect. I stopped feeling like I had to be interesting every single day. The content treadmill is a slow tax on your personality. When the front door works, you can go quiet for a week and nothing dies, and you come back with something worth saying instead of something you owed the algorithm.
That is what I actually bought. Not the March number. The Tuesday.
So here is the offer, plainly.
The thing I run now is called Go Midnight AI, and what we do is build that front door for people who already have something worth selling. Not beginners. People with a real offer, a real skill, an agency, a practice or a product that already earns money and has no cheap way in at the front.
We build the low ticket product out of what you already know. We build the funnel, the order bumps, the upsells and the emails underneath it so the arithmetic survives paid traffic. We build the ads at volume and the system that keeps producing them after the first ones fatigue. And we wire it into the expensive thing you already sell, which is where the profit actually lives. It is built for you and handed over live, and you own it.
Two tiers. Gold Partner is twelve thousand five hundred dollars. Diamond Partner is twenty five thousand.
The only guarantee I make is about our work, not about your income. We keep working with you, at no further fee, until you can profitably spend a thousand dollars a day on ads through your low ticket funnel, on the conditions set out in the agreement. I will never guarantee what you earn. I do not know you, and a guarantee about your income from a stranger on the internet is a marketing device, not a promise.
Everything I publish is educational and informational, including this.
If you want to see how the whole thing works before you speak to anyone, the workshop is free and it always will be. It is at gomidnight.ai/masterclass. Courses, workshops and meetups are free here. The only thing that is ever sold is the build.
If you want us to build it, go to gomidnight.ai/apply and book a call. You will speak to Ben. He will tell you honestly if what you already have is strong enough to put a front door on, and if it is not, he will say so.

bodyText:
Nobody on that plane wants to sit next to your baby.
At least, that's what the voice in your head keeps saying.

It's been saying it for weeks.

Every time you picture the flight, it plays the same scene. Wheels up. She starts pulling at her seatbelt. And the screaming starts right as the man in the aisle seat opens his book.

You see him sigh. You see the woman across the aisle turn around.

And you hear exactly what they're thinking: "Great. There goes the vacation."

So you've over-prepared. Snacks for every half hour. A tablet full of downloads. A little speech ready for whoever sits next to you.

And the voice still won't stop: What if she's that baby?

Here's what it doesn't tell you.

The people in those seats aren't judging the crying. Babies cry. They're watching what you do about it.

One traveler without kids put it plainly: when parents are clearly doing everything they can, they don't feel annoyed. They feel sorry for the parent.

So you don't need a perfectly silent baby.
You need something to hand her the second she starts to fuss.

That's why we made the Little Engineer's Busy Board.

A real key to turn. Switches to flick. A cable to plug in and pull out again. Eight real controls, and every one lights something up.

None of them make a sound. No speaker. No beeping. Nothing for the aisle seat to hear.

It's the size of a paperback, so it lives in your bag and fits on her tray table. Everything is tied on, so nothing rolls under the seat in front. Made for little ones 2 and up.

One parent's list of flight essentials put it simply: "toddler busy board a MUST."

Now let the voice play it one more time.

You walk down the aisle. She's on your hip, bent over the board, flicking a switch, watching a light come on. The man with the paperback glances up, sees a busy kid, and goes back to his book.

A busy baby is a quiet baby.

And the voice finally has nothing to say.
